name: Lands of the Nile

neighbours.name: The Pact of 1225
neighbours.summary: When most of the Cordovan sahirs joined the Order of Hermes in 925, one condition was that no covenant be founded in Africa for three centuries. Nobody now agrees why: to hide them from jinn they had betrayed, or to keep the settuten from becoming the Order's enemies. It expires in 1225, and some magi are eager to go.

stages.title: The pact expires
stages.ignored: Magi are free to found covenants in Africa.

neighbours.name: The Nile Valley
neighbours.summary:
The great river parts Africa from Asia, and Egypt, Nubia and, less so, Ethiopia are really the lands along its two banks. Men hold it to be the Gihon, one of the four rivers of Paradise; where it rises nobody knows, and scholars argue over it while expeditions go looking in Ethiopia Orientalis. Only a narrow fertile strip can be lived on, drowned each year from June to September under a rich black silt that comes of the rains in the Abyssinian Highlands. Palm gardens and orchards line the water, with broad fields behind them, then the desert. In much of Egypt and Nubia the river is the only water, and many years bring no rain at all.

Visitors marvel at its plenty: pastures, groves, forests thick with beasts, swamps and reed beds. Yet the place feels endless. One day is much like the last, the length of the day barely changes, crops grow all year, and only the flood marks the turning of the year, chiefly in Lower Egypt. Upper and lower follow the river's flow: Lower Egypt is the Delta in the north, Upper Egypt lies around Qus, Lower Nubia runs from the first cataract to the third, and Upper Nubia south to the Abyssinian Highlands.

Treasure is the land's great belief. Muslim scholars know that Herodotus lists more pharaohs than Scripture allows, and yet the tombs he names are where he says. Sufis and Christian mystics muse on this; most people hold that God filled Egypt with monuments to make men wiser, and that taking from them never lessens them. Every traveller on the Hajj through Egypt does well to see them. Every spot on the Nile is thought to hide a treasure, so firmly that the government licenses a guild of treasure hunters and takes a share, and in droughts has lived for decades on the tax. Where no treasure lies, a faerie may well put one there and help you find it, or help you suffer for failing to.

The West knows little of it. Traders come for gold, spices, ointments, stones and silks, keep fondachi in Alexandria, and ignore the Pope's bans on selling wood and iron to Egypt, but few pass Cairo. The Great King of Makuria forbids foreign trade, so Nubia and Ethiopia are almost unknown in Europe. Egypt is thought a storehouse of old lore, and some in the Order wonder whether the secrets of the first magicians lie in its tombs.

By the reckoning of the learned, the Earth was made 5278 years ago, in 4058 BC by Maimonides, and the Flood came 1656 years later, in 2402 BC. Misr son of Ham son of Noah was Egypt's first king, and his sons founded cities that still bear their names. Joseph was sold there in 1842 BC, and is said locally to have been a great magician, perhaps Imhotep himself. The Exodus followed in 1610 BC, and some say monument building slackened without the Jewish slaves. Pharaohs ruled for at most 2070 years, until Alexander took Egypt in 332 BC; the Ptolemies held it for 302 years, to 30 BC, and the Muslims finished their conquest in 641. Heliopolis, now a suburb of Cairo, is where Herodotus set the phoenix's death and rebirth.
neighbours.secrets:
Themes for sagas (pp. 6-9), none excluding another. The Red and the Black: Africa is the battleground of the Great Hunger and the Hope, and these lands lie in the Black's stronghold. The Kom, a giant who was the Red's chief servant, was slain and seeks to remake itself (at Pakhoras). The Cult of Dedun serves the Red indirectly by gathering power from death and decay, seeking immortality through decrepitude. Wesir, the first human to learn how to become a Daimon, is now a mighty servant of the Black. The old rites of death cleansed favoured ghosts of the Red and raised them as Daimons, allies of the Black. Egypt just grows marvels: the superabundance of tombs is another face of the Black's fertility. Secrets and mysteries: the Red devours secrets, so some mysteries no longer have answers, and others never had any, being plain marvels of God; players must expect that. Endlessness: see above. The Black's servants include the lector priests who were the pharaohs' magicians.

Why the Order might come here (pp. 127-128). The book puts no magi in these lands in 1220. A saga may loot the past with no neighbours and add other covenants later; a crusading or tired covenant may come to escape the Code or a Peripheral Code, until its actions bring magi from the Roman or Levant Tribunals; a covenant may join an existing Tribunal, if Redcaps or that Tribunal's members can reach it in good time and its Peripheral Code allows, or contest a border at Grand Tribunal, where no precedent yet exists, for vis or votes (Houses of Hermes: True Lineages p. 49; ArM5 p. 14). A Nile Tribunal needs at least twelve magi of four covenants and a Quaesitor, and a sponsor at the Grand Tribunal of 1228 or 1261. It must outlast the Fifth Crusade and, if history holds, the Seventh (1248 to 1254), against eremites, Moorish sahirs, treasure hunters and magi who want no new delegation.

Every monument of medieval Africa stands in Mythic Africa, with many more. The book follows thirteenth-century folklore, not modern archaeology. Tombs hold bizarre traps, strange creatures and puzzles, because people then believed they did: it explained why the treasure was still there. Old Egyptian magic is far weaker in attack than Hermetic magic; its priest-magicians excelled at healing and at commanding spirits.

Beasts of the valley with statistics elsewhere: the lion, in The Book of Mundane Beasts; a magical lion and the pard in Realms of Power: Magic pp. 60-61; other animals in Between Sand and Sea.

neighbours.name: The Abyssinian Highlands
neighbours.summary: The high country between Nubia and Ethiopia, also called the Land of Havilah. It takes in the Semien Mountains on the Ethiopian Empire's eastern border and Lake Tana with its many islands. Almost nothing else on the river's course rises so high, and its rains make the Nile's flood.

neighbours.name: The Deserts of the Nile
neighbours.summary: Three deserts hem in these lands, most of them ergs, rolling dunes swept by the wind. Travellers fear sun and thirst, sands that swallow a man and his mount, brigands on the caravan roads, storms that choke them or flay them, and the jinn and demons that show them palm-shaded pools. The first long drink may prove to be a mouthful of sand.
neighbours.secrets:
Hazards (p. 10). Deprivation checks for lack of water come every 4 hours here, and sun on bare skin does +1 non-combat damage (ArM5 pp. 180-181).

Dry quicksand: the victim is under within two rounds, then suffocates unless rescued. In the first round a Strength or Quickness stress roll against 9 frees him; a botch traps his arms for the next round. After that his companions must save him, and if his arms are free he may help in the second round, taking 3 off any further Ease Factors he faces. Then he has gone under.

Brigands usually leave a well-guarded caravan alone, unless desperate. Sandstorms and dust storms may be natural, made by sorcerers, elemental jinn, or even witches in disguise.

neighbours.name: The Libyan Desert
neighbours.summary: The vast desert on the western border of Egypt and Nubia.

neighbours.name: The Nubian Desert
neighbours.summary: The desert between the Upper Nile and the Red Sea, home of the headless Blemmyae, whose five tribes alone know where the gold lies that once made Egypt rich.

neighbours.name: The Danakil Desert
neighbours.summary:
The desert between the Nubian Kingdom of Atbara and Ethiopia.

Scorched salt flats on the south side of the Bab-al-Mandab, dividing Medri Bahri from Bet Amhara. Small communities hack out slabs of salt, and long camel caravans carry this 'white gold' to Adulis, Debarwa and Zeila.

neighbours.name: The Slavelands
neighbours.summary:
Nubians speak of the Slavelands as one country, but no such country exists. The captives sold to Egypt are taken from many separate places: some east of the Nile, some from the wilds between the Alodian city states, most from west and south-west of Upper Nubia. The name lets the Nubians think of free people as born slaves, and forget that they were once such a tribe themselves.

Fetid swamps and dry grasslands feed the tribes who live here, and Egyptian and Nubian expeditions raid them for slaves and cattle. Most slaves sold in Qus and Cairo come from them.

neighbours.name: The Land of Venom
neighbours.summary: A great rich pasture south of Ethiopia with nobody in it, because of the scorpions and spiders whose bite kills swiftly. The Cynamolgi graze their herds beyond it.

neighbours.name: The Copts
neighbours.summary:
The first people of Egypt, descended from the pyramid builders: dark of hair and eye, olive of skin, like Jews and Syrians, though they admire paler skin and some whiten theirs with pigments and bleaches. Red hair means bad luck. The most learned are said to read the old writing freely, for hieroglyphs are only another way of writing their tongue's ancestor; some become healers, oracles and magicians by it, and others use it to serve the Divine.

Copts are more curious about foreigners than Muslims are, and trade with them more: to know a stranger's needs is to know whom to send him to, and they approach his servants, since great men keep servants for such things. They forgive rudeness readily, being trained to it by Muslims who may berate them and in places spit on them, though an intermediary will still come to explain the fault so that the shame can be put right. Priests sway them more than clerics sway Muslims: faith marks them as a people and guards their standing as dhimmis, and a Christian priesthood is bound to its place as a Muslim teacher is not. Family counts for still more than among Muslims, and awkward matters stay within the community.

They keep festivals at the tombs of local saints, where the world works otherwise. At the moolid of Sitt Dimiana no thief can steal, and any man who looks on a woman meaning her harm is wounded in the eyes or lower down. At the Festival of Saint George nobody can stay possessed. Muslims and Christians go to each other's festivals, and when the flood looks poor the Sultan orders joint processions.

details.rules: All the notes on Egyptian characters suit Copts, save those marked as Muslim (p. 16). Festival miracles never fail, not even for a clever sorcerer, though people have been tricked into possession just after the festival ends. Western theologians find such certainty troubling; Copts do not.

neighbours.name: The Muslims of Egypt
neighbours.summary:
Egypt fell to the Umayyad Caliphate in 639, and its people turned to Islam slowly over the centuries. They are now a blend of Copts who converted and Arabs who settled from the east, and their faith is less strict than that nearer Mecca or among the west African dynasties. Of all Muslim lands, religion weighs least here on those who do not share it.

A good Muslim professes that there is no God but God and that Mohammed is His Prophet, before other Muslims, and follows the Qur'an and the sayings and deeds of the Prophet as jurists read them. He prays five times a day facing Mecca, between dawn and sunrise, after noon, in the afternoon, after sunset and after dusk, washing first; a mosque gives him water and a niche to face, and Friday noon is the great gathering. He gives alms, some rulers taxing for them. Egyptians hold that wealth does not reward virtue: Fate rules, and is not earned. He fasts, Ramadan above all, without even water, unless a child, old, pregnant, ill or travelling, and the evenings bring feasts hosted in turn. Pork and alcohol are shunned with more or less rigour. He goes to Mecca, and if he can Medina, once in his life, and comes back a Haji (a woman a Hajja), often in a green head covering; the poor visit nearer shrines, of which Cairo has many.

details.rules: The book's Islam is a simple guide for telling folktale stories, in which the rich and urban observe less strictly than the poor and rural (p. 12). For the Haj and shame, see Egyptian Manners.

neighbours.name: The Dhimmis
neighbours.summary:
Egypt surrendered to the Muslims rather than falling by force, and to a pious Muslim that bargain binds before God, so those non-Muslims allowed to stay fare better here than elsewhere, while they are useful. Most are Copts. Many Jews came from the Maghrib, among them the leader of a large community at Kairoun who fled a strict new dynasty. Some are freed slaves from the African interior, who should convert and often keep old ways besides. Few Zoroastrians live here.

They pay a yearly tax, though those in Alexandria by old agreement give only a little to the poor. They may not hold office, yet a Muslim may hire one to do the work of his; a Muslim port inspector, say, often pays a Christian to do the inspecting. They may not hold army rank, save mercenary captains; may not proselytize, nor touch or marry Muslim women; carry no weapons, though a knife is a tool and a shopkeeper keeps something handy. They must not plot with the ruler's enemies, nor testify against Muslims, though a Muslim friend may speak for them. Religious symbols are banned, though clerical garb is not and some places make them wear a mark. Prayer, bells and lavish funerals may not disturb, except in places such as Coptic Old Cairo. New places of worship need leave, and the authorities let new churches count as revivals of old ones, even of villages lost to the sand. Pork and wine stay out of sight. They should not ride horses or camels; in the towns they ride and dismount to pass mosques and great houses, and a Muslim knows he has arrived when dhimmis begin dismounting at his door. They bear contempt quietly.

Outside polite society, they may do what well-born Muslims may not. Trade abroad seems a little unsavoury, so Christian and Jewish merchants gather in the coastal cities, above all Alexandria, where taxes are lighter than for Muslims in Cairo, and sell to Europe, Sicily most of all. They lend at interest, and a dhimmi in the middle soaks up the sin when one Muslim lends to another. All Christians know a priest and all priests need wine, so many Muslims have a Christian supplier; most wine is imported, and nearly all the rest comes from monasteries.

details.rules: The Dhimmi Flaw, a Minor General Flaw, gives these duties (p. 13); custom softens many of them in Egypt. A character from Europe might take Outsider instead. City and Guild serves merchant characters.

neighbours.name: The Nubians
neighbours.summary: A black-skinned Christian people, descended from the Nobatae, a tribe who came into the Nile Valley about the fall of Kush, and much in debt to Greek culture. A unique treaty with Muslim Egypt, the baqt, keeps them safe from invasion for a yearly payment of slaves.

neighbours.name: The Ethiopians
neighbours.summary: Kin to the Nubians in looks, quite different in culture, and in their land since the dawn of time: the forebears of the Empire traded with the Greek cities, with Pharaonic Egypt and with Kush. South of the Empire lie sultanates of colonists from Yemen.

neighbours.name: The Churches of the Nile
neighbours.summary:
The Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria was founded by Saint Mark. It gave Christendom monasticism, and from its catechetical school came Origen, called the father of theology. It holds that after the Incarnation Christ has one nature, divine or a blend of divine and human, against the two natures upheld by Rome and Constantinople. When the Council of Chalcedon adopted that teaching in 451, Rome, Constantinople and Antioch agreed and Alexandria refused, so the Copts chose their own patriarch against the Melkite or Imperial one and were persecuted by the Byzantine governors. The Muslim conquest drove the Melkites out with the Greeks, and the Copts revived; six centuries of conversion have thinned them, but they remain a real presence.

The Nubian Church shares communion with the Copts and takes its bishops from Alexandria. Makuria was first converted by Melkites, and a good minority there still keep the Greek rite under Constantinople. The Ethiopian Church believes as the Copts do, but stands outside their congregation.

neighbours.name: The Tongues of the Nile
neighbours.summary:
Egypt speaks Arabic in its Masri dialect; travellers from North Africa use Maghrebi and those of Arabia Khaliji, all in the one script. Coptic, written in Greek letters with a few added from Demotic, has been failing since the conquest, though a century ago the country people still spoke it. Boharic survives in Lower Egypt; Sahidic has died out save among clergy in Nubia. Siwa speaks Siwi, a dialect of the Berbers' Tamazight.

The three Nubian kingdoms speak Nubian, written in an extended Coptic alphabet: Mahasi in Nobatia, Dongolawi in Makuria, Alwa in Alodia, Kenzi among the Banu al Kanz. Mahasi is close to becoming its own tongue. Masri is widely known in Nobatia, which trades with Egypt. The native clergy write and sing in Nubian Greek, which true Greeks think barbarous.

The Ethiopian highlands speak Amharic, from Ge'ez: Agaw in Agaw and Shewa, Amhara in Bet Amhara, Tigray along the escarpment of Medri Bahri. The lowlanders of Medri Bahri speak Tigrinya, with its own dialect in the Dahlak Archipelago. Oromigna, from Nubian, is heard in the southern sultanates and among the pagan tribes toward the Torrid Zone. All three use the Ge'ez script. Medri Bahri's merchants use Khaliji for the Red Sea, Yemen and the sultanates of Adal, Ifat, Hadiya and Dewaro.

The Blemmyae speak Beja, last child of Meroitic, and cannot write it, so Kushite monuments are closed to them. Each tribe of the Slavelands has its own tongue, but any one will make itself understood in the others. Slaves are taught Arabic by their Nubian masters to raise their price, and discouraged from their own speech.

Dead tongues: Ancient Egyptian, written in hieroglyphs and later hieratic, which became Demotic, in use until Roman times, still known to scholars, and the parent of Coptic. Meroitic, the speech of Kush, unrelated to Egyptian or Nubian, with a hieroglyphic and an alphabetic script that hardly anyone now reads. Ge'ez, the old tongue of Axum, still the liturgy of the Ethiopian Church, written in two hundred syllabic characters.

details.rules:
Living languages and their dialects (pp. 10-11): Amharic (Agaw, Amhara, Tigray); Arabic (Masri, Khaliji, Maghrebi); Beja; Coptic (Boharic, Sahidic); Nubian (Alwa, Dongolawi, Kenzi, Mahasi); Oromigna; Romaic Greek (Nubian); Tamazight (Siwi); Tigrinya (Dahlak); the tribal tongues of the Mythic Aithiopians. A dialect is a specialty; the Educated or well travelled may have shed theirs for a standard one (ArM5 p. 66).
Penalty to both speakers: same language, different dialects -1; Mahasi and any other Nubian dialect -2; Oromigna and any Nubian dialect -2; Amharic and Ge'ez -2; Beja and Meroitic -2; Ancient Egyptian and Demotic -2; Demotic and Coptic -2; any two Aithiopean languages -2.
Seekers learn key hieroglyphs of warning and curse by rote: the gist of a text is an Intelligence + Profession: Seeker stress roll against 6 for common curses or 9 for typical texts. A botch is a tragic misreading.

neighbours.name: Egyptian Manners
neighbours.summary:
Egyptians speak more formally than Europeans, even among friends and kin, though in the street they are surprisingly rude. Unsure of someone's standing, one says sidi to a man and lella to a woman, which grants higher rank, wealth, age or wisdom. It is dangerous to say it to a faerie or demon, for it gives them command. Any reasonable request must be met, and failure disgraces both sides, so requests go as opinions, suggestions, or gossip through a go-between. Asking for information counts, and a man who cannot answer loses face, as does the one who asked. Plans carry the words 'if God wills it', accepting fate; some say curses fall more easily on boasters.

To be known as disreputable shames a whole family, which can repudiate its member as a last resort. People expect mistakes, and public atonement. The learned and rich command others and keep to their class: they do no labour, for to hire nobody is to fail the community. Men's dress is loose trousers, which alone mark a poor man, with a long robe, head covering, tough slippers and a jacket. Women before men outside the family cover hair, body and arms, in many styles. The rich wear brighter, finer cloth and larger ornaments, while all pilgrims wear plain white.

Life is lived in company. To bathe or cook alone is to miss the news, and circumcisions, marriages and funerals are feasts held at home. A magus locked in his sanctum for months is thought shameful, mad, or seeking holiness. The Gift brings no shame of itself, but distrust soon brings bad Reputations that do.

Women's quarters are haram, forbidden to outsiders: wives, relatives, children, concubines and servants live there, with rivalries the folktales love. Women meet at the baths, at chores and on rooftops, and not to gossip is odd and rude, which gives them much news. A man may have four wives if he can keep them and treat them equally, and as many concubines as he can pay for, though this is not pious. A slave who bears a Muslim's child goes free and must be kept, so marriage usually follows.

details.rules:
Boasting (p. 14): a character who omits 'if God wills it' gives anyone envying him +6 on Hex rolls to spoil what he spoke of; saying the phrase cancels the bonus.

Shame (p. 15): a negative Local Reputation is bought down in the usual way, by building a rival Reputation (ArM5 p. 167), and here this is expected and right, not cynical. The Haj is a series of scenes giving Reputation experience against negative Reputations and a Haji +1 Reputation, with other benefits by what befalls. Shorter pilgrimages give less, which is why some are said to equal a fraction of Mecca. Religious insight from the Haj uses The Church pp. 15 ff., and is a separate process from the social one.

Women in disguise (p. 15, as the errata corrects it): a woman passing as a man has Dark Secret if discovery would ruin her, Gender Nonconforming if discovery recurs but only inconveniences, or no Flaw if it is not to make stories. A woman travelling with a false husband has Dark Secret if exposure would endanger the troupe, otherwise no Flaw.

Knows People (p. 13) is in the catalog.

neighbours.name: Words of the Nile
neighbours.summary:
Akh: a new soul made when ba, ka and khu fuse; the akhu are Daimons of the Magic Realm.
Ba: a dead person's travelling soul, ever seeking the khu.
Baqt: the pact that protects Christian Nubia from Muslim Egypt.
Cataract: a broad waterfall of the Nile, impassable by boat, some passed by carrying boats overland.
Domestikos: one of the thirteen kings who owe fealty to the megabasilikos.
Field of Reeds: a paradise in the Magic Realm where the ka live.
Ka: a dead person's ghost, going between the mundane world and the Field of Reeds.
Kentake: mother of a Kushite qore, sharing his power.
Khu: the Divine soul, which flees the body at death.
Megabasilikos: Great King, overall ruler of Makuria and Nobatia.
Mut: a ghost with unfinished business, like a shade.
Qore: a Kushite king; Alodia still uses the word.
Sahir: a magician working by summoning jinn, of the Order of Suleiman (The Cradle and the Crescent).
Serdab: the part of a tomb the ghost lives in while in the mundane world.
Ushabti: a statue of a person or animal to serve the dead in the afterlife; Egyptian ghosts can possess them.
Wadi: a seasonal stream or river.

neighbours.name: The Mythic Aithiopes
neighbours.summary:
The Aithiopes, 'burnt faces', are not the Ethiopians, though kin to them and to the Nubians, whose black skin and hair they share. Their many tribes live south-east of Nubia and east of Ethiopia, each with its own tongue, and were first written of in travelogs like that of Diodorus Siculus. The names the Greeks gave them are still used by the Nubians.

No missionary of any Divine faith has reached them, and most men would call them pagan, yet they believe in one Creator whose perfect world was spoiled by the first man and woman. They have no church or holy men, and appease or avoid the nature spirits cast out of Eden with that first couple.

details.rules: As characters (p. 122): Outsider applies automatically in Nubia, and in Arab lands they are likely taken for runaway slaves. Each tribe's intrinsic Virtue and Flaw come on top of the normal allotment. Or play one as a Magic Human (Realms of Power: Magic p. 32), the pair becoming a Minor Virtue Quality and a Minor Flaw Inferiority, perhaps with Inferiorities to cancel the immunity to aging and deprivation. The storyguide may treat their religion as Divine. These tribes are mythic, not the real peoples of East Africa.

neighbours.name: The Icthyophagi
neighbours.summary:
The fish eaters of the Red Sea coast live deep in the ravines, under arches of giant sea creatures' ribs woven with seaweed. When strong tides flood the shore the women and children throw small fish onto land, while the men band together against the large ones with goat horns and jagged rocks. The catch is pounded into bricks on cliff tops where the sun heats the rock red hot.

They drink only every fifth day, trekking inland to the Blemmyae's waterholes to bloat themselves and lie gasping. They raise children in common with no families, and are famous for enduring pain. Their dried fish is foul, but light, nourishing and never spoils.

details.rules: p. 123: Enduring Constitution; Weakness (drinking water). High Survival and Swim. A month of fish bricks is one Load.

neighbours.name: The Chelonophagi
neighbours.summary: Icthyophagi of the low Red Sea islands, which have no soil or fresh water, the outer ones breaking the waves so that the inner lie calm. The turtle eaters swim out to giant turtles sleeping at the surface, some as big as boats, flip them, tow them ashore and bake them in the sun. The upper shells become skiffs for trips to the mainland for water.

neighbours.name: The Rhizophagi
neighbours.summary:
The root eaters live in the marshes of the White Nile, digging out reed roots, pulping them and drying the balls in the sun. They live at peace with each other but are at war with the lions who come from the desert for the cool. They make no weapons. At the rising of Sirius, though, swarms of mosquitoes and flies descend, the people ward them off with marsh plants, and the lions flee, stung and terrified by the hum.

Taught at their mothers' knees, they are fine apothecaries and herb doctors, said never to sicken and to live very long. They make kombè for the Cynegi, in exchange for skins, and its antidote. At Egyptian markets a Rhizophagus is a prize, docile and skilled. The buyer should beware: he is also an expert poisoner.

details.rules: p. 123: Herbalism (Art & Academe p. 55); Noncombatant. Good Profession: Apothecary and Chirurgy; some have Mythic Herbalism.

neighbours.name: The Hylophagi
neighbours.summary:
Small, nimble, tailed and pale-furred, they live near the Rhizophagi, eating fruit in its season and otherwise chewing the tips of branches high in the trees. They leap from tree to tree like birds and never seem hurt in falling. They fight for certain trees with clubs and tear their victims apart. They dress in leaves or bark tied with vines; they make no tools, and simple made things baffle them.

Some live in vast hollow trees that hold a whole village, the leaves giving water and the fruit luring game. They are thought not worth importing, but some Nubian kings keep one as a gardener, tending the plants with teeth and nails. At home they sometimes live among the mouthless Astomi or the ear-winged Panotii.

details.rules: p. 124: intelligent monkeys, not humans: the Baboon block with Perfect Balance and Primitive Equipment. A village tree has about the inside of a Mystic Tower and could found an unusual covenant, from a seed grown by magic or a grown tree moved with Free the Striding Tree (ArM5 p. 139); Hylophagi make expert covenfolk for it.

neighbours.name: The Cynegi
neighbours.summary:
The Hunters of the inland country, unfit for farming, sleep in trees to escape the beasts and go by day to waterholes to kill. They use fire-hardened clubs, bows and bone-bladed spears, and wear a little leather, which is also their money: the more dangerous the beast, the more its hide is worth.

The Elephant Hunters are a western band. One grips the beast's tail, plants his feet on its thighs and hacks at the hind legs with an axe; when it falls the others rush in to cut meat, often before it is dead.

details.rules: p. 124: Puissant Hunt; Reckless. Profession: Prepare Kombè and the venom's rolls are on that page.

neighbours.name: The Struthophagi
neighbours.summary: The bird eaters live south and west of the Cynegi, small and tireless. Their homes overflow with fine baskets, furniture made with no saw or joint, painted pottery and great gardens, and they resent sleep for wasting time. They keep ostriches for meat, leather and riding, and the feathers are among Nubia's chief exports to Egypt. Legend says the ostrich was first given fire and hid it under its wing. The first Struthophagus persuaded it that it could fly, took the fire when its wings opened, and repenting vowed to look after it. A peaceful folk, they suffer badly from slavers.

details.rules: p. 124: Puissant Ride; Small Frame. Prized as light cavalry, their ostriches hurling stones while they throw spears.

neighbours.name: The Acridophagi
neighbours.summary:
The locust eaters live on the desert's edge near the Struthophagi, leaner and darker than other men. In spring the desert breeds swarms of locusts. The tribe drive them into ravines with fire, kill them with smoke, and salt them to last the year, growing no crops and keeping no stock.

They die young, and forty is a great age. Winged lice breed in their flesh as they age: first itching, then a thin acrid discharge, then the vermin bore out and pour away, each taking a morsel until nothing is left. Other peoples' flesh does not tempt them.

details.rules: p. 125: Greater Immunity to Thirst; Greater Malediction, which starts Aging rolls at 15. Nothing, even magic, cures or keeps out the lice.

neighbours.name: The Cynamolgi
neighbours.summary:
Tall bearded herdsmen beyond the Land of Venom, whose savage dog packs keep lions, leopards and hyenas off their cattle. Everyone covets the cattle, and Nubian slavers come for them, but seldom take the men, who are too much trouble.

A boy is suckled by a bitch and his milk-mates begin his pack. Only the man who raised the dogs can go near them. When he dies they must be killed and buried with him, or they turn wild and become the very predators they guarded against. They are solemn, slow to weigh a matter, decisive once it is weighed, and fierce in war.

details.rules: p. 125: Puissant Animal Handling; Compulsion (protect his pack). He leads his dogs as a trained group with Animal Handling for Leadership, and rarely has an Animal Companion Flaw.

neighbours.name: The Megabari
neighbours.summary:
Also called Trogodytes, they live east of the Cynamolgi and south of the Ethiopians, nomads with sheep, goats and cattle who follow the rains. They wear only loin skins and carry round oxhide shields, spears and bows, and their champions have huge iron-knobbed clubs.

Each band's tyrant owns the two pairs of beasts, bull and cow, ram and sheep, that it calls Father and Mother. When one dies its mate is killed and a new pair chosen, whose owner is tyrant-in-waiting; when the old tyrant loses the other pair, the new man rules, adopted by a second pair.

Women hold power and no man dares strike one. Only the tyrant has a wife; other women lie with whom they choose, and if his wife chooses a man he owes the tyrant a set number of sheep. In the rains they drink blood and milk left to seethe together. In the dry they fall back on the marshes and fight for the grass, first with stones, then with arrows, and so well that many die in moments. The women usually end it, running in to shield their sons. Some say their magicians make the carnivorous bull as vengeance on slavers.

details.rules: p. 126: men Puissant Bows and Prohibition (harming women); women Temporal Influence and Sensitive (to disrespect).

neighbours.name: The Polo Party
neighbours.summary: A nobleman's polo party rode down people in the market, and he needs every one of the injured found so that he can make amends.

neighbours.name: The Heiress's Father
neighbours.summary: An heiress's father died on a trading venture. She must find his remains so that he can be decently buried and his goods shared out among his heirs.

neighbours.name: The Sunken Cargo
neighbours.summary: A merchant's ship has gone down and his creditors are hounding him. He wants the magi to bring the cargo up from the sea bed.

neighbours.name: The Sicilian Sailor
neighbours.summary: A rich adulterer has talked a Sicilian sailor into taking the blame. Once the sailor has boasted of his conquests he must be smuggled out of town.

neighbours.name: The Learned Excuse
neighbours.summary: A noble drunkard needs a doctor of good standing to declare that sunstroke, not wine, was to blame for what he did. Is there such an expert to be found?

neighbours.name: Coastal Raiders
neighbours.summary: A tribe of Icthyophagi have tamed one of the great sea-eels of the Red Sea and are raiding merchant ships with it, very unlike that peaceful people.
neighbours.secrets: Who is really directing the tribe is left open.

neighbours.name: Tribal Medicine
neighbours.summary: A king's daughter lies ill with a disease nothing can cure. Rumour tells of a Rhizophagus healer of remarkable powers, and the characters are asked, or tempted by the reward, to find a cure.

neighbours.name: The Far-Away Tree
neighbours.summary: A tribe of Hylophagi live in a magically awakened village-tree that once wandered their own lands. Now it has turned toward the Nile Valley. Its rubbery bark and fibrous wood shrug off most weapons, it stamps flat houses and armies alike, and the tribe in its branches have clubs and rocks. The locals turn to the magi.
neighbours.secrets: If the characters cannot attack it directly, they should learn why the tree has turned north: perhaps the tribe's new witch-doctor.

neighbours.name: Famine of Ages
neighbours.summary: Acridophagi come into the Nile Valley seeking help and meet contempt. The characters may yet listen to them.
neighbours.secrets: Long ago a sorcerer bound a famine demon into an Acridophagus child, inking the bindings on his skin. The boy lived as a king, safe from harm: at his death the winged lice would each carry off a piece of the demon and destroy it. Now the tribe fear the sorcerer was corrupt, and that when the man soon dies the demon will be multiplied and borne to the ends of the earth. The answer may lie in finding the sorcerer, surely very powerful by now, or be as simple as killing the vessel.

neighbours.name: The Gamekeeper Turned Poacher
neighbours.summary: A bouda plagues the district around a covenant, and even a magus cannot kill what he cannot find. A Cynamolgus might be the answer, and a wanderer cut off from his homeland is rumoured to be nearby.
neighbours.secrets: His price is steep, and when the work is done he may prove more trouble than the bouda was.

neighbours.name: The Man-Eating Cow
neighbours.summary: All through Nubia cattle are dying mysteriously. Most just vanish, though now and then a skin or a bloodless body turns up. Magic is suspected, and the characters may fall under suspicion themselves.
neighbours.secrets: Every lost cow came from Megabari lands: stolen spoils among which came carnivorous bulls, now loose in the herds of Makuria.

neighbours.name: The Seekers' Guild (Al-Matalibeen)
neighbours.summary:
Explorers have stripped riches from Egypt's monuments for longer than anyone remembers. Old adventurers write popular books, sold in most towns, or take apprentices who pay in advance; desperate men try their luck untrained; in some districts digging for treasure is a sport, and a plague to those who would keep the monuments whole.

Centuries ago, in a time of drought or war, Egypt's impoverished rulers turned this trade into a guild. A man who gives steadily to the royal treasury has the ear of the emir, which brings humble folk close to the sultan's inner circle, and the emir or his allies may choose such men as agents.

The guildhall's scrolls tell how to disarm tomb defences, give charms against curses and rote readings of the hieroglyphs that matter, and describe the usual decoys and hiding places. Other texts list sites, both cleared ones ready for new residents and ones not fully looted.

Locals call hieroglyphs by many names: the Pen of Copts, of the Temples, of Talismans, of South Arabia, of Priests and of Hermes.

details.decides: An emir chosen by the sultan, often from his most powerful councillors, leads the guild. Its members elect a chairman, the Naqeeb al-Matalibeen, whom the emir must approve.
details.rules: Every tomb robber must belong. Membership costs a yearly fee and 20% of all valuables found, paid to the sultan.
details.offers: The guildhall in Cairo and its library of seeker texts; training from older members; rumours of sites; for members of repute, teams of specialists to attempt sites that have beaten earlier parties.

neighbours.secrets:
Rules: the guild's knowledge is the Ability Profession: Seeker; its site lists are Area Lore (LotN p. 24). A government clerk must be present at any digging for treasure (p. 25).

In a high-fantasy saga, members may hire magic items recovered from tombs, and the guild has supernatural allies or even mystical members (p. 24).

The book compares the guild to the adventurers' guilds of other fantasy games: a familiar way in for new players (p. 24). The Seeker manuals describe more, and less, dangerous versions of every trap listed under the Traps of the Tombs (p. 43).

neighbours.name: Gourneh
neighbours.summary:
The village of the finest tomb thieves, at Luxor. Its people have looted tombs since antiquity, when they built them by day and emptied them by night. Grandparents teach the young to excavate, tunnel, bargain and disarm traps.

Few of them fight well, so they hire mercenaries to face the guardians. When those die, as they often do, it counts as a mark of skill to bring back the corpses and the wages already paid.

Poor men who cannot pay the guild's fee, and others who will not give the sultan a fifth, work outside it. Their black market twines with the lawful trade, and ships artefacts abroad, often to wealthy pilgrims.

Gourneh families take work as labourers on lawful expeditions; once a dig is finished and likely to lie unwatched, the man summons his kin. They count themselves good Muslims and will not kill tomb guards, but will distract them or drug their food. Fiercely loyal to family and village, they could be fine allies to magi rich enough not to think of theft.

neighbours.name: The Pagan Monuments of Egypt (Birbah)
neighbours.summary:
Egypt is famous for its monuments, and a local proverb holds that every place has its treasure. The dynasties were buried at different places along the river, and the order of the tombs puzzles even learned Egyptians; it is thought pious to study it, and some old Coptic monks may have unravelled it entirely.

A tomb is a machine for keeping a ghost whole. At its least it has two rooms holding three parts. The mortuary chapel, the one room built for the living, is where priests and descendants leave offerings. It holds a statue of the dead, often striding out of a false door or seated in state. Later chapels shrink to a niche and a door that cannot open, or stand apart from the tomb. Later still, statues and then paintings of food replaced real food, and stelae outside the tomb order the gods to feed the dead whenever a passer-by reads them.

The serdab is the ghost's private home, often buried in the masonry with no passage a man could use, and is filled with grave goods or their pictures. A linteled door facing west, the stele, opens the way to Duat. It may be only a carving, or tiny, or in the oldest tombs a slit a few inches wide; later ones bear the owner's name, then a biography and advice on the afterlife, even spells. Sometimes a tunnel a few inches across joins serdab and chapel, to let incense and sound through.

Ghosts prefer a body, and animate statues that are good likenesses, flaws included: a courtier with the Dwarf Flaw is carved at his true height, with his crippled foot. Men have an older man's face over a young warrior's belly; women are younger and fair. There are spares, because robbers smash statues as a matter of course: it stops a ghost using them, and many are held with valuable copper clamps or hollow with treasure inside. The small servant statues, ushabtis or answerers, take a noble's turn at labour in the Field of Reeds, and they keep tomb machinery working.

The sepulcher keeps the body, for the refreshment of the ba, the travelling soul, as the serdab refreshes the ka, the ghost. The corpse is prepared so the ba may know it, and is wrapped in talismans and coffins inscribed with words of power. The texts say the ba is judged by its sins, then journeys through fearful places to the abode of the solar gods seeking the khu, the Divine spark that left the body at death. If it succeeds, ka, ba and khu merge into an akh. Grave robbers prize the body itself for the mummia that preserves it, a bitumen valued as medicine.

The earliest graves lay under mounds of soil or sand, and a warlord had to choose between a town, where people could watch his tomb, and the far desert. Limestone platforms, the mastabas, followed; then pyramids, jacketed in smooth stone or granite to hide the door. When the priests offered an afterlife to nobles, and in times of drought or invasion, smaller tombs were needed: black brick mastabas with a little pyramidion, a single sepulcher and a niche for a serdab, or tombs cut into limestone cliffs, with the sepulcher below the chapel at the foot of a shaft that could be filled with rubble.

Seekers argue over what the tombs hold. Some say gold, jewels and medicines; others say only early tombs do, and later kings buried gilded wooden copies, since the likeness becomes real in the Field of Reeds. Three things are never replaced by likenesses: writing, favourite possessions, and what preserves the body. Oddly, no true crown of Egypt has ever been found in any tomb.

Kanqahs, the schools of Egyptian mysticism, are often set in graveyards, and these have a Divine aura. Ancient temples may keep a weak Faerie aura from their pagan worship, if any remains.
neighbours.secrets:
Auras (LotN pp. 31, 40): ancient tombs often have Magic auras, from their preternatural tether and fine sites. Each century a grave site was in use gives a tether of 1, to a maximum of 5; the aura equals the tether, may be raised by impressive natural features, and is often lower where the monuments have decayed. The stele is a vestige of the Magic Realm, usually aligned to Mentem, of a level equal to the tomb's aura. An intact mummy is an Arcane Connection for its ka, giving a Familiarity Bonus of 15 to the Vestige Travel Total; mortals using the vestige gain nothing. See Realms of Power: Magic pp. 8-10, 20-24.

Ka-work (pp. 27, 30): a ghost can manifest as part of its form anything in its grave goods or painted on its walls, if not stolen or defaced, and these things can affect mortals at its choice. Hermetic magic cannot sense the ba, perhaps because of the Limit of the Soul, or use the spells written to protect it. Hermetic magi may use the serdab tunnel with shapeshifting or Intellego; treasure guides leave it out, as it is no use to thieves.

Carving equipment (p. 31): in a very few tombs the best grave goods are carving tools, with which a ghost makes likenesses that become real for it, including food, so it escapes the fate of the unfed. A rough carving of archers calls up faerie reinforcements. In later tombs a new object takes one round; in earlier ones, five minutes, as the carving must closely match known forms; in the earliest, a miniature statue, up to half an hour. Many tomb owners have a small servitor statue use the tools for them.

Unfed spirits (p. 31) travel the roads scrounging what humans have thrown away, which spiritually gives it to the next finder. They hate this, and may plague people with ill luck until offered libations.

Designing a tomb (pp. 40-44): a place marked as a tomb has a Tomb tab with the book's kinds, Build Points and costs; statistics are needed only for a tomb that will last in the saga. A library is usually wall inscriptions in Ancient Egyptian or Demotic, in hieroglyphs or hieratic: a history of the dead as Area Lore or Organization Lore, or spells as Magic Lore or Supernatural Abilities; a few hold scrolls in sealed jars. Specialists cost BP as usual; a tomb guardian costs its highest Martial Ability or Brawl; ghosts may be specialists or teachers.

Vis and Boons (p. 44): vis left as grave goods is paid for as a vis stock if the tomb becomes a character's home, and helps an akh offset the penalty of high Might on Study Totals for Transformation. Tombs may also be vis sources, Corpus most often. The Boons and Hooks of ArM5 pp. 72-74 and Covenants pp. 6-27 mostly suit; Wealth means the grave goods are intact, perhaps Unknown to the tomb's residents. In Nubia every tomb should buy Seclusion, for fear of the dead.

Dedun (p. 39): Temple Priests and Undying Ones of the Cult of Dedun use tombs as homes and temples, the font of power gained at Initiation as temple priest and the home of their ghoulish court; adherents gather there once a month. Detail the tomb's resources when a player character seeks that Initiation, or for an Undying One as villain or ally. Such a resident may hold altar priests and adherents as specialists (p. 42).

The book offers both simple tombs and labyrinthine necropolises; treat simple ones as early, poor, or built after a long drought (p. 27).

neighbours.name: The Field of Reeds
neighbours.summary:
The afterlife of the Egyptians, in Duat, called by some the Fields of Turquoise. Its ghosts live in great comfort but cannot stay for ever: at least once a year each must return to the mortal world to be fed, and to remember who it was from the offerings and inscriptions left behind. One that fails loses its memories and becomes a mut, or fades altogether.

It is called the ka of the Nile Delta: many islands, each the paradise of one ka, ruling as in life with the servants who followed him in death. Each island has a copy of its owner's stele. To walk another's island and leave by another's stele is possible, and a gross breach of manners.

The common dead expected no more than to farm here for ever; to be anything else took burial rites only great wealth could buy.
neighbours.secrets:
It lies in the Magic Realm, and most tombs' Magic auras ease the passage (LotN pp. 26, 32).

Wesir (Osiris) rules it: a powerful Daimon and ally of the Black, whose ordeals set the pattern for other ka, and perhaps the first human to reach apotheosis as a Daimon. He opened the path hoping to recruit friends for the Black. Those who become akhu may join, but none are forced to fight the Red (pp. 32, 37). Whether stories of Wesir inspired the faerie god Osiris, or the reverse, nobody knows; a faerie copy of the Field of Reeds, in the Faerie Realm, is ruled by that god and peopled by faerie ka (p. 32).

The ba is said to leave the boat of the sun god to visit its body (p. 30). Thoth judges those who would become akhu, and hearts heavy with evil feed the Devourer of Souls (p. 37). When the ba needs protection against the Great Serpents of the Hours it must have the true words (p. 32).

neighbours.name: The Ramaseum
neighbours.summary: The tomb of Rameses II, the pharaoh of the Bible, adorned with colossal images of himself.
neighbours.secrets: Most ghosts cannot possess statues far larger than they were in life, as these do not feel like true likenesses. Rameses, the very type of Pride, thought himself a giant bestriding the world, so might animate the vast images here. Other pharaohs who share his Personality Flaw might likewise manifest through huge statues (LotN p. 31).

neighbours.name: The Secret Valley near Alexandria
neighbours.summary: A hidden valley of rock-cut tombs close to Alexandria. Each tomb's mortuary chapel stands apart on the banks of the Nile, to keep the valley's place secret.
neighbours.secrets: The ghosts ride regularly to their chapels for offerings, or scrounge street rubbish if a chapel is destroyed or untended. Characters with Second Sight may follow them home; if spotted they are attacked, and on the Paths of the Dead the spectral weapons are entirely solid (LotN p. 31).

neighbours.name: The House of Life
neighbours.summary: The temple of Thoth where Imhotep's healers trained, the first known library of magical books and the first hospital. Others like it followed, but no House of Life has ever been uncovered.
neighbours.secrets: Its library, never found, is the greatest cache of alchemical texts (LotN pp. 39, 49).

neighbours.name: The Treasure House of Qarun
neighbours.summary: Qarun, a man of Moses's time, grew so rich that a train of strong slaves was needed just to carry the keys to his treasure house. God, disgusted by his pride, thrust it deep into the sands, and nobody has found it since. The seekers love the tale: it was buried, but not by its owner's order, so its defences should be weak beside those of dead kings.
neighbours.secrets: Where the keys lie is recorded somewhere in the guild's library. Characters with a clue find many eager young seekers, and many cynical old ones who chased it in their youth (LotN p. 25).

neighbours.name: The Treasure House of Moses's Pharaoh
neighbours.summary: God played the same trick with the treasure house of the pharaoh of Moses. It too has never been found, though its exact place is known.
neighbours.secrets: This may mean a Divine regio lies there (LotN p. 25).

neighbours.name: Curses of the Tombs
neighbours.summary: Most tombs have at least one curse, and some carry long maledictions promising many horrors to any who defile them. Lector priests laid them with magic now forgotten, writing them in a prominent place, usually in hieroglyphs, sometimes in Demotic. Each names a condition, such as defacing the inscription, breaking the seal, entering impure or disturbing the king, then one or more punishments.

tomb_curses.name: A Crocodile Shall Be Against Him in Water, a Snake on Land
tomb_curses.excoriation: Spend more than a night near water and a large crocodile comes; more than a night far from it, a venomous snake. Each is an ordinary beast bar its arrival; kill it and another comes. (Base 30, +1 Touch, +2 Room.)

tomb_curses.name: He Shall Be Destroyed by Sekhmet
tomb_curses.excoriation: Arrows of fire hit each target automatically for +15 damage. (Base 10, +1 Touch, +2 Room.)

tomb_curses.name: He Shall Capsize and Drown at Sea
tomb_curses.excoriation: Any boat the victim boards sinks; in more than a foot of water he cannot keep his head above the surface, and drowns. (Base 30, +1 Touch, +2 Room.)

tomb_curses.name: He Shall Have No Successors
tomb_curses.excoriation: Destroys the organs of generation. Other readings might drive off apprentices or proteges, as a Lesser Malediction. (Base 20, +1 Touch, +2 Room.)

tomb_curses.name: He Shall Meet Death by a Disease that No Doctor can Diagnose
tomb_curses.excoriation: A major disease (Disease Penalty -5); mundane medicine does not help Recovery rolls, only magic. (Base 20, +1 Touch, +2 Room.)

tomb_curses.name: He Shall Not Reach his Home, nor Embrace his Children
tomb_curses.excoriation: As the No Sense of Direction Flaw; in the desert it can kill. (Base 10, +1 Touch, +2 Room.)

tomb_curses.name: I Shall Cast the Fear of Myself into Him
tomb_curses.excoriation: Overwhelming dread of the tomb or its occupant; victims must flee at once. (Base 4, +1 Touch, +2 Sun, +2 Room.)

tomb_curses.name: I Shall Wring his Neck Like a Bird
tomb_curses.excoriation: Spectral hands choke everyone affected; use air deprivation (ArM5 p. 180) until cancelled or all are dead. Another may cut a hole lower in the neck: Dex + Chirurgy stress roll against 9, which leaves the Mute Flaw either way, and a botch kills. A victim who escapes the room and makes a Deprivation roll breaks the curse. (Base 30, +1 Touch, +2 Sun, +2 Room.)

tomb_curses.name: The Hollow Promise of a Swift Death
tomb_curses.excoriation: No curse at all, and a constant effect: magical detection sees a 30th-level curse. It may be made at other levels: a magnitude up or down in the base effect appears as two up or down. (Base 3 taint with magic, +2 Sun; +3 environmental trigger, +1 2/day.)

neighbours.secrets: How literally a condition is taken is left to the storyguide; it need not be one a Hermetic device could detect (LotN pp. 34, 40). All are 1/day, Pen 0, R: Touch, T: Room unless noted, and their levels serve for breaking them as well as for Build Points (p. 41).

neighbours.name: Wards of the Tombs
neighbours.summary: The favourite wards of Egypt hide a tomb from sight or nudge people gently away. The books of treasure hunters are full of ways round them: stand on a certain rock at dawn, say, wearing a headdress of red feathers. Against the strongest such tricks fail.

tomb_wards.name: Nothing But Sky and Sand
tomb_wards.effect: The structure seems a sand dune in every way. R: Touch, D: Sun, T: Str (Base 5, +1 Touch, +2 Sun, +3 Structure; +3 environmental trigger, +1 2/day). Avoided, for instance, by spotting a stray shadow or working out the stars that reveal it. It may fail from one angle or under sprinkled water (p. 42).

tomb_wards.name: Turn the Interloper
tomb_wards.effect: Spins anyone who triggers it, usually at a doorway, through 180 degrees (Base 10, +2 Voice; +10 unlimited uses). Avoided by bracing against it.

tomb_wards.name: A Sovereign Ward Against Robbers
tomb_wards.effect: Humans can hardly enter and cannot harm the structure from outside (Base 15, +1 Touch, +2 Sun, +3 Structure; +3 environmental trigger, +1 2/day). Overcome by forcing through, or throwing a stone to dislodge the amulet behind it.

neighbours.secrets: Wards (LotN pp. 35, 40). Most have a way to deactivate them for a while, and they are likelier than other talismans to have Penetration, since they are aimed at spirits. Books on bypassing the strongest are Initiation Scripts for Mystery Virtues, which may open a single site or, unknown to the reader, many: some grant Second Sight and teach regio crossing, others give resistance to talismans of one substance or school. A ward repels rather than harms, as when sand is about to turn to glass and seal the tomb, or an illusion has a flaw.

neighbours.name: Talismans of the Tombs
neighbours.summary: A talisman here is a small magic item set off by an expected act: step through a door and the lintel pours fire on your head. Most work on the gross elements rather than on emotion or luck. Their makers could not resist their own work, so built in a way to put each to sleep. Egyptian combat magic was poor, and Moses's contest with the pharaoh's magicians was a sort of primitive certamen, but their lasting curses, talismans and wards were sometimes exceptional, and always made of opulent materials.

tomb_wards.name: Apedemak's Strength
tomb_wards.effect: Animates a huge lion statue, which obeys one spoken order. Warped, it needs a Com + Leadership roll against 9 to override its last order: attack all who cross the threshold. Dogged, nearly indestructible, an unskilled fighter; to hide or run from it is the roll against its Ease Factor. R: Per, D: Conc, T: Ind (Base 5, +1 Conc, +1 stone, +1 size, +1 requisite; +5 maintains concentration, +10 unlimited).

tomb_wards.name: The Destroying Uraeus
tomb_wards.effect: A rearing cobra statue spews fire, +10 damage to one person passing without intoning the tomb owner's name. Unlike a Hermetic effect it can be dodged, by diving aside (p. 42). R: Voice, D: Mom, T: Ind (Base 5, +2 Voice; +5 24/day).
tomb_wards.deactivation: Intone the name of the tomb's owner in passing

tomb_wards.name: On The Presentation of Face of Lost Companions
tomb_wards.effect: After a fatal trap, an ochre-red image of the dead person's face comes out of a wall nearby. One known version shouts a warning in an old tongue against disturbing kings. Sinister versions enslave the ghost as a guardian. R: Touch, D: Conc, T: Ind (Base 2, +1 Touch, +1 Conc, +1 legible words and moving image, +1 requisite; +5 maintain concentration).

tomb_wards.name: On Lowering the Waters
tomb_wards.effect: Many tombs hold living water that strains to drown intruders. It is in effect a Might 15 water elemental (Realms of Power: Magic), and this talisman wakes and commands it; it may be tricked with a new command. R: Touch, D: Sun, T: Ind (Base 5, +1 Touch, +2 Sun; +8 Penetration 16).

neighbours.secrets: Talismans (LotN pp. 33-35, 41-42). Ancient Egyptians had no general Magic Resistance, so talismans aimed at people mostly have no Penetration: even young magi ignore them, but grogs and equipment do not. A particular spell effect usually renders one inert until sunset; in a laboratory a magus finds which, by trial or as with a magic item's triggers (ArM5 p. 100). Design them by the Hermetic item rules, or Learned Magic with the provisos of Chapter 5; few relied on one-use seals or temporary amulets. Though costed as Hermetic effects, they need not obey Hermetic limits. Left in a strong aura, enchantments take Warping.

neighbours.name: Traps of the Tombs
neighbours.summary:
The plainest defence is to bar the way. Iron was rare, so passages are choked with rubble, or in rich tombs with granite blocks so hard the manuals say to quarry round them through the limestone. Pits deter entry, and sloping passages may be filled with sand and lime, soaked until it sets into a rough cement.

Architects hide entrances behind stone jackets, leave unfinished chambers to send robbers home, and put a false wall or floor before the sealed way to the true rooms. Bronze clockwork, hidden in walls, floors, statues or arks, reloads projectiles, resets itself, moves great objects and answers to pressure plates and levers.

Some rooms can only be passed by a puzzle, a lock and trap in one, built to shut out those without leisure or letters: moves of a board game, or hieroglyphs touched in order, with a sign or riddle somewhere before the door. The favourite game was senet, played no more in Mythic Africa; many seekers report rooms themed on backgammon, though those who know its history doubt it, and some suspect faeries.

tomb_traps.name: Labyrinth
tomb_traps.text: A maze of tunnels and identical passages. Retracing steps takes three times as long as going in.

tomb_traps.name: Prison Room
tomb_traps.text: A dead-end chamber with treasure or inscriptions. The roll hears the mechanism in the delay; otherwise a door too heavy to lift drops. The treasure is painted wood, the inscriptions nonsense or taunts.

tomb_traps.name: Rock Fall
tomb_traps.text: Boulders roll on those climbing a slope: stress roll or +10 damage. Impact as ArM5 p. 181. Larger falls cost more: an avalanche +24 and perhaps suffocation (p. 180); rocks outweighing a character +21; about his weight +18; smaller, about +1 per 10 pounds. Spiked balls do more, sand, bones or the bodies of those left with the horses less.

tomb_traps.name: Medicinal Powders
tomb_traps.text: Fine poison in a sealed room, stirred by the door and by movement. It sears and disfigures, a Medium Wound, unless the roll is made. Others cost Fatigue, blind, paralyse, or burn.

tomb_traps.name: Head Wires
tomb_traps.text: Neck-high wires, +9 damage that most armour does not stop.

tomb_traps.name: Head Wires behind a Pit
tomb_traps.text: Strung behind an obvious pit, so a jumper hits them: +18 damage that most armour does not stop.

tomb_traps.name: Dead Drop
tomb_traps.text: A slightly less worn paving stone opens on a ten-pace fall to stone, +30 damage.

neighbours.secrets:
Spells that detect metal find mechanisms, and destroying one can seize the trap (LotN p. 32).

Puzzles: Hermetic magi can subvert them, say with Rego from outside the door. A dedicated magus might collect accounts to deduce senet's rules, or some ghosts know the game. As a minigame, play a real historical game; with combat-minded troupes put the characters on the board to fight the pieces; let magic cheat (p. 33).

Projectiles, cost varies: if not escaped that round, stress die + weapon Damage (ArM5 p. 177), soaked. Several projectiles are rolled and added; machines add +1 to +5 by human Strength equivalent. Many are poisoned (p. 180).

Pits, cost varies: falling damage (ArM5 p. 181), plus the nearest weapon's Damage for a dangerous floor: a 20-foot pit of sharp stakes is stress die + 20 + 5, against stress die + Soak. An architect's aim may add more.

neighbours.name: Ghosts of the Tombs
neighbours.summary:
Each tomb has a principal ka, the one it was built for, and perhaps the ghosts of those buried to guard or serve him. Muslim writers think of the ka as the body's ghostly double. They are resilient, well-found and dangerous, unlike Western spectres: transparent but fully coloured, the mightier the more solid. Other guardians are faeries, called up by long-dead lector priests or bound by talismans, still feeding on the stories told of them.

Akhu are the final state of the greatest dead, formed from ba, ka and khu. They need no food or prayer and no longer need a tomb, though some enjoy the access it gives. Imhotep is thought to have taken two thousand years to finish the change, which is not usual. Each is unique, many can take an animal shape, and all texts agree they can have children. Their names, placed at chapels and on monuments, feed them whenever read.

A just pharaoh kept the world in balance, so the floods came and food was plenty, and could enrich or ruin men by decree. All were thought to command spirits, though often by asking a divine patron to punish the disobedient. Some had strange powers from their lives: one, it seems, could slow time around him, so that his companions aged less and spells took longer to run out.
neighbours.secrets:
Quick ghost (LotN pp. 35-36). Take a mortal; Magic Might 5 to 25; Characteristics as in life, and it cannot fail Fatigue rolls. Remove Virtues and Flaws of social role or body, which need not balance. Most take Magical Monster, some Magical Friend; add Magic Spirit. Abilities stay, many useless. Intangible and unharmed by weapons or fire; Protection and Soak work against magic; vulnerable to Mentem. Add a +3 trait tied to mortal business. Few have Donning the Corporeal Veil (5 points, material until released, gear too). A new power is based on a Hermetic spell, at 1 Might per 5 levels, or per 10 for one that affects only itself, Init Qik - magnitude/2. Vis, usually Mentem, equals Might/5.

Possess Statue (Minor Power): 3 points, Init Qik -3, Terram or Herbam. Steps into and animates a statue at Range Personal, one at a time. Improved Powers often cuts the cost to 0. The statue's physical attacks must Penetrate. Wooden: ReHe 25 (Base 10, +2 Sun, +1 constant). Stone: ReTe 25 (Base 3, +2 Sun, +1 stone, +1 constant, +2 intricacy). Metal: ReTe 30 (Base 3, +2 Sun, +2 metal, +1 constant, +2 intricacy).

Quick animated statue (p. 36). As above with Might 5 to 25 (a possessing ghost's own Might). Rarely not life-size: -2 Str and +1 Qik per Size lost, the reverse per Size gained. Remove social Virtues; add Magical Monster and Magic Thing. Soak: wood +9; ceramic, soft stone or soft metal +15; hard stone +18; hard metal +21. Armour adds nothing unless harder than the statue. To destroy the face, announce it and inflict a Medium Wound; that drives the ghost out. Weapons of stone or bronze -1 damage; gilded wood in place of metal -2; alchemically hardened bronze as steel. Fists and kicks +1 for wood or stone, +2 for metal; brawling weapons unadjusted. Boost combat with Qualities as the story needs. Vis, usually the material's Form, is Might/5. Al-jazari, the automatons, use these rules on any reworked monster, and have no Might.

Royal ghosts (pp. 36-37): most dynasties claimed a faerie god invested the pharaoh when he begot his heir, giving the Major Blood of the Old Gods; other descendants have the Minor (Virtue, p. 36; Sympathy Trait usually Royalty, or a god's purview). The Ptolemies built their own god, Serapis, an ally but no ancestor. Longer rites and coffin texts allow Transformation after death (Realms of Power: Magic p. 52), and tombs were sometimes stocked with vis for it.

Akhu (p. 37; The Mysteries: Revised Edition pp. 82-86): a Daimon, an indestructible being acting through a self-sustaining Aspect. Build as Magic Spirits: Might 20 for a noble with the simplest coffin texts, up to 60 for the greatest pharaohs, the longer to finish the greater the Might. They have virtuous traits. All have long since gained all they can from readers of their names, so are Winter creatures, and may be summoned by name or relics. Offspring may have Mythic or Magical Blood.

neighbours.name: The Tomb of Imhotep
neighbours.summary: Probably at Saqqara. Imhotep, priest of Thoth under Djoser, the first king with a pyramid, is said to have invented architecture and medicine; the column and lintel come from his designs. Classical sources mention his tomb, but it has never been traced. He took every scroll he owned to the grave.
neighbours.secrets:
Its defences and writings would settle the Order's old dispute whether modern magic outstrips the ancient. Some magi hold that Bonisagus built on earlier traditions and that Original Research has gone further; others that the world declines from golden ages, and that research mostly fits old wisdom into Hermetic Theory (LotN p. 39).

Coptic magicians think Imhotep took great pains to leave no trace. Some magi think he was also Asclepius and Hermes Trismegistus, and hope those names lead to it; others dispute this.

neighbours.name: The Tomb of Marcus Antonius
neighbours.summary: Probably near Alexandria. The Romans never found it, for all their searching and the thousands who saw the funeral or helped to build it. Cleopatra meant to lie here beside him.
neighbours.secrets:
Cleopatra had at least two tombs made; this was the intended one, far closer to Alexandria than her final rest (LotN p. 39).

Hermetic magi want her resting places for Cleopatra's Book, and because some say the fire at the Great Library covered the hiding of its books from Rome, with the 200,000 books of Pergamon that Antonius took by force as a wedding gift for her.

neighbours.name: The Tomb of Queen Cleopatra
neighbours.summary: The prize of every treasure hunter: the resting place of Cleopatra VII, last pharaoh of Egypt. Hunters have sought it high and low, and many plundered pyramids have been claimed for it. The Romans never recovered her wealth, and it is believed to lie with her.

levels.name: The pool's regio
levels.enter: Open on the eve of the anniversary of Cleopatra's death, 12 August; at other times a Regio Sight roll against 23 (ArM5 p. 189).
levels.notes: Each year on that night hordes of asps with a small Faerie Might pour out to fight the mongooses. What lies within is left to the storyguide.

details.tomb_boons: Wealth (Resources, Major); Aura, Seclusion, Vivid Environment (Site, Minor); Edifice (Fortifications, Minor)
details.tomb_hooks: Regio (Site, Major); Crumbling (Fortifications, Minor); Guardians, Legendary Site (Surroundings, Minor); Dwindling Resources (Resources, Minor)
details.tomb_other: library 141, specialists 105, vis sources 70, vis stocks 9

tomb_curses.name: The Romans' Curse: boils
tomb_curses.condition: Anyone speaking Latin in the burial chamber
tomb_curses.excoriation: Boils that leave those who seek to disturb her hideous, but do no harm (Base 5, +1 Touch, +2 Room).

tomb_curses.name: The Romans' Curse: sickness
tomb_curses.condition: Anyone speaking Latin in the burial chamber
tomb_curses.excoriation: As the Fragile Constitution Flaw: a sickness no medicine helps.

tomb_curses.name: The Romans' Curse: no children
tomb_curses.condition: Anyone speaking Latin in the burial chamber
tomb_curses.excoriation: As He Shall Have No Successors.

tomb_curses.name: I Shall Cast the Fear of Myself into Him
tomb_curses.excoriation: Overwhelming dread of the tomb or its occupant; victims must flee at once. (Base 4, +1 Touch, +2 Sun, +2 Room.)
tomb_curses.condition: Anyone who breaks the clay seal on the treasure chamber

tomb_wards.name: The Shrouded Oasis
tomb_wards.effect: On the compound walls, as The Shrouded Glen (ArM5 p. 152). With Penetration 0 it only repels mundane hunters. A magus researching a breakthrough in enchanting Ritual effects can draw insight from it.

tomb_wards.name: First Statue of Sekhmet
tomb_wards.effect: As a Destroying Uraeus: bow drawn, it looses a fiery arrow a round at anyone in the temple.

tomb_wards.name: Second Statue of Sekhmet
tomb_wards.effect: As a Destroying Uraeus: bow drawn, it looses a fiery arrow a round at anyone in the temple.

tomb_wards.name: The Djet
tomb_wards.effect: A twenty-foot statue of Osiris in thirty fitted pieces of green stone: with burning incense in its hand it answers one question from each person, who must truly want the answer for himself. It knows only what some dead person knew, so nothing of the future, and answers at random otherwise. It lies scattered through the complex, one piece missing and unaccounted for; assembling it takes skill, and instructions are in hieroglyphs on the statue.

tomb_traps.name: The Soporific Corridor
tomb_traps.text: Two stone doors close off a stretch of corridor; opening them brings a faint floral smell and dust eddying in the light. All within must make the roll or sleep for as many minutes as they failed by, while immune mongooses swarm through ground-level holes to eat them: a Light Wound each, worse by a step every two minutes.

tomb_traps.name: The Covered Pit
tomb_traps.text: Before the burial chamber door: safe at first, but walking on it arms it, taking about a minute. Per + Awareness at +3 to the Ease Factor hears the arming; the roll leaps clear when cautious, harder for those fleeing the fear curse. Twelve feet deep with spikes: +12 from the fall, +8 from each of up to four spikes (simple die 1-2 none, 3-4 one, 5-6 two, 7-8 three, 9-10 four).

tomb_traps.name: The Sand of the Treasure Chamber
tomb_traps.text: Stepping on the threshold sends tons of sand from the roof, to bury the treasure; it can be outrun by those not yet inside.

neighbours.secrets:
It is no pyramid but a walled compound at Taposiris Magna, a lonely bay west of Alexandria, far from any trade route. A handful know the place, among them the jinniyya Nahrou, whose Might shielded her from the concealing enchantment (LotN p. 44).

The Garden: fifteen-foot walls with one great pylon gate, carved with Isis and with cows, cats, lionesses, vultures and hippopotamuses for the goddesses. Inside is a temple of Isis and a rich garden of food and medicinal herbs, dates, bananas and other fruit, feeding families of mongooses. Warping has made some of these Magic Animals, who rule the rival clans like royalty. The pool at the centre is the regio's entrance. The asps' bodies are vis, usually eaten quickly by the magical mongooses for Transformation.

The Temple: its roof rests on columns carved as four handmaidens, each face many times repeated. Walls hold spells of midwifery and healing in Koine Greek and Ancient Egyptian, some studied as texts on the Arts of Learned Magicians, though not quite the same Arts; Quality is what a 13th-century magician can draw from them. Two statues of Sekhmet, bows drawn, each loose a fiery arrow a round at anyone in the temple unless Cleopatra's name is intoned. Four priestess handmaidens died to guard her, and their ghosts haunt the place, sorceresses in healing, in destruction, in transformation and in control and enchantment.

The Tomb: an inclined passage from the temple levels off, with the soporific trap, then turns at the pit. The burial chamber, directly under the temple's statue of Isis, has a cursed door. The body lies under a net of pure gold, in a painted wooden coffin shaped like the queen, in a gold sarcophagus, in a stone sepulcher, ringed by four goddess statues with heads of vulture, lioness, crocodile and asp. A hidden way in the rear wall leads by a short corridor to a second, cursed door and the treasury of Ptolemaic Egypt: over ten thousand Mythic Pounds of gold, gems and ivory, a legendary source of income.

Library: later history of Roman Egypt, summa on Area Lore: Egypt, Koine Greek, Level 5, Quality 9. Medicinal herbs, tractatus on Medicine, Demotic, Quality 10. Healing spells, tractatus on the Learned Magician Form Salutem, Demotic, Quality 11. Magical wards, summa on the Learned Magician Technique Tueor, Demotic, Level 10, Quality 7. Eight formulae for pharmaceutical theriacs, Demotic, 5 BP each (Art & Academe p. 77). Creation myth, tractatus on Faerie Lore, Demotic, Quality 7. Handmaidens' diaries on crumbling papyrus: three tractatus on Charm, Etiquette and Intrigue, Koine Greek, Quality 5.

Specialists: four ghostly priestesses, each with the equivalent of one Hermetic Technique at 20; five mongoose monarchs, Leadership 5.

Vis sources, a year: 5 Animal (slain asps), 2 Aquam (the pool), 3 Herbam (exotic fruit), 1 Ignem (a potsherd exposed to a Destroying Uraeus), 3 Terram (an item worth at least 10 Mythic Pounds left a year in the treasure chamber). Vis stocks: 10 Creo (unguents, pastes, medicines), 5 Imaginem (cosmetics, perfumes), 30 Terram (gold objects in the treasure room).

neighbours.name: The Coptic Monks and Their Libraries
neighbours.summary:
Copts speak a descendant of the old Egyptian tongue, their priests a purer liturgical form. Most literate Copts can read Egyptian texts of the Ptolemies' time, in Greek letters, and scholars can read hieroglyphs, even in the oldest tombs. They seem to do little with this, because most scholars are monks.

The monasteries hold libraries of secret old knowledge. The monks can read the old spells but rarely use them: prayer is simpler, in the end stronger, and imperils no soul. They do not want to order gods about or dig for gold. Yet they hold powerful magic items, found when churches rise on old sites or given by believers; they are faithful and peaceful, but they have seen pogroms, and keep tricks for defence.

Egyptian magicians wonder what they want. They do not seem to use magic texts, so why collect them, and if the aim is safety, why not burn them? Many monasteries have Nilometers, for taxes they say, but their old religious role makes others suspicious.

details.offers: Spoken Coptic is easy to learn from the many Copts glad to teach it, in Mediterranean ports and on pilgrimage in the Holy Land, and some monks have written grammars for Arabic speakers. To read hieroglyphs one must find a skilled, probably ancient monk and persuade him to teach.

neighbours.secrets:
A few Copts practise Egyptian magic with saints or the Holy Family in the gods' places; these are Holy Magicians (Realms of Power: The Divine) (LotN p. 47).

They want to keep the writings of those who commanded spirits from undeserving hands (p. 56).

neighbours.name: Al-Quisir
neighbours.summary: The most famous Coptic monastery library near Cairo, on the Maqatam Mountain near Tura.

neighbours.name: Coptic Alchemists
neighbours.summary:
Whether the most studious monks or the sultan's personal alchemists are the world's best is disputed; each side names the other, citing the thousands of books the rival can reach.

Egyptian alchemy is practical and mechanical, grown from generations of magical medicine. Hermetic alchemy's goal of immortality makes no sense to these men: the faithful live for ever anyway, in greater bliss, so the Great Elixir is all but worthless to the devout.
neighbours.secrets: Hermetic magi may compare them to the Learned Magicians of Europe, who have one excellent book of Egyptian formulae. Medicines found in tombs can be designed as single-use Hermetic items (LotN pp. 47, 49). The Black calls on Coptic alchemists in its war with the Red (p. 57).

neighbours.name: The Sufis of the Enigma
neighbours.summary: A school of sufis in Egypt devoted to calligraphy and the beauty of the unread: they meditate on texts they cannot read, and find enlightenment in the attempt. They also study alchemy, only for substances that alter mood and body and so ease meditation and the channelling of the Divine.
neighbours.secrets: They hold the Wisdom from Ignorance Virtue (LotN p. 49; DE p. 116). The book gives this school no name; the record's name is descriptive.

neighbours.name: The Magical Treasures of the Ancient Egyptians
neighbours.summary:
So many ruins stand in Egypt, and grave robbing pays so well, that magic items of every kind turn up. Thousands of small ones are for sale at any time in the country's markets, to those who know whom to ask. Temples are so many and so various that a magus of 1220 could hardly exhaust them.

The ancients knew a force in all things and called it heka, which also meant a written spell. They found it in rare and strange things: resin for preserving, gold to hold it in amulets, iron, then scarce, for harming demons, and deformed things, which is why robbers find jars of pickled two-tailed lizards, and throw them away.

Most Egyptian religion was not about death. The Osirian hero cult, which built the great tombs, was an odd and exclusive thing even then: the oldest akhu claim kin with Osiris before his ascent, and only later were the richest nobles and merchants let in. Its artefacts survive best simply because they lay in graves.

The most common magicians were priests of small local spirits, much like the village witch or blacksmith of Christian Europe: not always Gifted, and of little power. Theirs is the only ancient Egyptian magic alive in 1220, renamed and aligned with Islam.
neighbours.secrets:
Heka is what Hermetic magi call vis (LotN p. 50). The tomb chapter assumes Magic-aligned practitioners; this one has Faerie-aligned priests served by Magic-aligned artisans. Use either as suits the story (p. 48). Troupes may let tombs give Guaranteed Insight into almost anything, or hold that Mercurian magic took in the Egyptian so fully that little new remains (p. 49). A parallel to nearly every magical tradition can be found in the ruins, even to troll-blooded magi, among the servants of old desert spirits (p. 47).

Local priests (p. 54): faerie-aided Murabits (see the Murabitin) may claim to venerate saints' bones but serve faeries of strong local stories. Design remnants with Virtues like Faerie Friend, as Faerie Doctors (Realms of Power: Faerie p. 118), Faerie Wizards in Weal (p. 129) or Faerie Bargainers in Bonding (p. 132). Their grave goods suit Mystery Quests; their ghosts may act as mystagogues, fading once they have saved their priesthood from extinction.
