neighbours.name: Books of the Lector Priests
neighbours.summary:
The lectors, or readers, performed the rites in the sacred books. Most knew few, for a god could be asked only certain things, at certain times, by people strictly prepared. Chief lectors were the librarians, keeping the books of rare and emergency rites; their title is the old word for any strong magician, and a ghost asked about magicians will mean them. The pharaoh, high priest of Egypt, appointed them. Each temple's book holds closely related effects, some just one.

Rites call for purity: shaving all hair, smoke bathing, natron mouthwash, gods drawn on the skin, new linen, abstinence; a space cleansed with incense, drawings or Nile water; things never used before, or dear reusable ones such as ivory wands and god-masks. Many spells are said four times. Some speak in code: the heart of a baboon is oil of lilies, Ethiopian soil is crocodile dung, the semen of Amun a kind of houseleek.
neighbours.secrets:
See the Lector Priests tradition. Usually Faerie Rite Wizards (Realms of Power: Faerie ch. 6), with Evocation p. 122, Grant p. 127, Weal p. 128, Ware p. 128 and Woe p. 130 popular, and always Ceremony (p. 115) (LotN p. 48).

Reading them (pp. 49-51). A magus usually cannot perform one; a character with the Faerie Method can make a Hermetic equivalent (Realms of Power: Faerie p. 121), so Merinita are sought. Ceremony must be followed exactly, perhaps Com + Leadership against 3 + 1 per follower. Then Com + Coptic against 3 + 1 per 5 levels, higher for symbolic language. A botch may misfire or bring a faerie's persecution.

Why rites fail: most need a powerful Faerie aura, as the god's presence was assumed; the Silencing of the Oracles voided foretelling; gods grow old and die; the rubric was left out as known to all; or no faerie nearby wants the role or notices.

Without Realms of Power: Faerie (p. 51): Range, Target and Duration are fixed. After preparation and the Com + Coptic roll, Casting total is Sta + closest Form + closest Technique + Aura + stress die, less spell level: 0 or more, cast, -1 Fatigue; -1 to -10, cast, -2; -11 to -20, cast, -3; -21 to -30, cast, -4 and a Warping point; -31 or less, not cast, -5, Warping equal to magnitude, and Twilight check if over 2. A book is a set of scrolls, one effect each, treated as casting tablets (Covenants).

Apparently unGifted: Egyptian accounts show no social effect of the Gift in lectors (p. 50); see the story of that name.

Those who threatened the gods (pp. 53-55): lectors, toward gods they did not serve, and rogues used a harsher Enchantment Rite, threatening to destroy the faerie and the world, usually with a faerie ally and a gate to Arcadia for escape. One such threat promises to turn the world over and drag up the afterlife: really a bargain offered to a second god, whose presence with the first weakens the world, touches Duat and allows Spiriting Away; Hermetic magi think the magician's unspoken wishes settle it. The Sun is said to have stood still for three days, beyond any but the Divine, so faeries faked or planted the memory. Their writings are scripts that Enchant; threat scripts that add a bonus to one Rite's casting total; and Initiation texts for Special Circumstances, Puissant Enchantment or Magical Focus.

neighbours.name: Transitory Magic Items
neighbours.summary:
Faerie-aligned magicians made things for a single use, not truly enchanted, often for one named user. Most temporary amulets are small painted linen bags of magic ingredients, medicinal or protecting against spirits, for childbirth or for fortune in war; skilled robbers can judge them by contents and writing. Many hold unclean things to scare spirits: preserved dog, dung, menstrual blood. Underworld demons live backward, mouths and anuses reversed; honey is bitter to them, and garlic drives them off by the sound of its name and the look of its cloves.

Popular amulets guarded against disease from the dead, demons or gods; spells of demons posing as foreign sorcerers; quarrying accidents; drowning and boat accidents; crocodiles; and death in battle.

Seals hold a spell until broken, touched, moved or lit. Some wizards carried ivory staves ending in hands, to touch things easily. Temporary potions were water or beer poured over a statue holding a faerie, above all the cippuses of Horus, or over words cut in a bowl.

The priests also trapped spirits in boxes, generally Apep's kin, who are said to get out, or the sun could not be reborn. Today's Muslim peasants dig up the boxes, and nearby faeries take the part of trapped djinn or efreets.

Some magicians made things from models. A magician-prince sailed up the Nile with a wax boat and crew; another left a wax crocodile with his steward, which dragged his wife's lover from a lake, and dragged him back from the afterlife for the pharaoh's questions, and away again.
neighbours.secrets:
Temporary amulets (LotN p. 51) are objects under a spell of the Until Duration, available only to Faerie Magicians, lasting until worn and discarded. Unlike modern ones they outlive their maker, perhaps being made by faeries, or mocked up just before their finders come.

Seals (p. 52) work much like Watching Wards. The ivory hands were talismans in some cults, a way to extend Touch in others, and in others a symbolic hand for the god.

Statues and potions (pp. 51-52): Merinita argue the statue is not magic. Water on a cippus is an open offer: a faerie that makes it medicine feeds on the family's fear and worship. If none takes it the sufferer gets water, and his death is blamed on hidden sin. Dying stories may be rekindled by dreams or a talking statue. Some bowls still work if faeries know the deal; others are only ceremonial casting at Touch and need a Gifted user.

Models (p. 54): grave goods still work when found: a faerie enters the model and aids the user, gaining vitality. With Realms of Power: Faerie, a faerie of the large form with a shapeshifting power; with core rules, an item with a shapeshifting effect.

Faeries in boxes (p. 55): they are no longer inside. Characters who know the old tales may tempt a faerie back into the role of Apep's servant. Use the animal-headed demons, or any dragon's statistics.

Unusual amulets (p. 54). Ib Scarab: made to let the dead lie to the gods at judgement, it replaces the heart, so works at Personal Range; lost, it is an Arcane Connection to its owner. Seals with royal names: a dead pharaoh's name has a little Magic Resistance, perhaps 5, so wearers hope curses that catch it are deflected. It protects only itself, so a curse that would drown a man through his boat's capsizing fails, while a scorpion's sting does not. Folk magicians know this. The royal ring is a shen, a rope laid in a protective circle; cartouche is a later word and unknown in Mythic Africa.

neighbours.name: Animated Statues
neighbours.summary:
Classical writers tell of Egypt's strange art of bringing temple statues to life. Two events destroyed most of them. The Romans, invading in 30 BC, knew they could banish gods by smashing images. Then when Christ fled to Egypt in 2 AD some writings say the earth shook and all the statues fell, though the Father of Dread plainly survived; perhaps only those then inhabited fell.

Others wore out with moving, for they do not heal; and healers could pass a person's injuries to a holy statue, moving the god to a new one when it was too hurt to hold him. When the art was lost, many old statues were spent that way.

Some priests consecrated statues for themselves, and in death took prayers to the gods in return for offerings. Guards and spies might be given statues likewise.
neighbours.secrets:
To secular magi, it means persuading a faerie to enter a statue and stay, feeding on those it touches and their worship; the statue is only matter it wears (LotN p. 52). Player characters can banish a faerie god by defacing its image. Ruined statues that held faeries often contain vis (p. 54).

Statue Consecration Mystery (pp. 52-53): lost to humans, but findable in an intact temple library, or from faeries. Great temples followed written steps; small sects were guided by a faerie. Such statues may attract demons seeking to replace the faerie, or Divine wrath. A few chief lectors made new rituals: a convincing narrative on which a faerie may feed, by Com + Folk Ken against 18. The texts are choreographies that aid the roll, as does a Faerie aura or rites by other priests.

Tongue magic (p. 52), in rare texts: The Drawing of Maat: a skilled portrait of the Goddess of Truth on the tongue stops the character lying or saying false words, and any weaker god must forgive mispronunciation. Whoever discovers it can make a tiny possessing faerie that corrects a magus's words, reducing botches, which may alter his personality.

Saliva and breath: spells work more easily on those spat or breathed on. Treat as Personal range but without circumventing Magic Resistance. People shielded themselves accordingly, and some faeries still use shared fluid or breath as Arcane Connections. It would ease some Spontaneous spells. Nobody bottled them to delay a spell.

neighbours.name: Magical Craftwork
neighbours.summary:
A caste of crafters served the temple priests, making amulets, which protect the wearer; talismans, which ease his life; and curses, which hurt another. Greek and Roman writers noted their skill, and it was a great export in Ptolemaic times. Robbers often recover their work, sold through the guild or the black market, and their writings can be read by those who know Coptic.

Colours matter. Black is the colour of magic, and green is widely used. Blue invokes gods. Yellow, orange and some reds are one colour to an Egyptian magician, and best for fire. Red is for evil: the names of Apep and Seth are always written in it, and spells to summon Seth's servants. Red stone amulets ward against them, and curses too are red.

The commonest amulet shape is a precious-metal copy of a linen bag. Others show a thing whose virtue the wearer borrows. Most bear the Wedjat eye, and many name Thoth, the Lord of Amulets.

The dead were thought to be like birds in some way, so people went to their graves with bird-snaring weapons against demons on the road: most often a throwing stick, and sometimes nets.
neighbours.secrets:
One Egyptian craft book, circulated in Europe, created the Learned Magician tradition (Hedge Magic: Revised Edition). Its protection, assistance and harm Techniques and Luck, Magic and Health Forms simulate much Egyptian work, but priesthoods had other Arts. Egyptian magic had no fixed Ranges, Targets and Durations and no Difficult Arts, relics of that single book. Spirit aid from the four realms came more easily. Assume very high casting and laboratory totals. Without that book, design amulets as Hermetic items (LotN p. 55).

Grave weapons: the throwing stick has an effect like Faerie's Eternal Oblivion; nets have ReVi effects that hold demons, so victims may flee or stab them.

neighbours.name: Contained Spirits
neighbours.summary: The most lasting relics of those who commanded spirits, wizards scarcer and stronger than the Keepers of the Books, who used their standing with mighty faeries to bully lesser spirits. They left creatures shut in mystic containers, able to speak with whoever holds them. A bargain with one binds, but only as to the words. Most are found in tombs, though in old times most were buried in sacred precincts, for the gods to watch.
neighbours.secrets:
Their magic resembles spirit masters', and they are an ancestral tradition of the sihr (The Cradle and the Crescent; a Hermetic variant in Houses of Hermes: Societates). Their writings, using the Magic Realm, suit Hermetic adaptation best: Insight and Mystery Initiations, prized by sahirs too (LotN p. 56).

A grateful spirit may forgo harm, and can be made a permanent ally by favours like Ordeals (The Mysteries), without Occult Lore. Most resent it. For a faerie, some magi advise instant, unconditional freedom: a gift many must repay with one worth as much, though the gift may cause trouble. A magical creature need give nothing, and may attack.

True names: Egyptians were casual with them. Tombs list the ka names of owner and servants, so that a dead man need not call his table-steward like a lost dog; a true name is also called a ka name or ren. Shabtis answered the owner's name for him, avoiding labour and turning aside curses laid through it.

neighbours.name: The Book of Thoth
neighbours.summary: All authorities agree the mightiest magicians of Egyptian folklore are the few who read the Book of Thoth, which holds every spell of the first great magician.
neighbours.secrets: Any character who finds it may read it, and can then cast almost any Hermetic spell's equivalent without effort. Within one day he dies or fades into Twilight; he cannot stay. The Book is then hidden again by forces reaching from deep in the Magic Realm (LotN p. 56).

neighbours.name: The Treasure of Qarun
neighbours.summary: Young seekers chase Qarun's lost treasure house, and the keys' place is written somewhere in the guild's library.
neighbours.secrets: See the place for what is printed (LotN p. 25).

neighbours.name: The Ramaseum
neighbours.summary: Colossal images of Rameses II may be statues that his ghost, for all their size, can animate.
neighbours.secrets: See the place; other proud pharaohs may do likewise (LotN p. 31).

neighbours.name: Following the Dead
neighbours.summary: Ghosts ride between the Nile bank and a hidden valley near Alexandria.
neighbours.secrets: Second Sight may let characters follow them home; see the place (LotN p. 31).

neighbours.name: The Search for Imhotep's Tomb
neighbours.summary: Hermetic wizards want this tomb, arguably the first of the Egyptian kind, to end the dispute over ancient and modern magic.
neighbours.secrets: See the place (LotN pp. 37-39).

neighbours.name: The Search for Antonius's Tomb
neighbours.summary: Hermetic wizards want this tomb, arguably the last of the Egyptian kind, for Cleopatra's Book and the lost libraries.
neighbours.secrets: See the place, and Cleopatra (LotN pp. 37-40).

neighbours.name: Conman
neighbours.summary: A rich man begs the covenant's help. A poor acquaintance showed him gold amulets from a find, took much money for supplies and labourers against half the treasure, and vanished.
neighbours.secrets: He is too embarrassed to go to the authorities. Having social standing, he might become an ally, pawn or front man (LotN p. 25).

neighbours.name: The Destructive Jest
neighbours.summary: A forged old document says a treasure lies under the covenant. Gangs creep in to dig the cellars, neighbours tunnel, mobs storm the gates, and passers-by strike the walls with picks, hoping for a hollow.
neighbours.secrets: An enemy forged it. The trick is old and famous among the ruling class, so its author is hard to trace; the characters may hunt the forger (LotN p. 25).

neighbours.name: Government Agent
neighbours.summary: A government clerk must attend any digging for treasure. One who has angered a nobleman is sent with the characters to a tomb known to be deadly.
neighbours.secrets: He is terrified and unskilled; they must keep him alive (LotN p. 25).

neighbours.name: Monastery or Mosque
neighbours.summary: An old scroll gives the place of a temple listed nowhere else, and so likely undisturbed; but a monastery or mosque has been built over it.
neighbours.secrets: Either its keepers welcome the characters, wanting the temple's troublesome beings destroyed; or they ban them, and the characters must sneak in, tunnel from nearby, or discredit the keeper for a more pliable one (LotN p. 25).

neighbours.name: Naqeeb Al-Matalibeen
neighbours.summary: Famous adventurers are useful to any candidate for chairman of the Seekers' Guild. Elections are usually civil, but sometimes rivals thin the field by assassination, with strange poisons, old magic items and death-traps.
neighbours.secrets: A player character who wins commands all the guild's resources, if he can keep the emir ignorant. A covenant secretly ruling the guild is a saga seed (LotN p. 25).

neighbours.name: Roman Notes
neighbours.summary: Many Egyptians believe the Romans hid treasure as they withdrew, noted the caches, and took Coptic, Greek and Chaldean treasure books to the cathedral of Constantinople. Crusaders sacked it in 1204, and most Arabs who know this think the Franks now hold the notes.
neighbours.secrets: Common folk might aid the new owners for a share; officials want to steal the books for the realm and for the thief's own safety. Characters who make gold by magic may be taken for the keepers, winning peasants and merchants but offending nobles (LotN p. 25).

neighbours.name: Medallion Removal
neighbours.summary: Many graveyard statues wear medallions showing a decapitator among bound, beheaded victims, and the same design seals tomb doors.
neighbours.secrets: Without these seals the decapitators hardly attack; near them, night is far deadlier. A robber may come by day, when they are less active, to remove or deface them unseen by the human watchers (LotN p. 28).

neighbours.name: The Mut for the Archmage
neighbours.summary: An archmage who will not leave his concerns in Italy offers to pay anyone who can capture a mut.
neighbours.secrets: He may lend a mirror that captures ghosts to those who cannot make such a spell or item. He thinks the Faerie and Magic realms had not yet parted when the mut were made. How will they know a mut from a recent ghost or faerie impostor? (LotN p. 29.)

neighbours.name: The Colour of Ghosts
neighbours.summary: Necromancers may notice the mut are never black like the ghosts of Greek and Roman sources, nor white like those of Mythic Europe.
neighbours.secrets: House Criamon says the shift came when the Axis Magica moved to the Cave of Twisting Shadows, and notes the ghosts older than Criamon there are all black. If so, what cataclysm drained the colour from the Classical world's ghosts? An ancient sorcerer's mut may know (LotN p. 29).

neighbours.name: Apparently UnGifted Magicians
neighbours.summary: The mightiest Faerie Wizards are always Gifted, yet Egyptian accounts show no social effect of the Gift among lectors, only among followers of dark gods.
neighbours.secrets:
Possible reasons (LotN p. 50). Faeries Stripped of Volition: the Egyptians may have made their gods machines, so a priest was anyone in the right robe; some may still be stuck in statues. Engineered Emotions: the right attention in a heightened state might win a mystical effect; such ecstatic cults were known, and forbidden darker rites called up things beyond Duat, dark faeries or demons, for anyone who repeats them.

A Source for the Gentle Gift: a Mystery Initiation may have given it to pharaonic priests; the ghosts of priests or the site could allow self-Initiation, and Jerbiton and Mercere might back it. If it spreads, offer a new Virtue to those who already took it. A Caste of Servants: true wizards may have cast through mortal proxies, whose symbols of office allow casting at a distance. Mystery Initiations: priests may have earned powers by Ordeals, known to faeries, the dead or old inscriptions.

neighbours.name: The Coptic Saga Arc
neighbours.summary: The monks gather magic texts and terrible weapons and keep Nilometers, and nobody knows why.

stages.title: Serving the Black
stages.clues: Monks give quests, rest under the Dominion, healing or training to characters who aid the Black.

stages.title: The Relics of Saint Simon
stages.clues: The characters carry the relics of Saint Simon the Shoemaker, famed for miraculously moving a mountain, to the Red's stronghold, a mountain in the heart of the Sahara.
stages.stopped: They move the Red's home to the depths of the sea, swinging the war decisively toward the Black.

neighbours.secrets: In this arc the Copts are allies of the Black, using their powers and items against servants of the Red (LotN p. 49).

neighbours.name: Egypt
neighbours.summary:
An old land whose great cities are young: Cairo, Damietta and Qus have held their present size and standing for only a few decades. Ancient landmarks stand among new suburbs, and a nobleman of today may have been a street thief or hired sword in his youth.

Most Egyptians live along the Nile and live by farming it. Under the iqta' the sultan parcels out his land by contract to powerful supporters, who owe him soldiers and taxes for the right to its produce. The grants are not hereditary, so that no noble can build a regional power: the whole class of landholders (muqta's) used to be moved on a timetable, until the rich threatened revolt, and now a family moves when its head dies. Each year after the flood a muqta's servant visits every village, measures how high the water came, grades the land, and gives out fields by witnessed written contract, usually with a loan of seed, tools or money and a stated return at harvest. Most contracts go to settled farmers; itinerant ones get land the flood does not usually reach, or work a new crop such as sugar cane. Village headmen answer for the contracts. The nobles move and the farmers have no tie to one piece of land, so a European covenant's familiar tricks, such as a tame nobleman, serve poorly here (pp. 69-70).

The farming year, in European months (p. 70). September: quince, winter grapes and dates picked, citrus begins, balsam tapped, canals opened, loan seed given out. October: rice harvested, trefoil and turnips planted, myrtle and nenuphar pressed for oil, the Nile at its height. November: wallflower, violet, narcissus and horseradish harvested, flax fields drained and sown. December: second-year cane cut and pressed, with narcissus, carrots, citrus, green broad beans and white leeks; trefoil sown. January: young cane cut, trees moved, cane waterwheels set up, fields weeded and ploughed, dykes breached. February: almonds, grapes, lotus fruit and turnips harvested, more ploughing, summer crops planted. March: broad beans, lentils and flax bought, African ships sail for the Mediterranean ports, summer crops tended, cane planted in long-fallow fields. April: broad beans, barley, cereals, cucumbers and roses harvested, flax seed threshed. May: balsam, sesame and rice sown, crops threshed. June: figs, peaches, pears, prunes, mulberries, dates and sour grapes harvested, flax soaked, indigo planted (ready in a hundred days), honey gathered; on the 18th the Festival of Saint Michael, when the Nile begins to rise. July: flax drained and dried. August: unripe dates harvested.

Trade from every quarter brings new crops, which are quickly taken up. Summer crops: cabbage, caraway, cotton, cumin, eggplant, green beans, indigo, lettuce, melons, Nile sesame, onion, radishes, sesame, sugar cane, taro and turnips. Winter crops: barley, broad beans, chickpeas, flax, garlic, grass peas, lentils, lupine, onions, trefoil and wheat.

Sugar cane is new here and still rare. It needs long-fallow land and great quantities of water and is hard to press, but Europeans pay fortunes for it, treating it as a spice, and if history holds it will spread across parts of the south (p. 69).

Auras (p. 57). Dominion: up to 10 at the holiest places and pilgrim sites; usually 4 at places of worship, 3 at the cemeteries and homes of People of the Book, 2 where monotheists work, and 1 where the call to prayer carries. Faerie: the Might of the area's strongest faerie divided by 5, or higher where two contest it; that faerie need not be the strongest the characters meet. Magic: at awesome natural places and tethered to human works, many old tombs among them (Tomb Creation, chapter 4). Infernal: usually small pockets the Dominion wears away, but places given over to sin can hold strong and seemingly permanent ones, such as the old customs house at 'Aydhab.

neighbours.name: The Nile
neighbours.summary:
Mythic Earth's greatest river. It rises in the Atlas, runs south through the desert to the edge of the habitable world, turns east through the lands of the Plinian races, and turns north again near Africa's east coast, through the lands of gold and black men. It floods Egypt yearly, leaving soil of almost magical fertility, and falls into the Mediterranean.

Even small European creeks may have elementals; the Nile's spirit is so vast it must make avatars or invest emissaries for people to understand it at all. The Copts call it Kheme, the Black, their word also for the colour and for Egypt. Elsewhere it is called the Hope. It is not Isis, the river's faerie goddess, though she perhaps served it and fed on its vitality. The Blemmyae of Philae, once her worshippers, often act for it; in the west of Africa a tribe of seven-headed rain serpents serves it, their shape perhaps mirroring its seven-mouthed delta; in Egypt it calls up horus-beasts, the ascended dead, Coptic alchemists, jinn and faeries for its endless war with the Red.

The Red, the Great Hunger, is desiccation and sterility, strongest at the heart of the Sahara; the Nile's encircling arm keeps its appetite from eating Africa. Its servants, detailed in Between Sand and Sea, include hedge magi fed by the decay of the land, set beasts, tribes of werehyenas and great afrits of smokeless flame. Some say every lie adds a grain to the Sahara and every liar serves the Red; others that no one who would escape the Black's notice should ever drink its water.

The Seven Heads (p. 57). Pliny lists seven mouths, not all of which can be found in 1220: some are silted, some are not where he says. The main one is the Phatmetic Mouth at Damietta, in the eastern Delta, for decades Egypt's chief port for Nile trade. The Delta itself is called so after Herodotus, for the letter it resembles on some maps; the Copts call it Ta-Mehu, Land of the Papyrus, a name close to the Field of Reeds in Duat (chapter 4), and many gates to Faerie and the Magic Realm are hidden there (p. 58).
neighbours.secrets: The Black has withdrawn some of the silted or missing mouths from the mortal world; others are coiled back as reflections of wounds taken from the Red. One, the Pelusiac Mouth, it has hidden as a safe base for its servants.

neighbours.name: Ayyubid Sultan of Egypt
neighbours.summary:
Al-Kamil, vizier of Egypt until the old sultan died soon after the crusaders landed in 1218, and sultan since. He wants the Crusade out of Egypt so that he can settle his hold on his own lands, and has twice offered Jerusalem to be rid of it (see The Fifth Crusade). After Damietta fell he drew back twenty miles south to Mansourah, and through the winter of 1219 he has thrown up defences there and waited for an assault that has not yet come.

So long as the Nile is high the sultan's ability to pay for things seems all but magical: the House, the Maristans, the tombs of Qarafah and Alexandria's mosques and bread all rest on it. He is legally entitled to his land taxes and tributes in any year the flood reaches full water. It failed in 1219, and with it his money (pp. 61, 66). Some suspect old Nile magic behind that purse; the Coptic monks say a failed harvest is explanation enough.

neighbours.name: The Mamluks
neighbours.summary: Slave soldiers. Copts may not carry arms, which the rulers enforce hard: a hadith calls Egyptians the finest soldiers in the world, and if that means a natural gift for war, an Egyptian peasant mob is far more dangerous than rebels elsewhere. Coptic revolts have been put down only with difficulty, so the sultans take Egyptian children from their Christian parents and raise them as Muslims and as slave soldiers (p. 59).

neighbours.name: The Hirranian Sabeans
neighbours.summary:
A people the sultan treats as People of the Book, perhaps through confusion with the Sabians. They say the great statue at Gizeh shows the god Horon and is the tomb of one of the three great scholars called Hermes, whom they equate with the Prophet Idris (Enoch). They bury their dead in urns around it and sacrifice white roosters to it (p. 64).

They claim to be Sabeans, and so People of the Book, with communities across Egypt and a fire religion much like the Zoroastrians'. They stand out in Cairo, for they venerate the Keeper of the Dead at Giza (p. 13).

neighbours.name: The Coptic Church
neighbours.summary:
Egypt's Christians fare better than those in most Muslim lands. Egypt surrendered rather than falling by force, making the Copts dhimmi and limiting what a ruler may lawfully take; hadiths call them the Muslims' instruments and help; Ismail's mother and one of the Prophet's wives were Copts; and the Fatimids were largely tolerant, as the present dynasty has been. Alexandrian Copts pay no tax but a compulsory charity for the poor. New churches, forbidden elsewhere, are often built, the jurists reasoning that they merely continue old ones. Copts may not ride, but here they often do, dismounting past the houses of Muslim nobles and legal officers. They remain third in standing, behind Muslims and new converts, and may not bear arms (pp. 58-59).

The Coptic Patriarch of Alexandria leads them in a moral sense. Since the capital moved it has suited him to live in Old Cairo rather than in his official see. He counts himself custodian of all Africa's Christians, but distance leaves the Churches in communion with him very independent, and a Greek rival for the See of Mark still lives in Alexandria. The finest alchemists in Egypt, the sultan's household perhaps excepted, are Coptic monks, and a suspicious number of old monks keep nilometers (pp. 59-60).

The see has been empty since 1216: one priest, Cyril ibn Laqlaq, has so much wealth and influence that no one else can be elected, and a core of opponents will not have him (p. 58). If this Mythic Europe follows history he will be ordained Cyril III in 1235, a notorious simoniac. The lack of a head weakens the Copts.

neighbours.name: Cairo
neighbours.summary:
The capital of Egypt for just over fifty years, a new and wonderful city that pilgrims from everywhere praise. Many locals call it Misr, the Arabic name for all Egypt, held to be the name of a son of Noah who was the land's first king after the Flood and whose sons founded its great cities.

Under Saladin and his first successors Fustat and Cairo were ringed by one wall, which is still being built by countless Christian slaves, Byzantines for choice, since Egyptians think them the best builders alive (p. 60).

Plot hook, printed without a name just before the Mosque of Ibn Tulun: one Cairo mosque stands where Moses duelled Pharaoh's magicians. See Ancient Works of Magic or Trickery?

neighbours.name: Coptic Cairo
neighbours.summary: The older quarter around Babylon Fortress, home to a large and prosperous Coptic community and, for convenience since the capital moved, to the Patriarch of Alexandria (pp. 58-59).

neighbours.name: Babylon Fortress
neighbours.summary: A Roman strongpoint in Old Cairo. From here, it can be argued, the Empire left Egypt and handed the land and the Copts into Islam's keeping (p. 59).

neighbours.name: The Hanging Church
neighbours.summary: The Patriarch of Alexandria's cathedral, set above the gatehouse of Babylon Fortress (p. 59).

neighbours.name: Fustat
neighbours.summary:
Egypt's capital until 1168, and one of Mythic Africa's largest and richest cities. The vizier Shawar had kept Syria and the Christians at bay by setting them against each other, but when Amalric of Jerusalem invaded he ordered Fustat emptied and burned, so that it could not serve as the invaders' base. His men spent 20,000 naphtha pots and 10,000 lighting bombs on it. The invasion stalled, and the Syrians then swept in and took Egypt for themselves (pp. 59-60).

The citizens could not carry away their goods. Many nobles buried their wealth, or stayed and died in the fire. The hoards still turn up for treasure hunters, and faeries and demons use them to tempt and reward people. The single wall has made Fustat part of the capital, but it was never properly rebuilt: it is where noxious trades are carried on and waste is dumped (p. 60).

Naphtha pots (p. 59). A pot is a ceramic grenade of petroleum held in gel. An incendiary pot is a thrown weapon: thick gel burns for minutes at +10 to what it touches; runnier fuel spreads a pool at +5 to everything flammable; plain liquid makes a one-round fireball, +5 less 1 per pace from the pot. An explosive pot does +10 on a hit, less 1 per foot, mostly by burning, and is often shaped for siege engines. A lighting bomb is a pot used as a fuse or to fire thatch, crops and furniture. A poison pot gives off toxic smoke and bursts only when it hits, good for sabotage and assassination, and handy against tomb spirits that incense repels. Veteran Egyptians do not panic at naphtha; untrained troops, foreign mercenaries and horses may break, and a Brave roll against 5 stands firm. Metal jackets and fierce blasts are beyond a bazaar alchemist, and are special items in stories.

Naphtha by magic (p. 59): a processed natural liquid, so Creo Aquam base 3, the Base Individual a pool a foot across and six inches deep (about a gallon and a half) whatever the viscosity. Made outside a container it lights at once.

neighbours.name: The Maristans
neighbours.summary:
The Cairo Hospital, among the world's finest, a place of treatment, research and teaching to which students come from far away. A royal palace given to the sick as charity houses it; the palace opposite became the women's hospital, and a third building was raised for the insane (p. 60).

It is a fine place to recover after hard events: besides its cures it has bath-houses, an excellent library and free lectures through which patients can improve their Medicine. Alchemists in the sultan's pay give out basic remedies and pass patients on to specialists.
neighbours.ruler: The sultan, who pays for them

neighbours.name: Mosque of Ibn Tulun
neighbours.summary: Cairo's oldest mosque and among its finest, built as a private mosque beside the palace of the governor Ibn Tulun. His capital, Al-Qatta'i, has been razed, and only this stands while later capitals grew round it. Over four tons of gold from one excavation are said to have paid for it. It is kept, on a subsidy from the sultan, for the free use of students and travellers from the Maghreb (p. 60).

neighbours.name: The Nilometer of Cairo
neighbours.summary:
A white octagonal marble column in a square well near the city, marked in 22 cubits called fingers: the legally official measure of the flood, though many keep their own. So many old Coptic monks keep nilometers that those who think they hold on to ancient magic call them ritual objects; the monks gently mock the idea.

At 16 cubits, 'full water', a festival begins and runs for several days; people are doused with Nile water for luck, a pharaonic custom oddly like Europe's Feast of Fools. The usual height is 17. Short of full water, perhaps one year in twenty, the sultan's purse begins to fail, and sometimes the flood fails for years on end, with famine in which, as ibn-Jabyr has it, God is the only hope (pp. 60-61).

neighbours.name: Saladin's Citadel
neighbours.summary:
The strong point at the centre of Saladin's wall round Old and New Cairo. Unfinished in 1220, it has been the seat of government for decades, and the bureaucracy keeps gathering into it. The sultan lives here (p. 64).

His library is among his countless treasures. Its last great census, under the Fatimids, counted 600,000 books, 18,000 of them on magic, astrology and alchemy.

neighbours.name: The House
neighbours.summary:
A school, said to lie in the citadel's grounds, that prepares agents for the sultan's service. It seems to take few students, perhaps twelve at a time, and no one outside is sure what they learn. Egypt's finest smith is trained here and kept on to teach his successor; so is an alchemist, though some Coptic monks might contest his claim to be the greatest; so are diplomats and, it is rumoured, assassins. Some think the teaching changes with the troubles the sultan's advisers foresee (p. 61). It is in effect a machine for intense teaching, which also trains specialists in how to teach.

Teacher of the House (Mystery Initiation path, p. 61). The mystagogue needs Lore of the House, an Organization Lore; its Ability also covers the House's history, students, missions and resources. Gifted initiates may have faster paths; most use these. Good Teacher: Presence + Lore of the House 6, a ritual Ordeal with items from the ancient House, the Flaw of loyalty; script +9 for the total of 15. Affinity with Teaching: Presence + Lore 8; a pilgrimage to find a great and charismatic teacher and a hard task spreading his message; script +7 (place and time +3, quest +3, loss of time +1). Improved or Great Communication: Presence + Lore 8; a rite at an ancient library invoking the goddess Seshat, whom the initiate must persuade with Communication + Charm against 12. Failure means being Spirited Away to keep her library in Faerie until the next solar eclipse in Egypt, which astrologers can foretell. Success, or escape, gives 3 Characteristic points for Communication, or the Great Characteristic Virtue if it is already 3; script +7. Errata p. 14: this path is for the unGifted, who must take an Ordeal at every Initiation, yet two of these have none; the errata leave it to the troupe.

Its pupils and agents take the Virtues Child of the House and Agent of the Sultan (p. 61).

details.rules: Teachers take a Major Personality Flaw of loyalty to the House's goals, which is not loyalty to the sultan or to its present head. Children of the House take the Code of Honor Major Flaw.
details.offers: Intense teaching, and agents for the sultan's service.

neighbours.secrets: Some suggest the House's leaders have undergone, or at least know, further Initiations meant for the priesthood they descend from.

neighbours.name: Tombs of Qarafah
neighbours.summary: A wide cemetery of the tombs of the Prophet's relatives and companions, with four great congregational mosques and many smaller mosques and theological colleges. The poor, scholars and travellers are welcome in the smaller mosques, and the sultan spends a couple of thousand dinars a month on upkeep and on keeping many of the residents, which pilgrims think a marvel. Magi count as scholars or travellers, and can live here at his expense if they like (p. 64).

neighbours.name: The Gizeh Necropolis
neighbours.summary:
Three great pyramids and a colossal lion with a man's head, a day's travel south of Cairo. Most Egyptians take little interest in the mastabas and pyramids here, thinking the plateau unusually dangerous even for a necropolis, and haunted, above all by night (pp. 62, 64).

Beliefs differ widely. Aristotle lies under one pyramid; the largest was made for Alexander, who was buried in secret elsewhere; a pharaoh raised them to save his people's wisdom from Noah's Flood; Allah, or a false god such as Hermes, made them by miracle. Saladin's son tried to pull down the pyramid nearest the statue, and it still shows the damage: he believed, as most do, that treasure lies everywhere, even where others have already taken it.

Herodotus and Manetho, widely read in Egypt, give each pyramid its own occupant. Cheops closed the temples, set all Egypt to work for ten years, and when money ran short prostituted his daughter; his brother Chephren ruled the same way. Cheops's son Mykerinos reopened the temples, judged fairly, and let people go home to their trades. As Egypt had been cursed to 150 years of suffering he was working against the gods, who took his only child and cut his life short. Told he had six years left, he set about making magical items to slow time (p. 62).

On the highest ground stand statues of marble crocodiles that keep real crocodiles out of their sight, guarding three miles of river either way. Some say the Third Hermes himself made them. No Hermetic magus has assessed them in a laboratory, so what exactly they do is unknown (p. 62).

Pilgrims widely report that the plateau's sand, the Sand of Hermes, raises Intelligence if carried as a talisman (p. 62).

Of all the guardians of the great necropolises the most powerful is Gizeh's, the Father of Dread: the great effigy of Harmarchis, Horus at Dawn, which Greek scholars call the Sphinx. It faces the opposite way from the one Herodotus reports, and nobody recalls when it turned or why (p. 28).

Between its forepaws lies a small Divine aura, from when Mary laid the infant Christ in the shade there while they rested (p. 28).

Abu 'l-Ahwa, the Father of Dread, is the colossal lion with a man's head. The Greeks call it the strangler, or sphinx, after the winged female monster of the Theban Tribunal that strangled those who failed its riddle. Some think it a solar god. It appeared to Menkheperure (Thutmose IV) to ask that its statue be dug from the sand, according to a stela said to stand between its paws. Some call it the grave of the Prophet Idris, or of Thoth, or both. If it were dug out and rites could again be held between its paws, answers might come (p. 62).
neighbours.secrets:
The plateau's greatest guardian is the Lady of the Tombs. Alexander of Jerbiton's few accounts suggest a potent faerie once worshipped as Isis, changed as her story has changed. She can call every faerie in the area and, worst of all, rouse a faerie variant of the Father of Dread (p. 62).

The effect of the sand may be faeries using Grant Virtue to give scholars at the tombs Improved Characteristics. They take the gift back when a scholar stops studying the ruins, so that the weak can be led to spend their lives on one confected tomb after another, feeding the faeries' need for attention.

Some say Mykerinos succeeded: his lamps make a room-sized Faerie regio where time runs slower. No one knows where they are.

The Divine aura between its forepaws may be what has locked the Father of Dread in place: it no longer gives predictions or warns of grave worldly events, but it protects the tombs in a subtler way, drawing trespassers into Faerie (LotN p. 28). The aura's strength is not printed.

neighbours.name: The Tomb of Aristotle
neighbours.summary: A pilgrimage site for scholars from across what remains of Alexander's empire. Only about a third of Aristotle's known works reach Mythic Europe, and those seem to be mostly esoterica: private musings, lecture notes and letters rather than the exoteric books meant for publication. Copies of the missing books may have been buried with him, and it is tempting to dig into the side of the pyramid; fear of its defences has so far been stronger (p. 62).
neighbours.secrets: A complete recovered set gives great Insight across many projects and rescales many Abilities: all readers gain +3 on all Artes Liberales rolls, and others as the books' subjects dictate. Incomplete sets still give Insight, and serve as books of very high level in their Abilities.

neighbours.name: The Isle of Gold at Gizeh
neighbours.summary: God sank the throne of the pharaoh who abused Moses deep in the Nile. It is still there, showing in famine years when the river runs low, and oddly no one has ever tried to raise it (p. 62).

neighbours.name: Alexandria
neighbours.summary:
An ancient city long faded and now reviving. Since Rome's rule ended its wealth and prestige have drained to Fustat and Cairo. Walls rebuilt in the ninth century took in only about half the old city, and it went on shrinking until Saladin refortified it in 1181 and founded new suburbs east and south of the walls (p. 65).

The loss of Damietta last year has made it the court's chief port and the sultan's main fleet base. Pilgrims avoiding Christian pillage land here and cross to the Nile, and it does not link directly to the river, so it is the less handy port despite its fine harbour (pp. 57, 65). The city is full of money and of the sharp, ambitious and well connected.

Its people pay nothing but the awqaf, a small poll tax, and yet the sultan pours riches through it. Between 8,000 and 12,000 mosques are said to stand here, more than in any city on earth, each with an imam on a 5 dinar stipend. Saladin's custom gives away 2,000 loaves a day: those who crossed the desert must take bread, even carrying their weight in gold, and many pass it on to the poor. While the Nile is high and he is rich, unlikely things happen in the sultan's name; a storyguide who needs a reason for almost any practice can say he pays for it (p. 65).

Alexandrians are as busy by night as by day. The port unloads without stopping, those who feed the workers keep late hours, and so do their suppliers, until the city barely slows down (p. 63).

It is one of the easier places for outsiders to reach, open to Iberian and North African pilgrims and to French and Italian traders, and so a good place to hire eastern-speaking servants and learn the roads east. Rich people of classical education wander its ruins with Diodorus or Arrian in hand and a guide at their elbow; the Jerbiton Itinerarium does not usually come this far south, but a skilled Jerbiton might bring apprentices (p. 63).
neighbours.secrets: No one has noticed that the city's nights make no economic sense. Lamp oil is why other ports sleep, and there is no satisfactory explanation for the cheap oil here. Pilgrims think it one of the sultan's bounties; his servants assume nearby farms make it cheaply, and do not look, since a tax-free city could grow diamonds on trees for all the law cares. Across the Mediterranean the Quaesitores would be looking for a magus making it with Creo. If a covenant settles in Alexandria they will ask for a full investigation, and if unsatisfied send Quaesitores and hoplites, a plain message that Hermetic law now reaches North Africa (p. 63).

neighbours.name: The Pharos of Alexandria
neighbours.summary:
The Lighthouse, one of the remaining wonders of the world, much damaged and rebuilt, its tower now short and capped with a mosque. Some magi claim a strong aura over the whole island; others say they tested and found none (p. 63).

Its mirror of Serican iron has long been gone. A man staring into it could pick out ships hours before the naked eye; by night its fire showed for miles; in war it could burn ships in the harbour. A Byzantine spy spread tales of treasure in the Pharos, stole the mirror in the riot that followed and, unable to destroy it, had it thrown in the sea. Some magi guess that a potent spirit of artifice defends it.

An inscription to the architect appeared on the side of the tower only centuries after his death: the masons had carved a flattering dedication to the king in thin lime plaster over it, which cracked away.

neighbours.name: The Library of Alexander
neighbours.summary: Burned by so many hands that the tales conflict, but many local tales agree part of it survived. Egyptians remember Cleopatra not as Rome's seductress but as a scholar and alchemist who took wise precautions when her kingdom was threatened, and many think her unfound grave may lead to a secret store of its books. Others say the land it stood on slid into the sea, and since Egyptians write by carving stone, magi with suitable spells might read any walls still standing on the seabed (p. 63).

neighbours.name: Damietta
neighbours.summary:
A port in ancient times that lost its trade to Alexandria, kept some standing as an Arab naval base, and rose again as Fustat grew, until by the thirteenth century it was the Nile's chief port (p. 65). Water and a stout chain across the navigable channel, running from the walls to a small island tower, guarded its approaches.

Of the 80,000 inside when the siege began in February 1219 only 3,000 were alive when it fell that November, and only 100 of those healthy (p. 66). The looted city came to the Christians with its defences whole, and the crusaders hold the sea.

In January 1220 the victors are falling apart. John of Brienne assumed it would join the Kingdom of Jerusalem; Pelagius says not, without saying whose it is, and has somehow offended both crusading orders, who now back John. Crusaders go about in squads of countrymen for safety, and in the last month some have fought to the death in the streets. The Italians pushed to force all Frenchmen out; the orders, who had stayed above what they took for a squabble over booty, routed the Italians (p. 67).

neighbours.name: Mansourah
neighbours.summary: A military city that has grown up twenty miles south of Damietta behind a tributary of the Nile, where al-Kamil has retired with his demoralised army. If it and the army fall, nothing stands between the crusaders and Cairo (pp. 66-67).

neighbours.name: The Papal Legate
neighbours.summary: Cardinal Pelagius, the Pope's representative, de facto leader of the Fifth Crusade since he took the credit for the sack of the Egyptian camp in 1219. He is no noble and has little experience of command in the field. He has twice turned down al-Kamil's offers, is waiting for Frederick II, and was raised up in part by a prophecy found in Damietta (pp. 65-67).

neighbours.name: The Fifth Crusade
neighbours.summary:
After the Fourth Crusade's disaster Innocent III preached a new armed pilgrimage led by the Church, not by kings, who were asked to come but control nothing. They were cool, and crusades against the Cathars and the Moors were nearer and looked richer. Honorius III at last mustered an army of mostly lesser nobles, with a fleet from Frisia. It gathered in Italy in 1217, the fleet was late, and in 1218 part of it landed at Acre. Told Jerusalem could not be held while Egypt stood, the crusaders sailed again and landed near Damietta, to take it as a base against Cairo. Some history-minded troupes start a few years before 1220 to play this through (pp. 64-65).

A relief force under al-Kamil, then vizier, held them on the defensive for six months to February 1219; the old sultan died soon after the landing and al-Kamil took his place. The Christians beat the relief force only through a strange chance (The Defeat of the Kurds), and the sack of its camp made Pelagius the real leader. Al-Kamil offered Jerusalem and all around it save two castles, and a thirty-year truce, for their immediate departure. John of Brienne, titular King of Jerusalem, and the Outremer barons wanted to accept; Pelagius, the Italians, and the masters of the Templars and Hospitallers, leading the French, refused, and refused again when 30,000 bezants were added.

In August 1219 the massed Christians drove at the sultan's fortified position; he fell back, they lost cohesion in pursuit and looting, and he struck. John and the military orders prevented a rout, but the defeat was heavy. Al-Kamil offered again: the truce, the land, the bezants, the True Cross, money to rebuild Jerusalem's walls (which his brother had pulled down in January) and his fresh prisoners. John favoured it; the Italians and French, believing the Emperor was about to come, did not. In November a few crusaders saw an ungarrisoned tower, climbed an unguarded wall and opened a gate, and the city fell. Al-Kamil, unable to assault or besiege it, withdrew to Mansourah, with the 1219 flood failed and his purse with it, and braced for the end.

The bezant here is the Italian word for a gold coin; these were probably dinars, which by law weigh 72 grains of barley but in practice vary. The sultan having 30,000 to hand shows what a raid on his treasury might bring: friends of the Crusade could help it hugely by finding them and making off with them (p. 64).

details.antagonist: The crusaders at Damietta, and the papal legate Pelagius

stages.title: The spoils are redivided
stages.clues: In February the factions agree to share out the sack of Damietta again.
stages.ignored: The soldiers make peace, though their leaders still cannot stand one another. The Pope lets John of Brienne leave to claim the throne of Armenia, and Pelagius, in sole charge, waits for Frederick II.

stages.title: Louis of Bavaria arrives
stages.clues: Frederick does not come; in May 25,000 of his soldiers do, under Louis of Bavaria, who urges an immediate attack.
stages.ignored: Preparations begin. John of Brienne returns in July and counsels against it, and again cannot move Pelagius.

stages.title: The march on Mansourah
stages.clues: The Egyptians, who have spent a year wondering at the gift of time to rearm, march out, take fright at the host and fall back behind the tributary at Mansourah. The Christians follow and fortify opposite, at Sharimshah.
stages.ignored: In August the Nile rises and a dry canal they crossed begins to fill. Egyptian ships enter it and cut their retreat and supply, and Pelagius orders a return to Damietta.

stages.title: The retreat
stages.clues: The Teutonic Knights burn most of the supplies; the wine will not burn, so to keep it from Muslims many crusaders get drunk. The burning camp warns the Egyptians.
stages.ignored: Al-Kamil has the canal wall smashed and the road turns to deep mud. At nightfall the Egyptians attack from firm ground. The Christians rally on John and the masters and get back to a camp with no food, to surrender or starve. Pelagius runs the blockade by boat.

stages.title: Damietta is handed back
stages.clues: Pelagius accepts the sultan's terms: Damietta returned, the Christians out of Egypt for at least eight years, all prisoners freed, the True Cross promised.
stages.ignored: On 8 September 1221 the Egyptians re-enter Damietta. Oddly, the sultan's servants cannot find the True Cross: it has been stolen.

neighbours.secrets: This is the real world's course and need not be Mythic Africa's: at any point the characters can change it, sometimes by very small acts (p. 67). If this Mythic Europe follows history, the Egyptians then pull Damietta down and build a new city of that name a mile and a half away (see Pulling it All Down).

neighbours.name: Qus
neighbours.summary:
The Greeks' Apollinopolis, long in decline and now in a century's rise the second city of Egypt. Three things raised it: the Crusade has pushed the pilgrim road across the Red Sea, and Qus is the last civilised place on it; a Christian rising at Qift ended with the sultan's brother putting 3,000 to the sword, so its market came here; and a gold rush at nearby Wadi Allaqi makes it the centre of mining supplies. New families have risen with trade and mining (p. 67).

Merchants of Egypt meet those of Yemen, Ethiopia and beyond here, and complain of unfair taxes: goods assessed for a year's tax though not owned for a year, no allowance for exempt tools of trade, and assessors who check for smuggling by piercing bags with sharp sticks. Yet the merchants feel safe: one whose camels sicken may leave pepper or cinnamon by the road and expect to find it untouched (p. 69).

The Qusian authorities are strict and the narrow valley is a choke point, so smuggling is hard, unless one can cross the desert. It is the nearest large settlement to old Thebes, its necropolis, and the temples of Luxor and Karnak (p. 68).

neighbours.name: Qift
neighbours.summary: Once the gateway for foreign merchants into southern Egypt, now a town of Copts impoverished by their failed rising, in which the sultan's brother killed 3,000. Magi can hire grogs, Coptic-speaking companions and people with influence among the clergy here (pp. 67-68).

neighbours.name: Akhmim
neighbours.summary: A city on the pilgrim road south to Qus. Arab writers say wizards live in a temple here, served by moving statues or by moving reliefs on the walls, which grant their desires; yet these magicians hold no political power, even over the town around them. The town is named for a god classical writers equated with Pan (p. 68).
neighbours.secrets: Theories abound. Some magi think their magic weak outside the temple's Faerie aura. Some Christians call them worshippers of Asmodeus, kept down by the imminent wrath of God. Some Muslims reply that they serve a Divine being and keep from the world for pious reasons.

neighbours.name: Thebes, Luxor and Karnak
neighbours.summary: The ancient capital, its necropolis and its temples, near Qus. The tombs near Thebes are cut into the rock and probably include those of the rulers who followed the strange heretic, monotheist pharaohs of lost Amarna (p. 68).

neighbours.name: Wadi Allaqi
neighbours.summary: The scene of a gold rush that Qus supplies (p. 67), and the reach of the north of Blemmyae territory, where some Blemmyae families mine gold and emeralds and control the flow of gold into Makuria and Egypt (p. 95). Shipping goods to the miners and carrying off untaxed gold might pay smugglers very well (p. 68).

neighbours.name: 'Aydhab
neighbours.summary:
A seedy Red Sea port of pirates and smugglers for centuries, lately rich as the place pilgrims leave Egypt for Jiddah. Travel writers tell pilgrims to keep to trusted groups, for the locals will rob and kill for money. The desert around gives nothing: no crops, and even the water is imported. Most older buildings are woven of reeds shipped from the Nile, a few new ones plastered. On paper its wealth is trade, the pilgrim traffic and the catch; in truth its traders prey at sea, the pilgrims are its prey ashore and few fish are landed (p. 69). The port lies in land the Blemmyae claim, but in Egyptian hands (p. 96).

Some pilgrims think the journey washes out sin and use it to indulge, and at a price most vices can be had here. Pilgrims are fleeced in three legal ways: famous prices for necessities, a fairly light tax of part of their food, and the hire of jilabs. A jilab is a rickety boat of planks sewn with coconut fibre, caulked with palm shavings, rigged with Theban palm-leaf sails and greased with castor or shark oil; it flexes on the reefs, so it is thought safer than a nailed hull. The hire is so high that the owner loses nothing if it sinks. Boats are often lost, crammed with pilgrims in a sea known for wrecks and sharks, and everyone in town who is not poor owns at least two.
neighbours.secrets: Most of the city seems to be falling under the sway of evil (p. 57).

neighbours.name: The House of Torturers
neighbours.summary: The old customs house at 'Aydhab. The Fatimids charged all who entered Egypt here seven and a half dinars, and hanged those who could not pay by the testicles, sending their names on to Qus and elsewhere, where the tax agents would do what travellers call only 'worse'. Sultans no longer charge pilgrims (pp. 57, 68).
neighbours.secrets: It keeps an Infernal aura, the book gives no figure, and minor demons living there urge locals to rob or murder pilgrims.

neighbours.name: The Pearl Islands near 'Aydhab
neighbours.summary: Islands whose seabeds teem with a silver bivalve that tastes of sea turtle, with mother-of-pearl shells. Pearls come in a brief June season from divers, about four to the ton of shellfish. Some divers black out as they surface (p. 68).
neighbours.secrets: Those who black out seem to sate creatures that guard the pearls. If magi make diving safer, the creatures may stop slumbering.

neighbours.name: The Red Sea
neighbours.summary: A sea of reefs, wrecks and sharks, home to immense creatures: sea-eels, sharks, whales, tremendous turtles, massive sea-centipedes and worms. They chase shoals up from the depths until the fish beach themselves in numbers or leap into boats (p. 97). Its ports, 'Aydhab, Badi, Qusayr and Sawakin, are old rivals.

neighbours.name: The Keepers of the Roads
neighbours.summary: Faeries who guard the goods merchants leave at the roadside and enforce the road's bounds and the rule against theft. They need not attack: they confuse a thief and hide the road, and he dies of exposure or thirst (p. 68).

neighbours.name: No Papa
neighbours.summary: The patriarchate has been vacant since 1216, deadlocked between Cyril ibn Laqlaq and those who oppose him. Characters who could break the deadlock might win the gratitude of the winning side (p. 58).

details.antagonist: Cyril ibn Laqlaq and his opponents

neighbours.name: Ancient Works of Magic or Trickery?
neighbours.summary: At the Cairo mosque built where Moses duelled Pharaoh's magicians, characters can call up the magicians' ghosts, given the right help or Hermetic Virtues. With no relic they must make an Arcane Connection to the dead; happily the two magicians' names are recorded, and one died in the Plague of the Death of the First Born Sons. Leadworkers (Houses of Hermes: True Lineages) and users of defixiones (Ancient Magic) can use names for this, and summon a pharaonic wizard here (p. 59).
neighbours.secrets: Some of their magic was only trickery.

neighbours.name: Perfect Ingredient
neighbours.summary: A plague breaks out in Egypt. It was last seen three hundred years ago and a scholar cured it somehow. A student's account in the Maristan library tells of a strange talisman that sealed the illness into the pit of the last victims, and gives away clues to the pit. The head of the Maristan sends an expedition (p. 60).
neighbours.secrets: Grave robbers have opened the pit and carried off the talismans. While they hold them they stay well but can carry the sickness. The Maristan and the Guild of Seekers combine to find them, study the talismans and copy them, and the player characters are urged to fetch a rare ingredient each one needs. Rivals who learn the plan mean to gather as much of it as they can and destroy the source, to make their stock priceless.

neighbours.name: The Magical Air
neighbours.summary: In Barcelona ordinary people have begun to develop the Magical Air Flaw. Strife follows, and churchmen who see the likeness to the Gifted blame the Order. A local Criamon suggests a contaminant but cannot find or treat it. The Tribunal tries everything it can, and sends a delegation to see whether the Maristan's records hold anything similar (p. 60).

neighbours.name: The Returnee
neighbours.summary: A young woman among the Maristan's insane makes wild claims that would be ignored if they were not in archaic Latin. A Coptic monk has heard such phrases only from a member of the Order of Hermes. She says she is Lucia of the line of Trianoma, back from Twilight. Her parents swear she is their own daughter, raised from birth (p. 60).
neighbours.secrets: How, then, does she know the Parma Magica?

neighbours.name: Pyramidions
neighbours.summary: Of the three main pyramids at Gizeh only one keeps its capstone. The other two were stolen, with great difficulty, and hidden. Pyramidions are powerful tethers that make Magic auras, yet are small enough for a spell or a cart to move. Who needs a mobile aura, and what have they used it for these few hundred years (p. 62)?

neighbours.name: Where is Alexander?
neighbours.summary: Most guides say the largest pyramid was made for Alexander, who never lay in it. By old custom whoever buried Pharaoh was the next Pharaoh, so Ptolemy stole the corpse and buried it secretly. For long a certain sarcophagus was thought his, a blind that really held the last king before the Ptolemies. Treasure hunters keep coming back to Cairo with coins, amulets and papyri that hint at his tomb (p. 62).
neighbours.secrets: Hermetic magi actually know Alexander was buried in Memphis and then Alexandria, and have some idea where. None of the local faeries care.

neighbours.name: The Library of Cleopatra
neighbours.summary: Find the unfound grave of Cleopatra and it may lead to a hidden store of Alexandria's books; or find the walls of the library on the seabed, and read what was carved on them (p. 63).

neighbours.name: The Lighthouse Mirror
neighbours.summary: A sedentary Verditius offers to pay the characters to find the Pharos mirror. Can they search the seabed, find ghosts who remember its casting into the sea, or get an Arcane Connection to it (p. 63)?

neighbours.name: The Island's Aura
neighbours.summary: A powerful magus planning an Alexandrian covenant has been distracted by the Christians feuding in Damietta. He pays the characters to live on the Pharos island for a year and find out why reports of its aura disagree (p. 63).

neighbours.name: The Second Inscription
neighbours.summary: Another sheet of lime plaster has fallen from the Lighthouse, showing a detailed prediction of events in the Order. Is it a hoax? If not, are other messages hidden on the building, and can whoever wrote them be trusted (p. 63)?

neighbours.name: The Mystery of the Oil
neighbours.summary: Where does the oil that lights Alexandria all night come from (p. 63)?

neighbours.name: The Itinerarium in Alexandria
neighbours.summary: A skilled Jerbiton leads a band of apprentices to Alexandria's ruins. The players act as guards, or as rescuers when something unexpected happens (p. 63).

neighbours.name: Peasant Revolt
neighbours.summary: Sugar needs far fewer hands than wheat or barley. Absentee nobles with no feeling for their land order as much of it grown as possible, leaving many without work, and if several in a district do so, each counting on buying a neighbour's wheat, there is famine. A horde of starving peasants threatens the magi's interests: can they turn its anger aside (p. 69)?

neighbours.name: A Wheel for the Verditius
neighbours.summary: A Verditius in the Greater Alps, curious about the waterwheels that crush cane, writes by redcap asking the characters to take apart the most efficient wheel they can find and ship it to him. Can they get it quietly, dismantle it unbroken and send it? Would it be easier to send Egypt's best wheelwright to the Alps? And if they go with it through Italy, how do they deal with nobles drawn by rumours of a Saracen siege engine (p. 69)?

neighbours.name: The Source of the Cane
neighbours.summary: Sugar cane appeared very suddenly in Egypt, and rumour says supernatural powers gave it to the first farmers. Did a demon of gluttony offer it to men? Are there really faeries that possess children who eat sugar and set them running mad (p. 69)?

neighbours.name: Aristotle's Lost Books
neighbours.summary: Dig into the side of Aristotle's pyramid, past defences no one has yet dared, for the books meant for publication that Mythic Europe has never read (p. 62).
neighbours.secrets: The Tomb of Aristotle's record gives what the books do.

neighbours.name: The Lamps of Mykerinos
neighbours.summary: Where are the lamps with which Mykerinos tried to slow time, and do they still work (p. 62)?

neighbours.name: The Sand of Hermes
neighbours.summary: A scholar who carries the plateau's sand for its gift to the mind has spent his life among the tombs and cannot be brought to leave (p. 62).
neighbours.secrets: Faeries grant the gift and take it back if he stops, feeding on the attention.

neighbours.name: The Crocodiles of Gizeh
neighbours.summary: No Hermetic magus has ever assessed the marble crocodiles in a laboratory. What do they do, and could they be moved (p. 62)?

neighbours.name: Raising the Throne
neighbours.summary: In a famine year the Isle of Gold shows above the low Nile. Why has no one ever tried to raise Pharaoh's throne (p. 62)?

neighbours.name: The Wizards of Akhmim
neighbours.summary: Who are the wizards of the temple at Akhmim, served by moving statues yet with no power over the town around them (p. 68)?

neighbours.name: Breaking the Chain
neighbours.summary: It took a month to break the chain at Damietta, and two groups are sure they did it. French soldiers remember assaulting the island tower from boats and rushing it with ladders, at the cost of many comrades. Dutch soldiers remember building a ship with a great saw beneath it, and ramming the chain in two; they have commissioned bells to ring the victory every year. Both carry pieces of the chain as keepsakes (p. 66).
neighbours.secrets: Some crusade leaders believe both stories in full, each with whichever group they are talking to; confronted, they cannot see the difficulty and soon forget the conversation. Is this a miracle hidden by Divine power, or two powerful faeries contesting the crusaders' vitality?

neighbours.name: The Defeat of the Kurds
neighbours.summary: The first Egyptian army was destroyed by infighting. Hearing that the general of the Kurds, his largest contingent, planned a coup, the sultan burst into the plotters' tent at the very moment their hands lay on a Qur'an, swearing to depose him. He took them prisoner and went to Cairo to secure his position. His army woke to find him gone and its general a prisoner, and scattered (p. 66).
neighbours.secrets: Was the plot mundane, born in the army or of Christian agents? Or a contagious madness from a demon, a faerie whispering promises of rule, or a battle between puppets of the Order of Suleiman?

neighbours.name: Pulling it All Down
neighbours.summary: As Damietta's buildings come down to supply the new city a mile and a half away, treasures and secrets come to light. Ghosts are disturbed, and the hidden cesspits of servants of the Infernal lie open (p. 67).
neighbours.secrets: If magi steer the choice of the new site, it might take in ancient tombs with Magic auras, leaving lacunae in the city's Dominion.

neighbours.name: Pelagius's Destiny
neighbours.summary: A prophecy in an old Arabic book found in Damietta foretold Pelagius's victory, and helped raise him up. No one knows who wrote it or how a crusader came by it. Characters who find a clearer copy can sell it to either side for valuable concessions, or use it to work events themselves (p. 67).

neighbours.name: Escort
neighbours.summary: A redcap or magus who means to explore Ethiopia or Arabia asks for an escort to Qus, to meet the merchants who come there, learn the distant country's language and hear the dangers of the road (p. 68).

neighbours.name: Lost Merchants
neighbours.summary: Someone asks the characters to find the bodies of merchants lost to the Keepers of the Roads, for burial; or to save a merchant who angered a keeper by theft and was lucky enough not to die of thirst (p. 68).

neighbours.name: Smuggling at Qus
neighbours.summary: Magi or servants able to cross the desert could make a great deal smuggling past Qus: goods out to the gold miners of Wadi Allaqi, untaxed gold back (p. 68).

neighbours.name: Infernal Site?
neighbours.summary: Pilgrims at 'Aydhab keep being robbed and murdered, and the trail leads back to the old customs house (p. 68).
neighbours.secrets: Minor demons dwelling in the House of Torturers encourage the locals to it.

neighbours.name: Pearls
neighbours.summary: Characters who want money quite legally might try the islands near 'Aydhab in the brief June pearling season (p. 68).
neighbours.secrets: If magi make the diving safe, the guardians that are sated by drowning divers may wake.

neighbours.name: The Bujat Road
neighbours.summary: Sailing back from Jiddah to 'Aydhab is dangerous: the winds blow ships south into the lands of the Bujat, the Romans' Blemmyae. Some travellers say the Bujat hire out camels and lead people north on purpose short of supplies, and then claim the goods of those who die of hunger and thirst. Their sultan lives in the mountains near Philae, and his family are said to be corrupt nudists who wear a loincloth at most. The al-Bujat once lived around Philae and worshipped Isis, and their wars made the Romans move Egypt's border north and garrison it (p. 68).
neighbours.secrets: It is unclear whether these are the Bujat, or headless faeries who have taken their name and story.

neighbours.name: Nubia
neighbours.summary:
The stretch of the Nile valley with a narrow, broken floodplain and six cataracts, the Arabs' bled es-Sudan, Land of the Blacks. Lower Nubia, around the first two cataracts, is almost rainless desert with a thin strip of river, farmed only with mule-driven waterwheels. Upper Nubia to the south has seasonal rain and much vegetation; where a river joins the Nile the land inside the confluence is rich, and people gather on these 'islands'. Savannah buffers it from the desert, and in the far south it merges into the Ethiopian Highlands. Its three kingdoms are Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia (p. 71).

History (pp. 71-73). Early kingdoms at Ballana near Pakhoras and at Kerma were absorbed by Kush, ruled by qores who descended from Nubian pharaohs of Egypt, and from Cush son of Ham. Kush broke from Egypt a thousand years before Christ. Its capital was first Napata, near the fourth cataract. In 591 BC Emperor Aspelta moved his palace to Meroë, partly to escape the priests, who as arbiters of ma'at, the order that made the laws, elected the king, made him a god and could order him to kill himself. He obeyed. Around 300 BC Emperor Arqamani had the Napatan priests slaughtered and made Meroë the capital, with a new royal cemetery; emperors then truly ruled but were no longer divine. Weakened by war with Rome and Axum and by rebellion, Kush faded. In 297 Diocletian used the desert Nobatae against the Blemmyae, and they settled the valley. A fifth-century Blemmyae revival at Meroë was crushed by Axum and the Nobatae, and three kingdoms emerged. Axum held Upper Nubia as a vassal for nearly a century from the early sixth.

In 540 Constantinople sent two missions, Justinian's Melkite and Theodora's Monophysite; the empress had the Melkites delayed in Egypt, and Julian spent two years in Nubia. His successor Longinus returned only in 567, when Makuria had gone orthodox, stayed six years in Nobatia, was exiled to Arabia, came back in 580, and crossed the Blemmyae lands to Alodia, which he converted wholly. The Umayyads failed twice to take Makuria, in 642 and 652, and the Baqt gave five centuries of accord. With the Melkites out of favour in Arab Egypt, Makuria had no Melkite bishops for over a century, and King Merkurios, the 'New Constantine', builder of Dongola, adopted Monophysitism. He also subdued Nobatia, which he suspected of dealing with Egypt's Muslims. Under the Fatimids (969 to 1171) Nubia thrived, supplying them with goods and soldiers, and gold found in the Red Sea hills paid for new ports.

When the Fatimids fell in 1171 Salah ed-Din sent his brother Shams ed-Dawla Turan Shah to invade Nubia. Nobatia suffered terribly and Premnis was held for some years. An emissary sent to weigh Makuria reported it too poor to be worth conquering, a lie, for it was and is at its height, and the Ayyubids withdrew. Trade returned but trust did not: the Baqt now goes unpaid more years than not, and demands for arrears are ignored. Bedouin tribes driven out by the Ayyubids are coming south into Upper Nubia, taking land from Makuria and Alodia and setting up warring principalities, meks, east of the Nile. Nobatia's desert is too poor to tempt them.

People (pp. 73-74). Nubians are black-skinned, with wavy black hair (curly hair is thought the mark of slave stock), and taller than most Europeans and Arabs. They wear light cotton trousers and loose smocks, brightly dyed in geometric patterns for church and feast days. Important people wear short tunics stiffened with reeds or ivory to flare at the waist, sometimes several layers of different lengths and colours. Both sexes wear gold and copper bangles and neck hoops, beads of ostrich eggshell, glass, cowrie and wood, and carved stone rings; parasols and walking sticks are common even among the young; hair is plaited in tresses or held in topknots with long ivory combs.

Warriors (p. 73). The Arabs call Nubian archers 'pupil-smiters' and 'archers of the eyes'. They use self bows and a compound bow with a bone core, with costly iron heads that punch through thick armour, spears, and short one-edged swords, and moulded oxhide breastplates, skirts, vambraces and greaves. Cavalry ride light horses or war camels. Exarchs command divisions of the royal guard or frontier garrisons; there is a levy in war, and Makuria keeps a small river navy under two nauarchs.

The dead (pp. 73-74). Nubians bury by Church rite but with no ceremony, and fear the dead deeply. A mask or plate covers the face so that death cannot infect those who see it; family and friends rarely attend, leaving it to a priest and hired pallbearers. Graves show where, not who. Houses have no windows towards a burial site, and graveyards have no roads near them. The same dread covers Kush's monuments: people who live by a pyramid avoid looking at it. Alodians will not even name a dead person or speak of his deeds.

Names (p. 74). A given name with perhaps a father's or town's (Abraam son of Kosma, Dawud of Dongola); women often by marriage (Eionngoka wife of Abraam). Male: Abraam, Adama, Anastasios, Athanasios, Chael, Dauti, Dawud, Douddil, Georgios, Iakobi, Iesou, Ioannes, Ioasse, Kosma, Mashshouda, Merkourios, Orinourla, Petros, Pisroel, Tapara, Tirsakouni. Female: Anthelia, Anna, Eionngoka, Eirene, Ekkir, Genseoua, Iannia, Maria, Mariham, Mena, Petrosinta, Songoja, Sophora, Theodora. Most Nubians laugh at long Kushite names, but Meroë's upper classes still sometimes use them. Male: Amanikhabale, Aspelta, Atakhebasken, Malewiebamani, Piye, Senkamanisken, Shabaka, Taharqa, Tanwetamai. Female: Amanitore, Aqaluqa, Gerarheni, Henuttakhebit, Kasaqa, Pebatjma, Qalhata, Shanakdakhete, Tabiry, Yuterow.

Economy (pp. 76-77). Several crops a year of sorghum, millet, barley and dates, with lentils, olives, sesame, vines, bananas, wheat and cotton. Sorghum makes bread and mizr, a staple beer; dates and grapes make drink; oxen drive the waterwheels. Sheep, goats, cattle and above all pigs are the livestock. Houses are of sun-dried brick. Pottery (at Pakhoras) and weaving (at Dongola) lead, with leather, metal and palm-fibre goods; gold and emeralds come from the Red Sea Hills. Cotton, and camel and goat wool, take dyes, and Nubian indigo gives light-fast blues the north envies. Exports: glass, ivory, ostrich feathers, cattle, emeralds, gold and above all slaves. Imports from Egypt: wheat, linen and wine. Downstream boats always pass; upstream, sail cannot get from Dongola to Abu Hamad against the prevailing wind, and the cataracts pass only at high water, so camels and donkeys matter.

Ancient auras (p. 83). The old monuments once had Faerie auras from pagan worship, which waned as the temples emptied. Centuries as cemeteries may have left a tether to the Magic Realm: a Magic aura of 1 for each century of continuous use, more at striking natural sites, less where the monuments have decayed (Realms of Power: Magic pp. 8-10).

neighbours.name: The Fortified River
neighbours.summary: Since the mid-twelfth century the kings of Makuria and Alodia have raised over fifty fortresses from Soba to Kalabsha, on nearly every lone hilltop with its own water, each big enough for the local people and with deep crypt-like stores of grain, in answer to their Muslim neighbours' growing aggression. Smaller ones have minimal garrisons and lie mostly deserted (p. 80).
neighbours.secrets: More than one has been quietly taken over by bandits, and sometimes something more sinister lives there.

neighbours.name: The Darb al-Arba'in
neighbours.summary: The road of the Arab slavers, from Asyut in Egypt by way of the remote trading town of Uri down into the Slavelands. It carries slaves past every major city on the Nile, so that Nubians can pretend the trade does not exist (pp. 77, 85).

neighbours.name: The Baqt
neighbours.summary:
The treaty of 652 between the Umayyad governor of Egypt and the king of Makuria, after a failed invasion; the name comes from the Greek pakton, agreement. It alone among Muslim treaties freed a Christian land from invasion and forced conversion, and Egypt did not invade for over 500 years despite many lapses (p. 73).

In 835, fourteen years in arrears, the caliph pressed King Zacharias of Makuria, whose son George went to Baghdad and made the slaves due every three years.
