The Fatimids demanded arrears too, an envoy came to Dongola, and it was renewed again. Since the invasion of 1172 it binds less, and the Baqt is more often defaulted than paid (pp. 72-73).

Copies are in every city of Nobatia and Makuria; the originals of 652 and 835 lie in Dongola Cathedral. A copy signed under authority from the King of Makuria and the Fatimid governor holds a pawn of Rego vis. The two originals are sources of Rego vis infused with the Divine, yielding only in years when Egypt does not attack and the tribute is not in arrears (p. 73).

details.rules: No war between the parties; safe conduct for each other's citizens; runaway slaves and Egyptian outlaws returned. Each year Nubia owes 365 slaves to the treasury, 40 to the emir of Egypt, 20 to the governor of Aswan, 5 to the judge of Aswan and 1 to each of the twelve guarantors; Egypt owes wheat, barley, wine and fancy cloth.

neighbours.name: The Nubian Church
neighbours.summary:
Nubia is overwhelmingly Christian, and it is illegal for a Makurian or Alodian subject to profess any other faith. Nobatia and Alodia were first Monophysite and Makuria Melkite; as Byzantine power in Egypt sank, Makuria too came over. The Church is one with the Coptic Church under the Patriarch of Alexandria, who appoints all bishops, many of them Egyptians, but its liturgy is in Greek, not Coptic (p. 74).

There are seven sees in Makuria and Nobatia (Kalabsha, Premnis, Pakhoras, Sai, Dongola, Shanqir and Kallama) and six in Alodia (Soba, Meroë, Kabushia, Kawa, Sennar and Goz Regeb). The ranks are many: bishops (papas), great priests (sorto daoul), priests (sorto or presbyteros), archimandrites, archdeacons, epideacons, deacons, liturgists and elders (gort). The typical church is a flat-roofed rectangle on timbers; larger ones are cruciform or domed. Monasticism is minor, its houses mostly founded and filled by Egyptians, and there are unrecognised communities called lawra (p. 76).

The archangel Michael is everywhere in invocations, inscriptions and dedications, and the common cryptogram chi-pi-theta stands for his name in Greek by number: 689 (p. 76).

neighbours.name: The Kushite Gods
neighbours.summary:
The old religion lingers in pockets, untolerated by the Church. Before creation water covered all; a mound rose, and on it Atum the first god was born and made the world from it. That mound is Dju Wa'ab (p. 76).

Atum is an old man, sometimes ram-headed. Anhur and Menhit were war gods Egypt took from Kush: Anhur, patron of soldiers, a bearded man in a kilt and four-feathered headdress with a spear, honoured with mock battles; Menhit, 'she who massacres', lion-headed, who rained fiery arrows. Mandulis, the sun, wears ram's horns, cobras, plumes and sun discs, and sometimes has a hawk's body and a man's head. Dedun, god of incense, was god of prosperity, guardian of the royal dead and special patron of the priests. Apedemak, perhaps the greatest, patron of royalty and of Meroë, was a four-armed man with three lion heads, or one, or a lion killing serpents, an allegory for Arqamani's triumph over the priests of Napata; he stood for courage, truth, light and fertility. His wife Amesemi was goddess of protection and the moon.

neighbours.name: The Ja'alin
neighbours.summary: Bedouin who have come from Arabia and Egypt over the last fifty years and now hold both banks between Abu Hamad and Berber. A dozen or so little principalities, meks, each founded by a prince exiled with Hamad, hold around a hundred human families and twenty or so jinn; each prince has an unGifted sahir of Hamad's line as vizier, who also mediates with the jinn. The jinn mostly belong to the Faerie Realm and are Muslims like their neighbours. Proud descendants of Abbas, uncle of Mohammed, men and women alike scar their faces in an H or T. They herd sheep and goats over thin pasture and sometimes fight over it, but quarrels are forbidden at Abu Hamad, which is neutral ground (p. 81).

neighbours.name: Banu al-Kanz
neighbours.summary: An Arab tribe that held the Aswan region under the Fatimids, one of whose rulers earned the title Kanz al-Dawlah, 'treasure of the state', which became hereditary. The Ayyubids drove them out, and they have made a semi-independent Muslim principality in northern Nobatia, including the land round Philae. Refugees from them built the island forts of the Batn al-Hajar (pp. 78, 80). The book also spells them Banu al-Kanuz.

neighbours.name: The Nubian Slave Trade
neighbours.summary:
Slaves are all three kingdoms' chief export. They come from the Slavelands, the vast pasture south and west of Alodia, with its peaceful unorganised herders, trekked hundreds of miles and driven north to Egypt (p. 77). Details of those peoples are in chapter 9.

The Christian kingdoms promote the trade yet abhor keeping slaves. Most bishops think it unbecoming and do nothing. The chief excuse is the Baqt, though it has weakened since 1172 and takes only a third of the slaves passing through; the rest are for profit. Promoters call the captives barely better than beasts, or say slavery is a better life than the Slavelands' wild beasts and cannibals. When the Baqt is missed it is rarely conscience, but refusal to pay the slavers' prices, no will to regulate them, and few ways to undercut them; sometimes famine or disease in the Slavelands, and rarely a whole lost expedition (p. 77).

Owning slaves is legal but not acceptable in any Nubian kingdom. Unlike Europe's, slave owners in Egypt and Nubia need no Virtue, and may hold what suits their wealth; a Christian owner in a Christian kingdom has a Local Reputation of 1. Slavers take Merchant if they transport or Mercenary Captain if they capture, and are likely Well-Traveled (p. 75).

Playing it (p. 75): slave stories need care for modern sensibilities. A slave character takes the Favored Slave or Chattel Slave Flaw (p. 76), which differ from Guardians of the Forests' Slave (p. 102). Reasons for a lax master: an inherited slave who cannot be freed without insult, a long loyal line, a vital skill, a self-sale to avert a worse fate. Stories for a chattel slave: escaped and hunted; seeking captured family; a dead master no one knows of; crimes hidden from the master or forced by him; a favoured slave envied; a master's enemies striking through him. Those truly free of their master count as free Aithiopians.

A free Aithiopian marks himself apart: Outsider if he keeps tribal ways, Outcast if he has taken local ones, in any saga outside the Slavelands. He will be taken for a slave in any Arab land, but without a Story Flaw that can usually be settled. Story Flaws may tie him here: Dependents or a True Love sold north, Close Family Ties, a former owner as Enemy, a Feud with his captor. A campaigner against slavery likely has Driven, Temporal Influence or Social Contacts, and Enemies. Abolishing the trade means renegotiating or ending the Baqt; petitioning the Church is a fine start, and what the bishops ask in return may make stories.

details.wants: Slaves and their cattle from the Slavelands.

neighbours.name: Nobatia
neighbours.summary:
A splinter of Kush that kept Kushite gods and customs, under Makuria's suzerainty for the last four hundred years or so but culturally its own and resisting every attempt to make it a province. It runs from the first to the third cataract, mostly desert, with the Libyan Desert west and the Nubian east; its people keep to the river, and eastern-bank settlements are the more heavily fortified against Blemmyae raids (pp. 77-78).

As in old Kush, inspectors collect all surplus and give it to those in need, first to those who have given before, so there is little poverty. It is a free trade zone, unlike Makuria: Egyptian coin is legal tender and Egyptians trade unhindered, but all cargo going upriver must pass to Nobatian factors. Trade with Alodia cannot cross Makuria, so caravans leave Nobatian towns across the risky desert. With the Ayyubid and Bedouin threats, people are moving from scattered settlements to walled hilltop and island towns, with stronger houses and inside stores (p. 78).

neighbours.name: The Eparch of Nobatia
neighbours.summary: The Lord of the Mountain, viceroy in place of a king, appointed directly by the King of Makuria, with judicial and financial control of the land. He can found churches and celebrate Mass. Each eparch is also anointed king of Dotawo, a Makurian vassal kingdom centred at Ado, which pays for him. He handles relations with Muslim Egypt, receives goods meant for the King of Makuria, and must deliver the Baqt's slaves or, more often of late, excuses. His emblem is a double-horned headdress, worn on formal occasions; his agents carry it embossed on an iron badge (p. 77).

neighbours.name: Ado
neighbours.summary: A hilltop fortress, with Premnis and Pakhoras one of Nobatia's three chief towns, and capital of the subkingdom of Dotawo. In the invasion of 1172 the Egyptians, who call it Jabal 'Adda, searched it for the eparch and failed to take him. The book calls that invasion Abbasid here, and Ayyubid elsewhere (p. 78).
neighbours.ruler: The Eparch of Nobatia, as king of Dotawo

neighbours.name: The Eparch's Church at Ado
neighbours.summary: The eparch's own church: no cathedral, but an impressive building with a complex geometric mosaic floor (p. 78).

neighbours.name: Batn al-Hajar
neighbours.summary: The 'belly of stones', named by Egyptian traders: eighty miles south of the second cataract where the Nile runs between high cliffs through barren mountains, with no floodplain, in places no more than twenty paces wide, broken by rapids, outcrops and small islands, and unnavigable even at the flood. Some islands hold miniature forts, raised into rocky towers against the floods by people fleeing the Banu al-Kanz. Otherwise it is all but uninhabited. It divides Lower Nubia, where foreigners are welcome, from Upper Nubia, where foreign trade is forbidden (p. 78).

neighbours.name: Dotawo
neighbours.summary: A vassal kingdom of Makuria inside Nobatia, centred on Ado, whose crown is given to each eparch to pay for his office (pp. 77-78).

neighbours.name: Akasha
neighbours.summary: A fortress in the Batn al-Hajar with a garrison guarding Nobatia from the Banu al-Kanz (p. 78).

neighbours.name: The Lost Temple of Ramses
neighbours.summary: Twin temples said to be carved from a mountain somewhere above Philae, under millennia of sand, which treasure hunters seek all over Lower Nubia. Pharaoh Ramses is said to have built them to intimidate his southern neighbours, claiming to have beaten them at Kadesh. The Great Temple was for Amun, Ra, Ptah and the deified pharaoh; the Small Temple for Hathor and his wife Nefertari (p. 79).

levels.name: The Temples
levels.enter: A troop of always twenty-two baboons, descended from those kept at the temple, raise their arms each dawn to worship the sun. A human who takes one's place in the rite sees the sun go through the sand to light the temple's guardian statues, and may approach.

neighbours.secrets: Explorers fail because the temples lie in a Faerie regio of aura 5.

neighbours.name: Menarti
neighbours.summary: A small island at the foot of the second cataract, 'island of Mei', Saint Michael. It is the upriver limit of navigation from Egypt (p. 79).

neighbours.name: Monastery of Menarti
neighbours.summary: A small monastery under Saints Michael and Cosmas (p. 79).

neighbours.name: Takoa
neighbours.summary: A small town on Menarti's southern tip, a customs post between Lower and Upper Nubia. No foreign merchant may pass: all cargo is given up here and goes on to the eparch (p. 79).

neighbours.name: The Tumulus Graves of Nobatia
neighbours.summary: Massive tumuli on both banks hold kings and princes, many enclosing palaces or compounds with rich grave goods and sacrificed animals, especially dogs. Most are pre-Christian kinglets', though the earliest Nobatian kings used them too despite their faith, for continuity. Each intact tumulus has a Magic aura of 1 (p. 80).
neighbours.secrets: A tumulus may hold a grave guardian such as a mummified dog.

neighbours.name: Kalabsha
neighbours.summary: Capital of the Blemmyae state after Kush, now the smallest of Nobatia's bishoprics. The temple the Blemmyae raised to Mandulis mostly still stands (p. 79). The northern end of the river's fortresses (p. 80).

neighbours.name: Temple of Mandulis at Kalabsha
neighbours.summary: The temple the Blemmyae raised to Mandulis at their capital, mostly still standing (p. 79).

neighbours.name: Pakhoras
neighbours.summary:
Bukharas in Arabic, sometimes called Faras: Nobatia's religious and cultural centre, though the eparch now rules from Premnis. Tons of sand blow in daily, and armies of 'sand-warriors' with buckets and spades clear the cathedral, the palace and the property of those who can pay. Dumped on the west side, the sand has silted the channel, turning the old island into a peninsula, and every few decades citizens raise their thresholds, and past generations their walls and roofs (p. 79).

Most of the city is Kushite and in fine condition. The wall, ten paces high and three thick with three gates, encloses three sides, leaving the east to poor defence by the river, and is extended upwards as the sand rises. The former king's palace, the highest point, lies empty at the centre, richly set with statues of lion-headed Kushite gods. One of two ancient Egyptian temples is mostly ruin, the other a warehouse.

It has a large monastery on a hill outside, a smaller one within whose pottery factories make fine vessels sold through Nubia and beyond, six churches around the cathedral, and a mosque for foreign traders, though the bishop forbids the public call to prayer. A large market sells exotic goods from Alodia and beyond. Outside the southern gate a tent city of drovers tends visitors' beasts, and escorts and mercenaries from Atbara will arrange passage over the river and south to Alodia without entering Makuria.

The town stands on the Kom, a hill that was the original island (p. 79).
neighbours.secrets: The first Nubians here slew the giant who embodied the Kom, a powerful servant of the Red. They crushed its bones and fed them to livestock, shredded its flesh for birds, fed those beasts to dogs and lions, then killed and burned those and scattered the ashes. Some believe the daily sand is the Kom, remaking its body. If so it is winning: more sand arrives than can be removed, and some claim the heaps ripple like muscles about to flex.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Pakhoras
neighbours.summary: A large and imposing cathedral, kept clear of sand by the city's sand-warriors (p. 79).

neighbours.name: Serra
neighbours.summary: An old pharaonic fortress across the river from Pakhoras, refortified and held by its soldiers. Pakhoras plans to evacuate here if invaded, and it keeps plenty of food and firewood (p. 80).

neighbours.name: Philae
neighbours.summary:
A pair of islands in the first cataract, the Pearl of Egypt. The smaller, Philae proper, was sacred to Egyptians and Nubians as a burial place of Osiris; 'The Unapproachable', it could be landed on only after the proper rites. No birds fly over it and no fish can be caught from its shores. The larger, Senmut or Beghé, bears monuments to the pharaohs and emperors who claimed Egypt (p. 80).

Pharaonic and Graeco-Roman building covers most of both islands, above all the temples of Isis, Amun-Osiris, Hathor and Horus. The land around, the Dodekachoenus, was the estate of Isis and kept the priests of the Great Temple. It is now held by the Banu al-Kanz, and the few inhabitants, mostly monks and lay brothers of a small monastery, feel besieged, though the well-fortified island has not been seriously tried. One of the first Nubian bishoprics, its seat moved to Kalabsha.

neighbours.name: Premnis
neighbours.summary:
Pedeme to Kush, Qasr Ibrim to the Arabs: a fortified hilltop town, Nobatia's administrative centre. It began as seven temples of the Nubian pharaohs; the Ptolemies circled it with a massive wall. With Nobatia's conversion, placed here in the seventh century, the temples became churches and it grew into a true town (p. 80).

Ayyubid forces took it in 1172. After their expulsion the defences were improved, secular buildings went up among the religious, irregular stone housing filled a large two-level piazza over one temple, and the eparch moved his administration here from Pakhoras. High above the valley, it need not be abandoned at the flood, though it does become an island. Foreign merchants usually pass on to Pakhoras.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Our Lady the Pure Virgin
neighbours.summary: The stone cathedral of Premnis, damaged in the Ayyubid invasion of 1172 (p. 80).

neighbours.name: Sai Island
neighbours.summary: The largest permanent island on the Nile, six miles by three. A large pharaonic brick fortress stands on its east shore, and a small town surrounds the cathedral of one of Nubia's bishops (p. 80).

neighbours.name: Makuria
neighbours.summary:
Perhaps the most important Nubian kingdom, from the third to the fifth cataract, covering the heart of lost Kush yet distinctly Greek in nature, with nothing Kushite left. It is peaceful and prosperous, with many towns and broad fertile fields, though people are gathering into defensible towns with stores of food, firewood and water, partly against the Bedouin who have entered the eastern desert (p. 81).

Foreign trade is a royal monopoly run through Nobatia, and no money circulates. Foreign traders may not sell here on pain of losing all their goods, even if they are only passing upriver.

neighbours.name: The Great King of Makuria
neighbours.summary: The megalobasilikos, whose ministers and court bear Byzantine titles. Each town is its own kingdom, and thirteen vassal kings, the domestikoi, pay him tribute. All of them, the great king too, are priests who say Mass for their realms, until a king takes a life and can say it no more. He can reduce any subject to a slave, guilty or not. He takes counsel from a host of ministers and a court of seven bishops. The succession is matrilinear, a king's sister's son before his own, and crises are common when no heir is clear (p. 81).
neighbours.secrets: Five years ago his armies uprooted and burned Abu Hamad. That night a visitor came to his bedchamber, and since then he has forbidden anyone to try again.

neighbours.name: Abu Hamad
neighbours.summary: A tent city at the end of the great bend of the Nile, the only Muslim settlement in Makuria by the book's account of it (though see Samna) and a thorn in the kingdom's side. Its people are Ja'alin Bedouin, who come and go to trade, arrange marriages, hold festivals and honour their dead, and Arabic is its chief tongue. Armies of the domestikoi and the great king have tried to clear it, and it simply reforms; the last attempt was five years ago. Makurian spies see that one set of tents at the heart of the camp never moves, and they have never got inside (p. 81).
neighbours.secrets: Those tents are the opulent home of 'Izz el-Afram Hamad, the Master of Abu Hamad.

neighbours.name: Atbara
neighbours.summary: A frontier town at the meeting of the Atbara and the Nile, fiercely independent of Makuria and Alodia and rich enough to stay so. It controls river traffic for the fifth cataract, ends the Pakhoras road that takes trade round Makuria to Alodia, and ends the only safe road to Sawakin. Its guides wear green turbans (p. 81).
neighbours.secrets: The Blemmyae spare caravans led by Atbarans, and in return their chiefs are told the route and goods of the occasional rich caravan that somehow cannot get an escort. The Atbarans have a like alliance with the Ja'alin at Abu Hamad, so that caravans for their rivals never arrive.

neighbours.name: Berber
neighbours.summary: The last Makurian town before Alodia, given Atbara's doubtful loyalty. It used to end the Pakhoras road, but the Ja'alin now attack caravans bound for it and leave those for Atbara alone, and it has shrunk to a tenth of its people. Many think Atbara pays them to keep it poor (p. 81).

neighbours.name: Kallama
neighbours.summary: A town grown up around Makuria's smallest cathedral, existing only to serve the bishop and the monastery attached to his see (p. 82).

neighbours.name: Galu
neighbours.summary: A Napatan fortress, ruined and half in the sand, over the Wadi Howar, once an important seasonal spring and road west. The wadi is dry, its settlements are gone, and the land is a desolate waste (p. 84).
neighbours.secrets: Galu caused the failure. It was built on the home of the wadi's spirit after Napatan priests slew it, hoping to take over the water's flow; the effect did not last, and the fortress was left guarding a road to nowhere.

neighbours.name: Ghazali
neighbours.summary: One of Nubia's largest monasteries, a large church of the Holy Trinity amid living quarters and a commemorative complex, inside a high whitewashed wall of stone faced with brick. Monks are buried in a barrel-vaulted crypt, and it has a hospice for visitors and a hospital for the sick and dying (p. 84).

neighbours.name: Kerma
neighbours.summary:
Capital of a kingdom older than Kush. The circular royal palace lies in ruins beside two deffufa, solid mud-brick towers thirty paces high; remains of a towered wall over two miles long enclose room for 10,000 (p. 85).

The cemetery runs over a mile north to south, with an estimated 25,000 graves: low mounds under thousands of pebbles, often clustered round a larger one, some white, some black and a few of both, for no known reason. Dozens of huge royal tumuli stand at the southern end, four over a hundred paces across. A Magic aura of 3 clings to those four, 2 to the rest of the royal cemetery and 1 to the other graves.

neighbours.name: Negila
neighbours.summary: A small oasis on the Darfur caravan road, claimed by Makuria on the edge of Alodian Bayuda. It holds a Makurian outpost with a unit of Struthophagi mounted on ostriches, swift messengers and scouts (p. 85).

neighbours.name: The Valley of Elephants
neighbours.summary: Marshes in a lush stretch of the Nile where elephants gather in great numbers for the food, above all a sweet rush they cannot get enough of. The serpents that usually hunt elephants do not come here, oddly. The herds wreck farming and have driven people to the marsh edges, where they raise what crops they can hide or protect and live in tents they can strike when sentries see elephants coming (p. 86).
neighbours.secrets: The sweet rush is hateful to the giant serpents of the gorges round about, or so the Old Man of the Forest says.

neighbours.name: Dju Wa'ab
neighbours.summary:
'The pure mountain', Jebel Barkal to the Egyptians: a small flat-topped mountain in a bend of the Nile, only a hundred paces high but sheer above a flat land, a landmark at one of the few crossings of the river and an opening for east-west trade. To Kush it was the world's centre, where the creator stood to bring the universe into being, and a huge free pinnacle at its south corner seemed a natural statue of a god. Around it lie the steep pyramids of Nubian pharaohs, Kushite rock tombs and tumuli of pagan Makurian kings (p. 82).

It has a Magic aura of 3 as a striking natural feature, and burial sites may be higher. The temples' Faerie auras may once have surpassed that, but most have gone with their worshippers.

Nubian pyramids (p. 84). Unlike Egypt's they are steep, seventy degrees against about forty-five, so one thirty paces high may be twenty wide where Egypt's would be sixty. Each has a pylon gate and temple at its base. The body lay ten or more paces beneath, down steep stairs, past an antechamber for offerings like an Egyptian serdab. Otherwise tomb contents are like Egypt's.

neighbours.name: Napata
neighbours.summary: The first capital of Kush, at the foot of Dju Wa'ab, dominated by the priesthood, with over two dozen temples to single gods and to combinations with sacred meanings. Incense and chanting once fed the faerie gods and kept a Faerie aura. The temples are empty and the priests long dead; no aura remains, though echoes of those gods linger (p. 83).

neighbours.name: Kurru
neighbours.summary: The first pyramid field of the rulers of Kush, in Dju Wa'ab's shadow. Over fifty pyramids remain, fewer than half still standing; five emperors' survive, with fourteen queens', some of them renowned warriors. Two centuries of use left a Magic aura of 2 (p. 83).

neighbours.name: Nuri
neighbours.summary: The later pyramid field, on the west bank opposite Napata, in use about five hundred years until Arqamani moved the royal cemetery to Meroë, which left a Magic aura of 5. The tombs of 21 emperors stand on two plateaus with those of 52 kings' mothers, wives and princes. The western plateau has the largest and oldest, that of Taharqa, king of Kush and pharaoh of Egypt, over fifty paces high, with the parallel lines of kings' wives' pyramids and the necropolis of the kentakes, the kings' mothers. The eastern plateau holds the other twenty emperors, each in a sarcophagus of a dozen tons or more (p. 83).

neighbours.name: Dongola
neighbours.summary:
Makuria's capital, built by King Merkurios on a bluff on the east bank where the Wadi Howar meets the Nile, at the south end of the fertile Letti Basin, and commanding all movement along that bank. Within a day's journey lie about thirty villages of fine buildings, churches and monasteries, palms, vines, gardens, fields and broad pastures (p. 83).

The high stone wall that first defended it is now the innermost of seven, one for each stage of growth, with a large suburb to the north. Over ten thousand are estimated to live here, in big houses often of two storeys on wide streets. It is a weaving town (p. 77). The royal palace alone is of red brick, several storeys above anything else, with domes on top.

neighbours.name: The Church of the Granite Columns
neighbours.summary: Dongola's cathedral, a square building whose sixteen polished granite columns stand in four rows, the wide nave crossed by a narthex to make a cruciform plan inside. They hold up a mighty dome, and a true master painted its vivid Biblical frescoes. Dominion aura 7 within. The originals of the Baqt of 652 and 835 are stored here (pp. 73, 83).

neighbours.name: The Church of the Angels
neighbours.summary: An impressive cruciform church in Dongola, famous for a many-coloured stone pavement that ripples like the river in the sun. Dominion aura 6 (p. 84).

neighbours.name: Darfur
neighbours.summary: A region far from the Nile yet firmly under Makuria, living on the slave trade. Its buildings are of distinctive red brick, built as flat-topped truncated cones up to fifty paces across at the base, twenty-five at the top and six high, each shared by several families (p. 85).

neighbours.name: The Tajuwa
neighbours.summary: The people of Darfur. They look like the slave races they capture, with tight curly hair and scant beards, but have Nubian height, suggesting old mixing. Both sexes wear ankle-length smocks copied from the Arab djellebah, often striped linen; those who need freer clothes wear loose trousers and no shirt. Their warriors are mostly caravan guards with weapons and armour to personal taste, swords being uncommon. They are lax Christians at best: their churches, staffed by Nubian priests, stand nearly empty at the Eucharist, and they have sought no other gods (pp. 85-86).

neighbours.name: Uri
neighbours.summary: The royal palace of the chief of the Tajuwa, Makuria's vassal, and a long-distance market at the crossing of the Darb al-Arba'in and the Tarik al-Sudan, the savannah route west across the Great Desert (Between Sand and Sea) (p. 85).

neighbours.name: 'Ayn Farah
neighbours.summary: A red-brick monastery and church of Egyptian Copts, founded to convert the slaves. Every slave on the Darb al-Arba'in is in theory offered baptism, but slavers rarely stop, so the monks stand on the walls and shout Christ's salvation at the passing lines. The slaves seldom understand; the monks try to learn the Slavelands' many tongues but get little practice (p. 85).

neighbours.name: Fasher
neighbours.summary: The main starting point for expeditions into the Slavelands: an oasis with few lasting buildings, a camp of slavers, caravan guards and camel and cattle drovers, with a thriving rope-making trade. Slaves from the south are penned here like the stock taken with them (pp. 85-86).

neighbours.name: Samna
neighbours.summary: A town of Tajuwa red brick, with one of Makuria's only mosques, for the Arab slave traders (p. 86).

neighbours.name: Alodia
neighbours.summary:
The most remote Nubian kingdom, from the fifth cataract to beyond the meeting of the Blue and White Niles. It is held to be stronger than Makuria: richer in gold, more fertile, larger, with a bigger and better-armed army (pp. 86-87).

Its nine subkingdoms are Atbai, Bayuda, Butana, Gezira, Kabushia, Kassala, Keraba, Meroë and Soba.

neighbours.name: The Great King of Alodia
neighbours.summary: A great king like Makuria's, ruling nine subkingdoms from Soba. His army has a strong presence in rebellious Gezira. Royal Meroë has resented his rule through several failed coups (pp. 86, 88, 90).

neighbours.name: The Mortuary Society of Kassala
neighbours.summary:
The society that cares for Alodia's dead, based at Kassala with offices in every city. Its members are shunned as unlucky and respected for doing what must be done. By law they wear plain white linen smocks with a black sash; most add a black fez-like hat and a glass bell, and all carry a pouch of powder that wards off the dead (p. 88).

Every Alodian pays a mandatory burial tax in gold dust, most of which pays the society. Should a foreigner die in Alodia his family or friends must pay for the body, or it is usually left to scavengers, and the unburied dead are the likelier to haunt those who did not bury them (pp. 88-89).

Kassalan Exorcists (p. 89) deal with the dead who will not accept their place. Their Virtue, tradition and Kassalan Dust are the Kassalan Exorcists' chapter.

details.wants: To limit the power of the Cult of Dedun.

neighbours.secrets: The society's upper ranks know of the Cult of Dedun, and much of its work is designed to limit it: church burial for everyone, in anonymous graves so the famous cannot be found, guarded mausoleums, and magic that counters the cult's sorcerers. Its assassins killed Artanyeszame's master.

neighbours.name: The Ministry of Works
neighbours.summary:
The department that keeps and improves Soba, employer of most of its alchemists, who wear red robes and can be seen leading building crews or restoring public works and art. State alchemists teach the next generation at the Ministry buildings. Summae and tractatus on Soban Alchemy exist in Nubian Greek, many jealously held by rich families (p. 93).

Alchemist of Soba and Soban Alchemy (Virtues and Ability) are the Soban Alchemists' chapter, pp. 93-94. Alchemists tend to set up in the lacunae of the city's Dominion to spare themselves its penalties. Some believe the art is the last of the magic that raised the monuments of Egypt and Kush.

details.offers: The wonders of Soba, and training in Soban Alchemy.

neighbours.name: The Qore and Kentake of Meroë
neighbours.summary: King and queen mother of the city-state of Meroë, who rule together. They have often risen against Soba and failed. They are widely believed to be pagan worshippers of Apedemak: the lion is their symbol, they sit on a lion throne and they keep lions as pets (p. 90).

neighbours.name: Atbai
neighbours.summary: Alodia's easternmost, driest and poorest kingdom, with no minerals to trade. Its people are mostly herders, with some Red Sea fishing villages. The northern border is disputed with the Blemmyae, and its king has left the villages he cannot afford to defend to their mercy (p. 87).

neighbours.name: Goz Regeb
neighbours.summary: Atbai's only town of size, seat of a bishop, with a cathedral modest for Alodia (p. 87).

neighbours.name: Taflin
neighbours.summary: A fertile area where Atbaik nomads bring their flocks in the rains for a month-long festival of stock trading and marriage arrangements. Ball games are discouraged, out of respect for the Dihi (p. 87).

neighbours.name: The Dihi
neighbours.summary:
Children of Blemmyae and humans in northern Atbai. They look like the human parent, but have Blemmyae ears on the upper torso, and at their first great shock or excitement the head falls clean off the shoulders. This does not harm them and it can be put back, if they live. After that it may fall in any strenuous effort or emotional stress. Some lions of Atbai have learned to ambush Dihi, since a headless body is easy prey. A Dihi careful enough to keep his head on before having children has normal children; an afflicted Dihi's are afflicted. Most think it a curse; a few have found uses for it (p. 86).

Rules (p. 86): take Lesser Malediction. In physical or emotional stress roll a stress die: on 9 or more the head comes off, and also on any botched physical roll, when it may roll away. The head is deaf and the body blind, but a head that can see its body can shout it commands. Reattaching takes a round. Dihi often have Magical Blood (Realms of Power: Magic p. 46) to balance it.

neighbours.name: Bayuda
neighbours.summary: Unlike its fellows, a kingdom of countless small villages scattered through sandy desert into the Gilif Hills, with no one city. Each village seems to have its own language, unrelated to any neighbour's or to Nubian (p. 87).
neighbours.secrets: They all speak one language, but under a magical curse no native Bayudan can understand another speaking it. An outsider who learns it from any village is understood by all.

neighbours.name: The Gilif Hills
neighbours.summary: Deep ravines and jagged crags, an unforgiving land said to be haunted by leopard spirits. It does hold uncommonly many leopards, and some may have supernatural powers. For the Gilif leopards use the lion's statistics (The Book of Mundane Beasts) with Size +1, which takes 2 from Strength and adds 1 to Quickness (p. 87).

neighbours.name: Butana
neighbours.summary: A sheltered kingdom between Keraba and Soba, Alodia's main farmland, well watered by tributaries of the Nile and the Atbara. Its people are known for hard work and helped by Soba's alchemists, who rely on Naqan glass (p. 87).

neighbours.name: Naqa
neighbours.summary: Capital of Butana, an old city of Meroë's age on the seasonal Wadi Awateib, where lesser wadis come down from the plateau, thirty miles from the Nile. It is a trading city on the way to Ethiopia, and many slaves from the south get their first taste of civilisation here. It is famed for glass: unusually pure sand gives a clear glass with a slight green tinge, traded north in ingots, and its glassblowers are justly respected (pp. 87-88).

neighbours.name: Gezira
neighbours.summary: The southernmost and newest kingdom, between the White and Blue Niles, the least Nubian, sharing blood with Ethiopians and Aithiopes, and poorer than the others. Known for rebellion, many of its people see their vassalage as conquest, and the great king's army may provoke more riots than it prevents (p. 88).

neighbours.name: Sennar
neighbours.summary: Capital of Gezira, home of a dynasty of Nubian and Megabaran blood (chapter 9). Men and women are equal among the Gezirans, the monarch is as often a queen as a king, and a quarter of the army are warrior women quartered here (p. 88).

neighbours.name: Kabushia
neighbours.summary: The Gates: the northernmost and among the most heavily fortified subkingdoms, its city full of warriors, its outer districts growing food for the standing army, with whole villages of smiths turning Meroë's iron into weapons. No friend of Makuria: in the Umayyad invasion the Makurian royal family, sent south for safety, were seized by its king and ransomed at an extortionate price, and it has never let its great neighbour forget it (p. 88).

neighbours.name: Kassala
neighbours.summary:
Home of the Mortuary Society and a city of the dead, with more dead than living among its tombs, cemeteries and monuments. Some graves are ancient, most from Christian Alodia, belonging to those deemed worth remembering for money or fame. No trade route comes near it; one road crosses the plain from the west (p. 88).

Other cities pay Kassalans to take their corpses. Porters gather the bodies for morticians to prepare, hired pallbearers carry them, and priests do little but the burial rite. Others make shrouds, death masks and incense, or work as mourners and grave guardians. With so small a congregation it has no Dominion aura, and some parts have a weak Magic aura.

Embalming is rare: most are wrapped in plain shrouds, with a clay or metal mask, and the wrappings often bear protective texts of folk-magical value. For more, the flesh is taken from the bones, which is held to speed the soul to redemption, ward off ghosts and foil sorcerers.

neighbours.name: Keraba
neighbours.summary: A kingdom ruled from el-Hobagi when power drifted upstream after Kush, then eclipsed by Soba in the sixth century and made a vassal. It is now ruled from Sufra (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Sufra
neighbours.summary: The present seat of the kings of Keraba (p. 89).

neighbours.name: El-Hobagi
neighbours.summary: A huge tumulus, one of Alodia's last pagan royal burials, among other high-status tombs. It has never been entered, despite tales of wealth; if it is like others, the entrance is at the summit, with a shaft going down. Beside it a temple of ram-headed Atum is in remarkable repair, with a Faerie aura of 3, as though still used, though no one has ever been seen to enter (p. 89).

neighbours.name: Kawa
neighbours.summary: One of Alodia's six episcopal sees, named only in that list (p. 76).

neighbours.name: Shanqir
neighbours.summary: One of the seven episcopal sees of Makuria and Nobatia, named only in that list (p. 76).

neighbours.name: Meroë
neighbours.summary:
Medewi to its builders, raised by King Aspelta of Kush six centuries before Christ as his chief palace, capital after Arqamani took the empire from the priests around 300 BC. At its height it ruled the whole Upper Nile; now it is a city-state within Alodia, and the Island of Meroë is the vast triangle between the Nile and the Atbara that it rules (p. 89).

It is famed for iron and then gold. Its outskirts look almost industrial with bloomeries and blast furnaces, and Meroitic ironwork is prized far and wide. Its people have a superior air, born of their ancient heritage (pp. 89-90).
neighbours.ruler: The Qore and Kentake of Meroë
neighbours.secrets: The Initiation Script of the Undying Ones survives only among the writings on the monuments here, a site the Mortuary Society patrols (p. 100).

neighbours.name: Taqasi
neighbours.summary: The chief residence of the King of Meroë, a palace of about twenty rooms on two levels round a courtyard, with a ramp to a podium, amid luxurious grounds. A pride of lions roams the manicured 'jungle', fed on live prey released within the walls, so it is unwise to come uninvited. From the podium the king and kentake receive visitors and watch the lions feed; if a meeting goes badly, the two may be combined (p. 90).

neighbours.name: Begarawiyah
neighbours.summary:
The royal necropolis outside Meroë, the widest of Kush's three (with Kurru and Nuri) (p. 90).

Southern cemetery: the oldest, of the same age as Nuri, with nine pyramids, four of them emperors' and five princes' and queens', and 195 unmarked tombs of commoners. Magic aura 4, from over four hundred years of royal burial.

Northern cemetery: used after Arqamani moved the capital. His pyramid stands with those of 29 other kings and 27 kentakes, queens and royals, and just three non-royal tombs. Magic aura 5, from six and a half centuries.

Western cemetery: 113 tombs, none royal and so no pyramids, simple and poorly preserved. No Magic aura.
neighbours.secrets: This is the haunt of Alodia's most powerful devotees of Dedun, and some pyramids are occupied, with higher Magic auras aligned to the dead. Artanyeszame excludes all other Undying Ones from the southern cemetery. Two more dwell in the northern and a third in the western.

neighbours.name: Soba
neighbours.summary:
Alodia's capital, on the east bank of the Blue Nile just above its meeting with the White, spread over a gently rolling plain cut by shallow streams. People live on the mounds between them, with wide open land around. Gravel mounds hold big wooden houses coated in white clay that glitters with mica, each in a lush garden. Red-brick mounds bear seventeen churches decorated with gold leaf, chief of them the Church of Manbali, the cathedral. The Dominion is 3 near these, with many lacunae where it does not reach. Small monasteries, each of a few monks, stand around the town and on the banks. It alone in Alodia has a mosque, for a sizeable population of Muslims from Egypt and the southern sultanates (p. 93).

The city is famous for its alchemists' wonders. Corner poles shed light at night to rival the moon. The streets are unusually smooth for wheels, and some Soban vehicles hover just off the ground. Streams, sometimes canalised, carry stone barges that float miraculously with grain and timber. Fountains run upwards, stone statues in gardens are tethered lest they float away, bridges are of transparent metal, and roof tiles make the city smell sweet.

neighbours.name: Church of Manbali
neighbours.summary: The most prominent and luxurious of Soba's seventeen churches, and its cathedral (p. 93).

neighbours.name: The Red Sea Hills
neighbours.summary: The land between the Nile valley and the Red Sea, broadly the Blemmyae's, with the Pakhoras road to Atbara as its western border. Gold was found here under the Fatimids, and gold and emeralds are mined here. Treaties between Blemmyan and Makurian kings fix the limits but last only as long as the signatories' lives. Blemmyae and Makurians have lately found a common enemy in the Ja'alin (pp. 72, 77, 96).

neighbours.name: The Blemmyae Tribes
neighbours.summary:
A nomadic, warlike race of magic humans of the Red Sea Hills and the Nubian Desert, and of the Libyan Desert in the west, with no head or neck and a face on the upper chest. Libyan Blemmyae are merchants who lead camel trains. Nubian Blemmyae are aggressive and rightly feared. They herd camels for wool, leather, meat and milk, and hunt gazelle and ostrich. They raid caravans between Nobatia and Alodia for luxuries, and as their reputation means no resistance from Nubian merchants, most victims escape alive, often with their bulky goods. Bedouin get no such mercy: there is no treaty with them, and they are interlopers. Regular tribute to the Makurian and Alodian thrones is thinly veiled fines for past raids or bribes for future ones (pp. 95-96).

Five tribes, named for five cities they once held: Phoinikon, Khiris, Taphis, Talmis and Prima. One king rules all, sometimes at Sawakin but more often among his family like any other Blemmya. He is respected and usually obeyed, but relies on the five phylarchs, tribal chiefs. On taking the crown he names as heir one phylarch, not his own tribe's, and cannot change it; if that phylarch dies the honour goes to his nearest male relative. Under them hypotyranni lead bands of about fifty families.

Men outnumber women ten to one, but women do not age and bear for many generations, and bloodlines are watched lest a woman marry her descendants. They have resisted Christianity and Islam, worshipping the stars and Kushite gods, Mandulis above all. Their language, Beja, descends from Meroitic.

Characters (p. 96). Their faces are larger than a man's between wide shoulders, their hearing is poor as their ears are under their arms, and their hairless bodies, bare above the waist, resist damage. Women have no breasts and feed children goat or camel milk. Armour needs eye holes or a visor, so must be rigid, and large shields are of little use; warriors tend to be mounted skirmishers with slings. They are Magic Humans (Realms of Power: Magic p. 32) with the inherited features the rules cite: Puissant Thrown Weapon, Tough, Hunchback and Poor Hearing, and for men Age Quickly, giving a human lifespan. They take a Social Status suited to their tribal role, or to their magical nature among humans.

neighbours.name: Badi
neighbours.summary: Abandoned by honest merchants, a fetid pit of lawlessness whose long quays serve the pirates who prey on the Red Sea. Anything can be had here, and men can be hired to get what cannot be bought. The Blemmyae keep land travellers away for their own good, and few captains dare the sea: by standing order of Egypt and Arabia, ships known to have docked here forfeit the lives of captain and crew, and passengers are sold as slaves (p. 96).

neighbours.name: Sawakin
neighbours.summary:
Ptolemy's Limen Evangelis, Port of Good Hope; both Sawakin and the Beja U Suk mean 'prisons'. Solomon is said to have banished his most troublesome jinn here, and as far as anyone knows they still sit in a magical jail no one can find (p. 96).

A round island at the end of a long inlet, a fantastic town built wholly of bands of white, pink and red coral. Its lighthouse is so shaded from white at the base to red at the top that it can hardly be seen at dawn or dusk. Red coral has a strong sympathy with controlling demons (ArM5 p. 110), which might guide those seeking the prisons. It is the end of the only safe road from Atbara (p. 81).

It rivals 'Aydhab, Badi and Qusayr, and is rising at Badi's expense on trade with Arabia, Persia and distant Hind and on passage to Mecca for the hajj. It sometimes exports coral, mostly 'snake's tongue', forked twigs of rough red stone (p. 97).
neighbours.ruler: Sometimes the King of the Blemmyae

neighbours.name: The Prisons of the Jinn
neighbours.summary: The jail beneath Sawakin of the jinn Solomon banished, whose whereabouts no one knows (p. 96).
neighbours.secrets: There are 111 jinn in prisons of coral beneath the town, all hostile to man. Most are petty nuisances Solomon would not free; a few are truly terrible. One is rumoured to be Ashmodai, Prince of Temptation, one of the ten mightiest demons save Satan himself (Realms of Power: the Infernal p. 27). No one knows, and any number of jinn claim to be him.

neighbours.name: The Cult of Dedun
neighbours.summary:
Dedun, the Egyptians' Dedwen and god of incense, was to the Kushite priests lord of what is gathered in this life for the next: prosperity, as the dead were buried with their goods; fame and reputation; the patron of priests who kept the dead's memory; guardian of the dead and lord of the fields of prosperity; god of salt, natron, naphtha and all that preserves. His chief centre was Napata. The struggle of priests and kings is often shown as the uraeus, his sign, fighting the lion of Apedemak (p. 97).

Under this cult the pyramids of Napata and Meroë rose and the fields of the dead were tended. By holding the dead it ruled the living, until Arqamani, with the priests of Apedemak, stormed Napata, killed the priests and took the royal dead (p. 97). Few in Nubia now suspect it survives.

details.wants: Bodily immortality, and the return of its temporal power.

neighbours.secrets:
The priesthood of Kush included Canaanite necromancers (Ancient Magic, chapter 2), some come with the Tribe of Dan, others after Saul's purge of Canaan's priests. Those seeking that Mystery may find clues leading here. Holding the royal dead, the priests held their living relatives, by the threat of wracking their spirits after death (p. 97).

The cult lurks in graveyards and forgotten tombs. It now cares less for keeping the dead than for power over them, and the Red's subtle influence has made it, knowingly or not, a corrupting force serving oblivion. It is a Mystery Cult in informal districts, each worshipping at a grave site under a temple priest; those priests meet every few years. Most members above adherent seek magical power, not worship; its Mysteries are of the Magic realm, not Faerie. Some priests are fanatics, but none deceive themselves: it is a way to eternal life, once offered after death as an akh (chapter 4), and now as lordship over one's own decaying flesh (pp. 97-98).

Adherents come from every walk of life, some from families loyal for centuries, some wooed by friends in the priesthood, some through curiosity about Kush's graves or research into long life or necromancy. They attend night rites at the local temple, usually four times a year, favour each other in daily life, and help when a temple priest asks. Altar priests assist the temple priest, keep the temple and the discipline, and silently kill an adherent who endangers secrecy; there are rarely more than four to a temple. A temple priest usually leaves family and normal life to live in squalor in his temple on what can be scrounged, sometimes on the bodies he steals, and gathers a court of noted corpses, each prepared by his own rite and bearing his name in Meroitic, which makes each a permanent Arcane Connection to him. There are currently a dozen Undying Ones along the Nile (pp. 98-100).

The cult teaches no magic of its own, but draws the unsavoury. Sorcerers among it are often Learned Magicians, or have Corpse Magic, the Goetic Arts (Summoning and Commanding, in a version that reaches ghosts and bears an Infernal taint), or curse magic such as Hex, Cursing, the Vulnero Art or Malediction (p. 102).

The ranks, Initiation Scripts, Virtues, court strength, the loss of the Gift, the common powers of the Undying Ones and Corpse Magic are the Cult of Dedun's chapter and rules/africa.py (pp. 98-102). The errata (p. 87) correct the temple priest's script: she will not necessarily become bedridden and die of old age at Decrepitude 5.

Under the Empire of Kush a body was embalmed, coated in molten glass and set on a pillar, visible for all to see, and by some magic not burned. After the priesthood of Dedun fell that secret was lost, and the body was first put in a hollow statue of its likeness, gold for royalty, silver for princes and the rich, earthenware even for the poor, and then in glass (p. 88).

neighbours.name: The Pyramid of Arrakkamani
neighbours.summary: A royal pyramid in the southern necropolis of Begarawiyah. A curse in Meroitic is written at the tomb's entrance (p. 92).

details.tomb_hooks: Evil Custom (Site, Minor), Inhuman Covenfolk (Residents, Minor), Seed of Madness (Residents, Minor)

tomb_curses.name: Those That Enter My Tomb in Their Impurity
tomb_curses.condition: Those that enter the tomb in their impurity
tomb_curses.excoriation: Their flesh shall decay and their bones perish: the Enfeebled Major Flaw. Written in Meroitic on the entrance. Artanyeszame's Might makes him immune, and his purification rite protects his servants. (Base 30, +1 Touch, +2 Room.)

tomb_wards.name: Shroud of Sands
tomb_wards.effect: A cloak of sandstone disks on twine, moving up to ten thousand cubic paces of sand, enough to bury the pyramid or dig out the tunnel to the burial chamber; slow, and a threat only to the immobile (Base 1, +2 Voice, +1 Conc, +1 Part, +3 Size; +5 24 uses/day).

tomb_wards.name: Glory of the Royal Lion
tomb_wards.effect: A statue of Apedemak whose lit eyes hold one looker a round, until its uses end, motionless save to keep facing it, even out of sight; they starve unless released (Base 5, +1 Eye, +3 Moon, +1 release; +4 12/day, +6 Pen 12).
tomb_wards.deactivation: A command word in Meroitic releases those held

tomb_wards.name: Sovereign Ward Against Wandering Shadows
tomb_wards.effect: No spirit of Might 25 or less enters or leaves the pyramid if it Penetrates. Queen Weteriken, trapped by it, claims to have enchanted it herself; Artanyeszame gained his Might inside and is immune (Base 25, +0 Touch, +0 Sun, +3 Structure; +1 2/day, +3 environmental trigger, +13 Pen 26).

tomb_traps.name: The Receding Steps
tomb_traps.text: The steps to the burial chamber recede into a smooth 20 pace ramp ending on a hard floor, +30 damage; the roll catches the sides.

tomb_traps.name: The False Burial Chamber
tomb_traps.text: Filled with fake treasure, and good for an ambush; the roll sees through it from outside.

tomb_traps.name: The Rain of Poisoned Darts
tomb_traps.text: Each person is struck by 1-6 darts, each a Light Wound unless the roll is made (average 3 Light Wounds).

tomb_traps.name: The Falling Slab
tomb_traps.text: A massive stone slab, +15 damage, which traps people on the wrong side; the roll dives clear.

neighbours.secrets:
Artanyeszame's home. His court of the dead, of strength 181 over four dozen corpses, among them King Arrakkamani and his mother Weteriken, is posed in a chamber as if at audience, paying homage to the central throne where he broods. Magic aura 6, aligned to the dead. The book scores the lair as a covenant site, for 259 Build Points overall (p. 92); the Tomb tab holds its curse, enchantments and traps.

Covenfolk: the three bouda sisters and a dozen magical hyenas, some with Magic Sensitivity, who can find Corpus vis in the necropolis's long-buried dead, and are prone to bouts of madness.

Library (45 Build Points): Inscription on Petitioning the Dead, a summa on Corpse Magic, Level 8, Quality 6; Initiation Script for Corpse Magic, Script Bonus +15. Specialists (56): two altar priests (Magic Lore 5), four grave guardians (Single Weapon 4), the ghost of Queen Weteriken, the three bouda. Vis (35): 2 pawns of Vim a year (paint flecks from magical texts), 4 of Corpus (bodies robbed by hyenas), 1 of Ignem (glass exposed to the dawn sun on the rising of Sirius).

neighbours.name: The Master of Abu Hamad
neighbours.summary: A merchant friend of the characters is being ruined by a rival with an endless supply of their trade goods, from a magic reed basket that seems to create them permanently without vis. The trail leads to Abu Hamad (p. 82).

stages.title: The Magical Basket
stages.clues: A rival's endless goods; a reed basket; the trail to Abu Hamad.
stages.ignored: The merchant is ruined, and the characters are left a mystery.

stages.title: Attempted Regicide
stages.clues: Having met Hamad and lived, the characters interest the Great King of Makuria, as Hamad makes sure. They are summoned to Dongola with the basket, and run into court politics stirred by his agents.
stages.ignored: Before the king the basket's true purpose shows: a fearsome jinn comes out and attacks him. Even if it is beaten, the characters may be blamed for endangering him and lose any favour they had.

stages.title: The Demons of Sawakin
stages.clues: Hamad seeks to master the jinni imprisoned at Sawakin, creatures Solomon himself thought too dangerous.
stages.ignored: With them he could smash any Aegis of the Hearth and defeat even Hermetic magi. The characters must race to the Coral City for a showdown of Hermetic and Solomonic magic.

neighbours.secrets: Hamad arranged this to meet and weigh the characters. He insists they keep the basket as compensation. It works by a bound jinn, which fetches the goods from elsewhere, and a power makes it read to Hermetic Investigation as a normal enchantment, like a Shell of False Determination. Other clashes with the Ja'alin and his minions should fill out the arc.

neighbours.name: The Siege of Berber
neighbours.summary: The characters are hired to break the blockade of Berber, or something they need is trapped inside. Three Ja'alin meks hold the three landward approaches, each with two score warriors and a dozen jinni; given notice, three more lie a day away and six more within three (p. 83).
neighbours.secrets: The characters are the first outsiders here in three years. The people are enslaved to Ja'alin overlords and set to digging under the town. For what, and for whom? 'Izz el-Afram Hamad is the obvious mastermind, but by no means the only possibility.

neighbours.name: Theft by the Dead
neighbours.summary: Robbers, probably foreigners, exploit the Nubian horror of the dead by faking their deaths and going about as their own walking corpses. No one reports them, and no one follows them to their graveyard haunt (p. 73).
neighbours.secrets: Their work has drawn faeries or demons, who take the look of real corpses and copy the crimes. The characters are drawn in when one robs them in the shape of someone they know to be dead.

neighbours.name: Six Hundred and Eighty Nine
neighbours.summary: A crazed old man has for years sold clay amulets marked chi-pi-theta and spent the money on used swords, over six hundred now, fixed to his outer walls. His house is a local landmark. One day the swords are gone (p. 74).
neighbours.secrets: He is hiding them across the city, muttering in Aramaic, believing that with all 689 in their exact places he will summon Michael, archangel of the sword, to cast out the city's evil. Will it work? Will it bring an archangel? Will Michael define evil as men do? Sodom and Gomorrah were the last cities he cleansed.

neighbours.name: Freedom Fortress
neighbours.summary: The characters stop for help at a small fortress of the river (p. 80).
neighbours.secrets: Its garrison are escaped slaves posing as soldiers. Some would kill the characters if they guess the truth; another faction warns them and may want to leave with them or use them to take the fort. The characters could gain useful allies.

neighbours.name: The Soul Exchange
neighbours.summary: Seeking something rare, the characters visit a fortress famed for its black market, and find it a den of every vice (p. 82).
neighbours.secrets: Its people are ghosts, trapped by the demon that killed them. Each is promised freedom for winning a soul for Hell, but the demon just consumes the ghost and traps its victim instead. Only slaying the demon in the caverns beneath the fort frees them.

neighbours.name: The Blind God's Eyes
neighbours.summary: Treasure hunters have long searched Napata for the Kushite priests' lost wealth, and legend says the missing statues of the gods show the way. The priests' last act was to wipe the paint from the statues' eyes, making them mere stone (p. 84).
neighbours.secrets: Wind has uncovered one, and a merchant's daughter, waiting for her father at the well, idly coloured in its eyes with kohl. The faerie that lived in it has returned, and it now walks slowly and inexorably to its destination. There is a town in the way.

neighbours.name: The Hawk That Thought It Was A God
neighbours.summary: A desert hawk circles Dju Wa'ab crying, and lands on a temple roof every day at noon (p. 84).
neighbours.secrets: A faerie animal with the merest scrap of Might, once emissary of Mandulis. If characters are near at midday it takes them for the old priests and gives his last message, that Anhur's Spear lies where the sun meets the sea and the waves lie still. What does it mean?

neighbours.name: Thirty Centuries
neighbours.summary: A character is visited, by vision, Second Sight or vivid dream, by the ghost of an ancient warrior in a black tabard. His unit is surrounded and needs help. He can lead the characters to Kerma, where the battle can be seen on the night of a new moon (p. 84).
neighbours.secrets: Kerma died in a civil war, and the stones mark each side's fallen. Every new moon the ghosts fight again; a black soldier killed joins the white, and vice versa, and his grave's stones change colour over the year, making the mixed graves. If one side stands unopposed the army will unite under one commander, free to leave. White holds most graves now and gains yearly, the work of a temple priest of Dedun. What will he do with 25,000 ghostly warriors?

neighbours.name: Valley of Elephants
neighbours.summary: An Old Man of the Forest, a magical elephant and guardian of the valley, appears before the characters. A local king plans to drain the marshes for farming and drive off the herds. The sweet rush, he says, is hateful to the giant serpents of the gorges; without it men and elephants alike will feed them. The king will be hard to convince. Is it true? Can there be a compromise (p. 86)?

neighbours.name: Black Coral
neighbours.summary: Someone comes to Sawakin for coral, to trade or to enchant, and buys stone that draws evil spirits instead of warding them off (p. 96).
neighbours.secrets: An earthquake cracked the coral under a warehouse, and an Infernal jinn reached a labourer clearing the rubble, who now leads a cult of 'Ashmodai'. The cult corrupts the coral and tracks its buyers, and recruits the demons they attract, once the buyer is dead or corrupted.

neighbours.name: Grandmother Lion
neighbours.summary: The characters meet an Aithiops slave escaped from Taqasi, with poor Nubian, who begs them to free her grandmother from the king (p. 96).
neighbours.secrets: The 'grandmother' is a magical lioness of Taqasi, the lion's equal of a sorceress, with powers including human shape. The king found her out and holds her cub to ensure her behaviour. She has the Gift, so some pet lions distrust her and may betray her. If she and her son go free, she might let the cub become a character's familiar or companion.

neighbours.name: The Green Stone Hand
neighbours.summary: The characters come by a hand of green stone (p. 90).
neighbours.secrets: It is the missing part of the Djet in Cleopatra's Tomb. An agent snooping in their things tells Artanyeszame, who realises the Djet can show him the Book of Thoth. He has only to trick them into wanting to find the tomb.

neighbours.name: The Queen's Ghost
neighbours.summary: A junior member of the Mortuary Society asks the characters to help free the ghost of a Kushite queen and lay her soul to rest (p. 90).
neighbours.secrets: He omits that Queen Weteriken is Artanyeszame's ally and tutor, in his pyramid. The society hopes the characters will weaken or destroy him for them.

neighbours.name: Theft of the Dead
neighbours.summary: A vis source of the characters is being raided by a man plainly not taking it for himself. This may be their first sight of the Cult of Dedun (p. 102).
neighbours.secrets: He is an adherent. His Prohibition stops him naming his master or leading them to his temple if he suspects he is watched, and forcing him triggers it.

neighbours.name: Help from the Black
neighbours.summary: Soon after a clash with the cult, a potential ally approaches the characters. She has been fighting its corruption, and asks help to free a friend captured by an Undying One (p. 102).
neighbours.secrets: She is secretly a knowing servant of the Black, and her friend is an akh (chapter 4), who could be another strong ally.

neighbours.name: If You Can't Beat Them, Join Them
neighbours.summary: The characters' ally seems ever better informed about the cult's rivals, and steers them against those rivals (p. 102).
neighbours.secrets: She has joined in secret. She tells herself she is bringing it down from within, but immortality has seduced her, and she hopes the characters will find where the Initiation Script for the transformation lies.

neighbours.name: Ethiopia
neighbours.summary:
Punt to the ancient Egyptians, who thought it the home of the gods and the Sun's resting place, then the Empire of Axum, Ethiopia in 1220 is a Christian empire of smaller kingdoms under one emperor, cut off from Europe by hostile tribes and Muslim tributaries. Agaw, Bet Amhara, Medri Bahri and Shewa are its core. Dahlak holds the islands off the coast, Muslim merchants and corsairs hold the Red Sea, pagans and Blemmyae fill the north and west, and the sultans of Adal, Dewaro, Hadiya and Ifat line the south. Beyond them lie sweltering jungle and the Torrid Zone (Art & Academe p. 27, BS&S pp. 13-14).

The empire runs from the Semien Mountains and the Takkaze in the west to the Blemmyae hills in the north, the Ganale and Wabe Shebele rivers in the south, and the Danakil desert and the Bab-al-Mandab in the east. The cliffs and salt flats of the Great Rift Valley part highland from lowland. It is not the land of the Mythic Aithiopes, though in antiquity the two may have been one realm. Greek writers placed it beyond Nubia and gave it King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia, of the Perseus story.

Axum grew as Rome declined, trading with Rome, Persia and southern Arabia. When Kush fell its armies crushed the Blemmyae at Meroe, and in 525 Emperor Kaleb's generals took the Jewish city-states of South Arabia. For 250 years its emperors struck gold, silver and copper coin. Islam closed the Red Sea and Constantinople to it; the sultan of Cairo charged a fee before a new abuna could be sent; Southern Arabia, Nubia, Adal, Ifat and Yemen broke away; and the last coins bear Emperor Armah's name, in 614. In 960 the Jewish queen Gudit, called Isat or 'Fire', burned the churches and left a patchwork of small hereditary fiefs. For nearly two hundred years only the Church held any wide authority.

In 1137 Takla Heymanot beat Gudit's heirs and claimed Axum's inheritance for the Zagwe dynasty. Five brothers and sons ruled in order after him, Kedus Harbe from 1180, and revived the custom of shutting up young heirs on a mountain. Lalibela's reign now turns isolated fiefs into something like one state. Records are so thin that borders, rulers and great men are mostly guesswork, free for the storyguide to shape.

Lord and commoner live much alike, on grain, vegetables, hunting and livestock (cattle, donkeys, goats, chickens, camels). Communities store surplus against famine and the emperor's wandering court; few merchants exist without a lord's backing. Agaw, Amhara, Tigray and Tigrinya dialects mark the only ethnic lines, forgotten at any outside threat. Lowlanders wear loose cotton, linen or silk, the bright woven shemma, shawls, sandals; highlanders wool, skin and fur, heavy vests and boots, the men trousers and long thin sticks. Men favour round flat caps and short hair, seldom a beard; women wear their hair long or in small braids. Faces mix African, Mediterranean and South Arabian features, light to dark.

No one eats pork or shellfish. Wat, a thick stew of meat and vegetables, is served on injera, sour teff flatbread, in place of plates, and only the right hand touches food. People drink katikala from millet, tela beer and tej, a honey wine. Coffee is known in Agaw and Shewa, whose warriors march on balls of ground bunn in lard or butter; a few Sufi sects near Harar praise it. A minority keep several wives, whatever the Coptic Church's letters say, and answer for every child they father.

Highland and Red Sea lowland are two cultures. The plateau has many climates, with dry alpine country and hard water; the Tigray-speaking lowlanders live by the sea in constant heat. They raid each other's herds and feud over land. Farmers grow teff above all, with millet, barley, carrots, lettuce and onions. Ethiopia trades north and west with Nubia, and little by sea, for Asir and Yemen wink at piracy. It sells skins, spices, elephants, ivory and pagan slaves, to Nubians and to the markets of Harar and Dahlak. Gold comes from the southwest, the west and the escarpment; salt from the Rift is valuable enough to pass as money in places.

Sheer slopes, few fords and no reliable bridges make land travel slow, and landing places are too scarce for much river traffic. Horses, camels and donkeys cope; anyone who can goes by sea. Beyond the old gods Astar and Mahrem, whose shrines Christianity razed or converted, no pagan community is tolerated. Tribes beyond the Takkaze and south of Damot raid for captives; enslaved pagans live like animals, standing decrees in Agaw and Shewa let anyone kill them, and the Church does not try to convert them.

Baboon troupes of five to 250 and hyena packs of four to twenty are common. Elephants and the serpents that eat them, gazelles, hippopotamuses, leopards, lions, antelope, rhinoceroses and zebras thrive; giraffes and flying foxes live in the south, painted dogs and pangolins near the Semiens. Traders take hides and live beasts.

The Periplus of the Erythean Sea, known in Latin and in the Classical Greek of Arrian of Nicomedia, charts this sea's ports in 66 short chapters. It tells of Azania near the Torrid Zone, a kingdom far to the east, the heirs of Alexander in their fortresses, and the Pyralaoi or 'Fire-people', with Arab slaves for clerks; of strong iron, pearls as big as a fist, lakkos chromatinos, spikenard and bdellium. Copies are rare, mostly in private hands at Alexandria, Constantinople and Jerusalem.
neighbours.secrets:
The Periplus is a tractatus in Latin or Classical Greek on each of Area Lore: Ethiopia, Area Lore: Erythean Sea Coast, Area Lore: Red Sea Coast and Magic Lore, Quality 5 (p. 107).

A Jew or Falasha is unusual but not an Outsider unless also a blacksmith (p. 110). A large polygamous family might take Close Family Ties (p. 109). Infantry bear sword, shield and an 8-foot spear, thrown about twenty-five paces; cavalry wear heavy mail, most others the equal of quilted armor; the Amharic word for 'spear' and 'war' is the same. Militias have a shield and a dagger or spear (p. 110).

neighbours.name: The Bleeding Trees of the Red Sea Coast
neighbours.summary: Small, jealously hidden stands of frankincense and myrrh grow along Ethiopia's Red Sea coast, and their keepers cut long wounds in the thorny trunks to gather the dried resin, as in Yemen and Asir. The jaculi that nest in such trees in Arabia are not found here, so some think the trees were planted. If they were brought from Yemen or Soqotra, no one tends them now. Yemeni merchants may be spoiling them to protect their own trade.
neighbours.secrets: The jaculi are in The Cradle and the Crescent pp. 116-118, Soqotra in Rival Magic p. 110 (p. 113).

neighbours.name: The Mountains of the Moon
neighbours.summary: Vast, towering peaks past the southern jungles, which Herodotus gave as the Torrid Zone's border.

neighbours.name: The Semien Mountains
neighbours.summary: The high range between Bet Amhara and Agaw, cut by the Blue Nile. Painted dogs and pangolins live here. Somewhere in them is the cave where Saint Yared spent his last years, still undiscovered.

neighbours.name: Medri Bahri
neighbours.summary: The northern coastal kingdom, of Upper and Lower Bur along the shore, Eritrea to the north and Tigre in the middle: most of Ethiopia's lowlands, hot, humid and full of mangroves, with farmers and fishermen, rising to the plateau as far as the Takkaze. Its ruler, the bahri negus, ranks second only to the emperor. Rectangular cut-stone churches are commonest here.

neighbours.name: Bab-al-Mandab
neighbours.summary: The strait between Ethiopia and Yemen, held by Yemen's Muslim navies, friends of the sultan of Adal.
neighbours.secrets: Passing it requires a story, as with the straits of Gibraltar (p. 114).

neighbours.name: Erta Ale
neighbours.summary: 'Smoking Mountain', an active cone of black basalt in a hollow of the Danakil, its pit holding a lake of molten rock that spits burning debris or spills over the rim. Its low bare slopes grow almost nothing. A fiery, capricious ifrit jinni lives here.
neighbours.secrets: An ideal site for the volcano magic of Hermetic Projects (p. 115).

neighbours.name: Adulis
neighbours.summary: The old port of Axum, sacked in the eighth century when Yemen occupied the Dahlak islands to punish piracy, and never truly recovered. Once a great trading port, it sees far fewer merchants now, though caravans from Nubia and Egypt and ships of the Red Sea still end here. Bishop and governor both live here; the bishop's large Byzantine church stands in the northern quarter. It keeps a large slave market. Teachers of Amharic, Arabic, Ge'ez and Artes Liberales are easy to find.

neighbours.name: Debarwa
neighbours.summary: Capital of Tigre and of all Medri Bahri, on the Mereb river some twenty miles from the plateau's edge. The bahri negus lives here, grown rich on the copper, gold and iron mines of the escarpment, the coast roads and a large Saturday market, and his army is strong and well equipped. Bouda faeries roam its roads and wild forests, driving those they meet to lust and murder, so hyenas are hated here. He pays a bounty on live hyenas, hoping to catch the faeries.
neighbours.secrets: The bounty is unlikely to work (p. 115).

neighbours.name: Massawa
neighbours.summary: A trade port on two islands and the shore, fifteen leagues northwest of Adulis, which rose after Adulis fell. Sheikh Hanafi, a Muslim sworn to the bahri negus, has built a mosque of carved white coral on the larger island, sends missionaries into Ethiopia, and brought shipwrights from Yemen and the Hijaz to grow his fleet. His captains carry Mecca-bound pilgrims free.

neighbours.name: Negash
neighbours.summary: A modest hamlet of Christians and Muslims on the road from Axum to Zeila, some thirty leagues east southeast of Axum. It has a small stone mosque and the tomb of Emperor Armah, called here Ashama ibn Abjar al-Najashi, who sheltered the Prophet's daughter. Devout Muslims come as pilgrims, and the neighbours leave them in peace by old custom.

neighbours.name: The Tomb of Armah
neighbours.summary: The grave of the emperor who gave refuge to the first Muslims.

neighbours.name: Abba Garima Monastery
neighbours.summary: Built north of Adwa by Abba Garima of the Nine Saints. They say a nearby spring rose where he spat on the stones, and that its water grants long life.

neighbours.name: The Church of Kulubi
neighbours.summary: A pilgrimage church on the Feast of the Angel Gabriel, Tahsas 18 or December 16, when clergy baptize children born by the archangel's help, who are often named for him.

neighbours.name: Bi'isa Monastery
neighbours.summary: The northernmost of the Nine Saints' houses, built by Abba Alef on the south bank of the Mareb.

neighbours.name: Bet Amhara
neighbours.summary: The rich, fertile breadbasket of the empire and the old heart of Axum, running from the Semiens across the plateau into the Rift. Lesser realms make it up: Wag guarding the north against the Blemmyae, Begemder and Falasha, Lasta and the lands of Amhara. The Jamma parts it from Shewa, the Abbay from Agaw and the Takkaze from Medri Bahri. Its lords above all hold the Kebra Negast true. Round timber churches are common here.

neighbours.name: Axum
neighbours.summary:
The old imperial capital, almost 4,000 strong, a religious centre where emperors are crowned, proud of its past. When he visits, the emperor leaves his tents for two stone palaces of the old days: Ta'akha Maryam, 120 by 80 meters with 50 rooms, and smaller Dungur, called Queen Makkeda's home.

A low wall sets off the necropolis and its thirteen monoliths, among them the three great stelae, taller than any Egyptian obelisk. Ezana's Stone stands here, repeating one message in Ge'ez, Classical Greek and Ancient Sabaean: King Ezana's deeds and his conversion by Saint Frumentius. North of town, Gudit's Field is a pasture of old tombs and man-high stelae, near the rock-cut reservoir called Sheba's Bath. On a small hill Abba Pantelewon and Abba Liqanos's monastery, a pagan temple nearly 750 years ago, is still at work.
neighbours.secrets: Knowing one of its languages, a reader may study Ezana's Stone for a season as a Quality 5 tractatus on one of the other two, or on Area Lore: Ethiopia. Ancient Sabaean is also found at Petra, at Yeha and in Yemen and 'Asir (p. 116).

neighbours.name: Church of Maryam Tsion
neighbours.summary: Built in the fifth century within a thick, lush forest, this church is said to hold the Ark of the Covenant in its sanctuary, brought here from Tana Qirqos. Pilgrims come on Axum Tsion, Hadar 20 or November 18, and many go on to Roha.
neighbours.secrets:
The Divine aura here depends on whether Axum truly holds the Ark (p. 116).

The Ark has Faith Score 10, 10 Faith Points and Divine Might 100 for any Ethiopian, Falasha or Christian; for other Christians and all Muslims its Faith Score is 7 (RoP:D p. 44; p. 112).

Prester John does not rule Ethiopia, but anyone leaving this church at sunrise on Easter morning may enter a Faerie regio much like his lost kingdom (p. 120).

neighbours.name: The Kingdom Beyond Maryam Tsion
neighbours.summary: A pleasant, vivid land whose people look like whoever has entered it. They say a wise Christian king rules them, and that the law forbids them to name him.
neighbours.secrets: A Faerie regio entered on leaving the church at sunrise on Easter morning. Whoever sleeps here wakes in the church of his baptism or in Maryam Tsion, which makes exploring it hard (p. 120).

neighbours.name: The Hidden Palace of the Great Stelae
neighbours.summary: The hawilti, begun in the worship of Mahrem and Astar, were carved with doors and windows as houses for dead kings, with vaults below where the living honoured them. Ezana raised the last just before his conversion and never entered it.
neighbours.secrets: Nobles and priests who knew the way once passed the false doors into an afterlife regio. It was submerged under the Divine aura, not destroyed, and its secret died with the priesthood. On the night of the winter solstice the Divine sinks enough for Faerie to show and entry is easier. Inside is a vast palace of gold and ivory scented with myrrh, where ghosts of the old kings lounge, speaking Ge'ez and fluent Latin. They might describe the Roman trade, teach Ge'ez or reveal lost pagan and magical sites (p. 107).

neighbours.name: The Stone Lion and the Quarry
neighbours.summary: A league west of Axum, in dry scrub by the quarries of the great stelae, a rock bears the life-size etching of a lioness in mid-stride. Legend says Gabriel threw her against it so hard that only the mark remained. The quarry's trenches look cut like meat, and three half-worked stelae lie half in the ground. Locals guard both and answer defacement with force.
neighbours.secrets: An animal corpse laid at the lioness's feet on the night before the first day of spring, and kept from scavengers until dawn, yields 5 pawns of Animal vis in some part of it. Chips from the partial stelae gathered at noon on Timket hold 5 pawns of Rego and 5 of Vim (p. 117).

neighbours.name: Amba Geshen
neighbours.summary: A roughly cross-shaped hilltop of wild cedars and a spring pool, once an Axumite fortress and treasury, then a prison for imperial heirs from the third Zagwe emperor on. Lalibela ended that, vowing no more sons of Zagwe would wait here for an emperor's death, and raised the church of Egzyabeher Ab, 'God the Father', on the southern edge. It is a fortified treasury again, its long narrow halls housing guards and stores. A single-file path, the Macaraquer, reaches the gatehouse; cattle and timber are hauled up by rope. Goats and oxen live above, and escaped monkeys and rabbits raid the gardens until they reach the pot.

neighbours.name: Debre Damo
neighbours.summary: Abuna Aragawi of the Nine Saints founded this house of about 100 monks on a mountain plateau once held by a serpent cult. Tradition and the carvings of its cut-stone church say a giant serpent carried him up the cliff in its coils, under the fiery sword of Gabriel, set him on a stone and left; its cult turned Christian. Everyone arriving kisses that stone. The way up is an 80-foot braided leather rope, with a basket for the old and infirm, and it has kept the monks safe for over 700 years. Up top are the church, curiously forestless, with a great store of illuminated manuscripts, nearly two dozen shared houses with gardens, a pen of cattle and rabbits and six stone cisterns. Kedus Harbe retired here, and heirs were once held here.
neighbours.secrets: The whole community has a Dominion aura of 3 (p. 117).

neighbours.name: Lake Hayq
