neighbours.summary: A large, deep lake in southeastern Amhara, of bony catfish and hippopotamuses, with lemons and oranges on the shore and a small Muslim fishing village. Tradition says God raised it to drown a haughty young princess and her train for insulting a pregnant woman; the woman's seat and the village behind her became an island.

neighbours.name: Istifanos Monastery
neighbours.summary: On the western shore; emperors have long kept their letters, documents and land grants here.

neighbours.name: The Island Shrine of Lake Hayq
neighbours.summary: A small shrine on the island where the wronged woman sat.

neighbours.name: The Empty Palace of Lake Hayq
neighbours.summary: A large stone palace across the lake from the monastery, built by a forgotten Axumite emperor. No one lives in it or takes its stones. A melancholy Axumite princess haunts it.

neighbours.name: Yeha
neighbours.summary: A village of about two hundred, with a Falasha blacksmith, a potter and a weaver, in the lush plain of an easily defended vale held sacred even before the Nine Saints. Abba Aftse's monastery here failed.

neighbours.name: The Temple of Yeha
neighbours.summary: A crumbling temple on a high outcrop a third of a mile from any other building. Faded graffiti suggest a later church or monastery, before the roof fell; walls and square pillars bear Sabaean carving. A ruined shrine stands at the foot of a natural stone stair, and three rock-cut tombs sink into the slope to the south.

neighbours.name: Zeila
neighbours.summary: A walled port of polished white coral just beyond the Bab-al-Mandab, a rich meeting of Ethiopia, Yemen and the wider seas. Its governor keeps a strong army and shifts between the sultan of Adal and the ras of Amhara. Merchants press him toward the sultan, for easier passage through the strait and more power of their own. An imam from Harar has lately converted him to Islam. Its mosque was built by the Prophet's companions, exiles of 613.
neighbours.secrets: The mosque has a Divine aura of 5 (p. 117).

neighbours.name: Roha
neighbours.summary:
A modest-looking village of mud-brick and red stone in dry, rocky country, the emperor's birthplace and official capital of the empire. Sunk beneath it, reached by tunnels, are its eleven churches, each cut from one stone between 1188 and 1200: a symbolic Jerusalem, for those Saladin's conquest shut out, with a channel called the River Jordan, a small stone cross at the place of Christ's baptism, and a Mount of Olives above. Angels are said to have helped build it.

North of the Jordan stand Bet Denagel, Bet Golgotha Mikael, Bet Maryam, Bet Maskal and Bet Medhani Alem; south of it Bet Abba Libanos, Bet Amanuel, Bet Gabriel Raphael, Bet Lehem and Bet Qeddus Mercoreus. Bet Giorgys stands alone, joined to the rest by trenches. Bet Golgotha holds copies of Christ's tomb, Adam's tomb and the crib of the nativity.
neighbours.secrets:
The whole complex has a Dominion aura of 7 (p. 117).

A framework for pilgrimage (p. 118): a season walking the tunnels, praying at each church, fasting and defeating the trials of demons in possessed locals or of bouda faeries calling temptation from the rims completes a pilgrimage story (The Church pp. 16-19).

neighbours.name: The Village of Roha
neighbours.summary: Small clusters of houses around the tunnels, in the Lasta country. The Ethiopian capital in name; the emperor's true seat is his travelling camp.

neighbours.name: Agaw
neighbours.summary: The realm of the negus of Agaw: Agaw proper on the west shore of Lake Tana up to the Semiens, Gojjam south of the lake, and Damot in the far south, beyond which the Jamma parts it from pagan tribes. Good rain, clear water and rich soil make it the province that suffers least in famine. Its warriors are famously fierce; an old emperor raised a monument to how hard it was to subdue. The Zagwe dynasty was forged in its hills, and Na'akueto La'ab of Gojjam, next in line to the empire, is its true power.

neighbours.name: Lake Tana
neighbours.summary: Fifty-two miles long and forty wide, bigger than any lake in Mythic Europe and mostly over 40 feet deep, fed by the Gumara, the Lesser Abbay and the Reb. Sixteen of its islands are settled, seven with fishing villages and nine with monasteries of timber or Axumite stone. Dek, the largest, is ten miles across with three villages and two churches. On holy Daga, just southeast of it, the monks bar women and livestock. Solomon's ring, Menelik's, is said to be hidden on one of these isles, the place long lost.
neighbours.secrets: The ring is a relic of Faith Score 7 for Jews, Falasha and Ethiopian Christians, 5 for other Christians. It adds its Faith Score to a Solomonic practitioner's casting total (Cradle & Crescent pp. 33-37) or an Ars Notoria recitation (RoP:D p. 98), and a Gifted student may study it as a Quality 5 tractatus on Ars Notoria. Where it lies is unknown (p. 112).

neighbours.name: Tana Qirqos
neighbours.summary: An island near the Gumara's mouth where tradition says the Ark rested before going to Axum. The ruins of a large temple stand on it.
neighbours.secrets: Anyone with Judaic Lore who studies the ruins for a season finds they follow the proportions of Solomon's temple (p. 119).

neighbours.name: The Blue Nile
neighbours.summary: The River Abbay leaves Lake Tana over a fall and cuts through the Semiens, carrying the silt that feeds Egypt. There are few easy crossings and no stone bridges, and the rains cut off Agaw and Gojjam until the flood falls.

neighbours.name: Tis Abbay
neighbours.summary: The 'Smoking Waters', the fall where the Blue Nile begins. Rich plants grow in its mist.
neighbours.secrets: As the flood first starts, mist caught here at sunrise yields 3 pawns each of Aquam, Creo, Imaginem and Perdo. Unharvested, it feeds the flora; Plants and Beasts of Virtue are common (p. 117).

neighbours.name: Shewa
neighbours.summary: The southern highland kingdom: Shewa proper in the north, Bale in the southeast and Fetegar in the southwest, the last two wetter and more forested thanks to the Wabe Shebile on the border. All three fight pagans to the southwest and sultanates to the south. Its negus rests on a cluster of very old towns on ridges about five leagues long, 3500 to 4000 feet above the Rift.

neighbours.name: Asbari
neighbours.summary: A town on a rocky spur at a high cliff's edge, often raided by pagans. Houses and workshops surround a large walled church on a small hill, which doubles as a redoubt; hundreds of rock-cut tombs cover the north slope. A straight wall two paces high and thick shuts the town off from the plateau, and a half-mile road winds from it to the gate between terraced farms.

neighbours.name: The Terraces of Asbari
neighbours.summary: Three terraces deep along the road to Asbari's gate, growing many sorts of plant.
neighbours.secrets: They grow various Plants of Virtue (p. 120).

neighbours.name: Masal
neighbours.summary: Three neighbouring walled hilltops between Asbari and Nora, each with a church and about five hundred people, known for good pottery and razor-sharp obsidian tools and arrowheads. Near each lies a vast ancient cemetery of nameless tombs, many with Axumite decoration. A great obelisk carved with medallions of Solomon's star bears vague Ge'ez lines hinting at a royal tomb.

neighbours.name: The Caves Under the Masal Obelisk
neighbours.summary: The obelisk marks a way into caverns deep in the earth, some with signs of old habitation.
neighbours.secrets: It marks the tomb of an Axumite Falasha wizard who helped found these towns. Frost on its shaded side on the first day of Passover holds 4 pawns of Rego. In old sampling pits of an abandoned, brittle obsidian seam, chips gathered once a year yield 3 pawns of Terram and 3 of Ignem (p. 121).

neighbours.name: Nora
neighbours.summary: A dense city of walls on a rocky outcrop, about 3,500 strong, the seat of the negus of Shewa, though he is usually away hunting pagans and raiders. Elders and priests built its rising patchwork of homes, gardens and courtyards. The stone wall follows the mountain, the streets climb in stages along walls, and 30-foot round towers guard the way. Inside are ornamental tiles and packed rectangular houses. The main church, an Axumite building behind 15-foot walls, has a lush forest only 10 feet deep and 20 tall. Outside, a mound of raw stone holds hundreds of carved tombs.
neighbours.secrets: The church has a Dominion aura of 3 (p. 120).

neighbours.name: The Sultanate of Dahlak
neighbours.summary: Four large islands and 200 small ones just off Adulis, the Periplus's Alalaois, home to about 2000 people. The sultan lives on Dahlak Kebir in a village of cut stone and coral, and grows rich on water, his channels filling cisterns for passing ships. Nahaleg lives by fishing, Nakura by pearls and tortoise shell; the wealthy make beaded glass and trade hides and spices. Some 3,000 to 4,000 slaves a year pass through its markets. Yemen occupied it in the early eighth century to punish its pirates, and used one island, 'The Isle of Thorns', as a prison. The people turned Muslim, and missionaries start from here. The sultan pays Ethiopia tribute, is independent in name, and loves the elephants of the nearby coast. He wants a herd of his own.
neighbours.secrets: The main mosque is a converted Axumite church; the Divine aura of 3 covers the whole of the islands (p. 121).

neighbours.name: The Sultanate of Hadiya
neighbours.summary: West of Shewa, bounded north by the Abbay: small fertile hills of fruit, grain and good pasture for horses and elephants, with thick jungle in the south, eight days' journey long and nine across. Its people use pieces of iron as money and pay tribute in ivory and exotic skins.

neighbours.name: The Sultanate of Dewaro
neighbours.summary: Between Hadiya and Ifat, below the strong Christian kingdom of Bale. Rather than clear their jungle hills, its men raid south for elephants and slaves. The sultan prefers infantry, mostly veterans.

neighbours.name: The Sultanate of Ifat
neighbours.summary: Ten days' journey long and six across, bounded by the Awash, growing hotter and more forested southward. Dunya-huz, a man of Zeila, rules it with strong cavalry, and raises his son Umar Walashma to dream of a greater Ifat uniting Dewaro and Adal.

neighbours.name: The Sultanate of Adal
neighbours.summary: The largest of them, from the Awash across the Rift into the Danakil and to the Red Sea, dry and growing drier eastward. Clerics from Yemen have made its people the most devout of the sultanates, and its priests preach against the tribute and for war on Ethiopia. It courts Zeila, and an imam of its capital, Harar, converted Zeila's governor. Harar has a slave market, and Sufi sects nearby praise coffee.

neighbours.name: Negusa Negast of Ethiopia
neighbours.summary:
Gabril Mesqa Lalibela, king of kings, negus of Bet Amhara, ras of Lasta and bitwoded of Axum, in full Moa Anbessa Ze Imnegede Yehuda, Atse Lalibela, Negusa Negast, Seyoume Igziabeher. To the sultanates he is also Negus Tsion. He is addressed Girmawi or Janhoy, and his household is the Getochu.

Born at Roha, named for the bees that swarmed at his birth, he survived his half-sister's poison, went to Jerusalem instead of exile and, at Alexandria in 1187, saw in a vision Saladin's conquest and God's command to rule and build a new Jerusalem. Kedus Harbe gave way that year, saying angels had told him to. The emperor never speaks in public. He holds his lords to him by travelling among them with his tent camp and armed retinue, the real seat of power; many nobles think him weak.

neighbours.name: Bahri Negus of Medri Bahri
neighbours.summary: Second man of Ethiopia, rich in mines, trade and soldiers.

neighbours.name: Sheikh of Massawa
neighbours.summary: Sheikh Hanafi, a rich Muslim merchant lord sworn to the bahri negus; see Massawa.

neighbours.name: Governor of Adulis
neighbours.summary: Keeps some three hundred men, about fifty cavalry and three small ships, which clear small threats from the district. The bishop leads him easily.

neighbours.name: Governor of Zeila
neighbours.summary: A convert to Islam, caught between sultan and emperor; see Zeila.

neighbours.name: Negus of Shewa
neighbours.summary: Spends most of his time abroad hunting pagans and raiders.

neighbours.name: Negus of Agaw
neighbours.summary: Rules Agaw, Damot and Gojjam, overshadowed by the ras of Gojjam.

neighbours.name: Ras of Gojjam
neighbours.summary: Na'akueto La'ab, the emperor's scheming cousin, freed from Debra Damo as a mercy. To show his loyalty he built two fine churches in Lasta, Wagra Sehin, 'among celestials', and Ashetan Maryem, 'among terrestrials'. Many nobles suspect him of waiting for his moment.

neighbours.name: Sultan of Dahlak
neighbours.summary: A Muslim ruler who pays the negus a grudging tribute.

neighbours.name: Sultan of Adal
neighbours.summary: A Muslim ruler who pays the negus a grudging tribute.

neighbours.name: Sultan of Dewaro
neighbours.summary: A Muslim ruler who pays the negus a grudging tribute.

neighbours.name: Sultan of Hadiya
neighbours.summary: A Muslim ruler who pays the negus a grudging tribute.

neighbours.name: Sultan of Ifat
neighbours.summary: A Muslim ruler who pays the negus a grudging tribute.

neighbours.name: The Ethiopian Church
neighbours.summary:
Two brothers of Tyre, Edesius and Frumentius, enslaved at the Axumite court, taught Prince Ezana; Frumentius, consecrated by Athanasius, baptized him and became first abuna, Abba Salama, 'Father of Peace', and Kesate Birhan, 'Revealer of Light', and died in 386 (feast August 1). After Chalcedon came the Nine Saints (Abbas Aftse, Alef, Aragawi, Garima, Guba, Liqanos, Pantelewon, Sehma and Yem'ata), monophysites who spread the Rule of Pachomius and the monastic life.

It is monophysite, like Nubia and the Copts, with Christ's human nature 'dissolved like a drop of honey in the sea'. Believers pray to God and to the Kidusan, angels and saints who carry prayers up and do God's will. What is holy is not the building but the tabot, a consecrated copy of the Ark, usually of Moses' tablets and not a relic, dedicated to a saint, kept where only priests go and paraded on holy days. Its liturgy is in Ge'ez.

Only three kinds of church are allowed: cave or hypogeum churches, mostly of the bad years between Axum and the Zagwe; rectangular cut stone; and the newer round timber. Stone and timber churches must keep a thick forest around them, which carries prayers to Heaven. The abuna, always an Egyptian named by the Coptic patriarch for life, often arrives knowing neither Amharic nor Ge'ez and feeling exiled. He names bishops, who name priests and some debterah. The emperor pays the sultan of Cairo before a new abuna can be anointed.

The year starts on August 30 with twelve 30-day months in Ge'ez (Meskerem, Taqamt, Hadar, Tahsas, Tarr, Yekatit, Megabit, Miyazya, Ganbot, Sane, Hamle, Nehase) and Pagume, five or six added days. By the Julian calendar they start August 30, September 29, October 29, November 28, December 28, January 27, February 26, March 29, April 28, May 28, June 27, July 27 and August 26, Miyazya and those after it a day earlier in a leap year such as 1220 (p. 108). The four-year cycle is named for John, Mark, Matthew and Luke, Luke's being the leap year, and the count of years runs eight behind Europe until the new year, then seven: January 1, 1220 is Tarr 5, 1212. Feasts are Enkutatash (August 30, Sheba's return), Maskal (17 Meskerem or September 15, the True Cross, with a daisy-decked bonfire), Kulubi Gabriel (Tahsas 18 or December 16), Gena (Tahsas 28 or December 25), Timket (Tarr 10 or January 6, three days with the tsellats paraded on Ketera), Faseka (in 1220, Miyazya 2 or March 27) and Axum Tsion (Hadar 20 or November 18).

details.rules:
In a town with a church forest the Divine aura gathers in the forest, leaving the land outside one lower, even around a church in mid-town; a particularly lush forest usually raises the aura one above the standard (RoP:D p. 10). The tabot focuses the aura and keeps it when carried out of the forest, for as long as it was in the aura (p. 111).

Soot from the Maskal fire, marked on the forehead, grants a temporary Faith Point lasting until it is washed off or spent (p. 110). Spells with Year durations follow the solstices and are unaffected by this calendar (p. 108).

neighbours.name: The Debterah
neighbours.summary:
Saint Yared of Axum, taught by his uncle Gidewon, three divine birds and Abuna Aragawi, made the zema chant of the Ethiopian Church. An emperor, rapt, once dropped his spear on Yared's foot and neither noticed until the song ended; offered any reward, Yared asked for solitude and went to the Semiens. His feast is 11 Ganbot, May 8 or 9.

Debterah (singular debtera), lay deacons of Christian and Falasha communities, sing, teach noble children, make protective amulets, cast horoscopes and drive out evil spirits by The Magic Star Book, handed down from teacher to student. Falasha kahens often become debterah before they are confirmed as rabbis.

Yared's five volumes are The Books of Digua and Tsome Digua, The Book of Meraf, The Book of Mewasit and The Book of Zimare.

details.rules:
A holy societas (p. 114). Favored Abilities: Adjuration, Blessing, Craft Amulets, Invocation (RoP:D pp. 34, 37, 48-50, 137). Without that book: Clerk or Educated, Enchanting Music, and Sense Holiness/Unholiness or Wise One; suggested Abilities Artes Liberales (astronomy), Chirurgy, Organization Lore: Ethiopian Church, Medicine, Music, Teaching and Theology, with Divine and Infernal Lore for a Wise One, who can exorcise only through ceremonies and the auras of tabot and forest.

Yared's books together are a summa of Organization Lore: Ethiopian Church, Level 5, Quality 8.

neighbours.name: The Beta Israel
neighbours.summary:
The 'children of Israel', called Falasha, are a distinct Jewish people who marry among themselves, chiefly in the Falasha province of Bet Amhara and in Agaw and Gojjam. Gudit's fierce army came from them, but a century of Zagwe rule has eased that and many serve the emperor loyally. Christian neighbours help with burials, since Falasha may not handle corpses.

The Kebra Negast, 117 chapters in Ge'ez, tells how Solomon seduced Makkeda, queen of Sheba, how their son Menelik came north and proved himself with Solomon's ring, and how the firstborn sons sent home with him stole the Ark, which carried them miraculously to Ethiopia. Menelik became the first negusa negast, and those sons the Falasha. The Ethiopian nobility believe every word, and it helps protect them.

neighbours.name: The Mesafint
neighbours.summary:
The nobility of Ethiopia, in descending order: negus, a high king made only by the emperor; ras, the highest noble rank, used by lesser kings and minor princes; bitwoded, like a duke; dejazmach, 'gatekeeper', a count; fitawrari, 'leader of the vanguard', a baron; gerazmach and kenyazmach, equal older titles for favoured commanders, often given in pairs; balambaras, a local governor; ato, 'sir', woizero for a woman. Noble children are lij, a noble's wife emebet hoy.

A title passes to surviving brothers first, each in turn, then to the eldest ruler's first son. Some nobles try to get round this.

The emperor's court, the makwanet, includes two Afe Negus, the 'Mouth of the King', who speak as him; the Blattengeta, master of the retinue; the Blatta, pages; the Enderase, 'Regent', a title also used by his envoys; two Lique Mekwas, who dress as him and ride into battle beside him as decoys; and the Tsehafi Tezaz, 'Minister of the Pen', keeper of the great seal, of records, laws and treaties. The consort is respectfully Itege.

neighbours.name: Siwa Oasis
neighbours.summary:
A depression some 50 miles long and 5.5 to 18.5 miles wide, 500 feet below the desert plateau, a patchwork of sand, date palms and springs around sterile salt lakes, the largest being al-Zaytun. It was the oracle of Ammon, visited by Alexander, and its priests dwindled away, hastened by Justinian's decree of 532. Its people resisted the Arab conquest and took Islam only late in the twelfth century. By 1200 there remained seven families of about 200, whose forty men could not hold the old temple village and built a fortified one. Though Cairo claims it, no governor has ever come.

Alexandria is eight days east by the Sikkit al-Sultan, Bahriyah twelve southeast, Awdjila 75 leagues west on the Garamantian Road through the Great Sand Sea. Caravans rest here on the way to Cairo and Alexandria, some bound for Mecca.

The people grow dates, olives and wheat, keep goats and camels, and brew intoxicating lagbi from palm hearts. Men shave their heads; women wear silver and tiny braids. Outsiders rarely pass the gates, and most people speak only the Siwan dialect of Tamazight. Seven to ten sheikhs, wealthy elders, rule as a council. The thirty or so zaggalah, 'club-wielders', men of twenty to forty, sleep outside the walls and work the fields until they marry, when a new home rises on top of the walls. The khadim, drawn from them, guard the sheikhs and enforce the law, unmarried until released. Old women keep the stories, and an old firekeeper watches the gate and the fire that lights every hearth.
neighbours.secrets:
Boons: Difficult Access (Minor Site); Edifices (Minor Fortification); Important Building x3, the Aghurmi temple fort and the lesser temples at Abu Sharef and Bilad al-Rum (Minor Fortification); Peasants (Free Residents); Strong Community (Minor Residents); Ungoverned (Minor External Relations). Hooks: Poverty, Multiple Sites (Minor Resources; pp. 128, 131); Road (Minor Site); Tribunal Border (Major External Relations); Unsafe (Minor External Relations). The book counts seven of each, and would give Castle and Ringworks only if the Bedouin matter to the saga. It suggests Castle, minor Natural Disaster (locusts on the dates), or a minor Regio holding a version of the temples (pp. 128-130).

Multiple Sites (Major/Minor Resources Hook, p. 131): facilities at several sites must go without the Aegis, share tokens or take several rituals in a day, at the cost of vis, of unguarded sanctums or of more tokens to steal. Major with five or more sites.

Resources (pp. 131-133): up to four lab sites, a working covenant needing at least two: Siwa Village and any of Aghurmi, Abu Sharef or Bilad al-Rum. Income: 20 Mythic Pounds a year from dates, and 20 from caravan barter and rest fees. Think of it as between Manor and Farm and Grand Castle (Covenants pp. 45-46). Few craftsmen; true specialists must be brought in. Scores in Tamazight count one less unless Siwan is the specialty.

Vis (pp. 133-134): Alexander's Camp, 4 Herbam a year, 20 points: cut the first fronds to sway on the Ides of February, Magic aura 2. Alexander's Stele, 6 Vim, 30 points: a prism, gem or glass set atop it to catch the sunrise on the Ides of February, Magic aura 3. Crypts of Jabal al-Mawta, 5 Corpus, 25 points: a lone skull in the tomb with two cobra-headed pillars, on the winter solstice, ending if the tombs are emptied, Magic aura 2. Spring of the Sun, 6 Aquam or 6 Ignem, 30 points: fill an amphora on the full moon between late October and early November, at noon for Aquam or midnight for Ignem, Magic aura 2.

Story themes (pp. 134-135): exploring deserts, native traditions and lost ruins from a safe distance; scarcity and survival when isolation turns dangerous. The caravans bring the slave and salt trade and the Great Desert's adventures to the door (BS&S).

neighbours.name: Shali
neighbours.summary: The walled village of Siwa, built in 1203 of salt mud that sets like cement, two or three storeys of homes forming its wall, its lanes wide enough for one laden donkey. Near it is the conical Jabal al-Mawta, the Hill of the Dead.

neighbours.name: Aghurmi
neighbours.summary: The abandoned village three miles east of Shali, with the main oracle temple, a cut-stone fort on a very large rock, among a dozen lesser buildings, a brick watchtower, part of a wall, and Alexander's Stele, raised by Ptolemy to make up for denying Siwa the king's body. A staircase in the temple leads down to a deep well. Close by is the Spring of the Sun, coolest at noon and boiling by midnight.

neighbours.name: Abu Sharef
neighbours.summary: A crumbling abandoned village 28 miles east of Shali, across the salt lake, the edge of Siwan land, with a lesser temple of Ammon of dressed stone, walls over a meter thick, with chambers enough for sanctum and laboratory.

neighbours.name: Bilad al-Rum
neighbours.summary: On the western edge 13.5 miles from Shali, by abandoned Khamisah: a rectangular lesser temple of dressed stone with three grand halls, a brick outbuilding, old quarries, and rock-cut tombs in the hill.

neighbours.name: The Zenata of Siwa
neighbours.summary: Berbers, who call themselves Imazighen, 'Free People', and speak Tarifit Tamazight: fifty-five warriors with two or three camels each, camped by the springs of al-Zaytun. They raid caravans and pilgrims and sell loot and slaves at market.

details.wants: Goods, wives, excitement and regular spoils.
details.offers: A hardened host who know the desert, after a show of force.

neighbours.name: Ikhmindi
neighbours.summary:
A walled refuge above the Nile in Nobatia, seven leagues south of the first Cataract and Philae, where the routes of the Great Desert, a splinter of the Darb al-Arba'in and the Red Sea road meet. Greek missionaries built it in the mid-sixth century, to shelter farmers and spread the faith. It stood mostly empty as a caravan halt until escaped slaves moved in ten years ago, joined by local families. Its people, from all over Africa, the Slavelands and even Europe, stay because no one governs them.

It measures about 360 feet by 300, on a hill between two ravines, with ten-foot walls, two towers a side and one at each corner. The main gate faces southwest to the caravan trail; the Fishermen's Gate leads northeast down to huts by the river, flooded each year. About a hundred two-storey family houses pack the five-foot alleys, half of them occupied, and an open space fifteen feet wide surrounds the central cut-stone church with its catacombs. The southern church is built into the wall. Livestock sleep in stables by the gate. The central well runs cool and fresh and seems to invigorate all who drink.

Women, children and the old work inside, boys help the fishermen, and the men farm thin fields along the streams, together for safety. Nothing is wasted, even dried dung. The men are bowmen, like all the 'Archers of the Eye'.
neighbours.secrets:
Hooks: Castle (Major Fortification); Fragile Vis Sources (Major Resources; two sites, the mine unrepairable); Poverty (Minor Resources); Ringworks (Free Fortification Choice); Road (Minor Site); Unsafe (Minor External Relations). Boons: Edifices (Minor Fortification); Difficult Access (Minor Site); Healthy Feature (Minor Site; the well, +1 to Aging Rolls for those who drink from it most of the year); Missile Weapons (Minor Residents); Important Building x2, the two churches (Minor Fortifications); Peasants (Free Residents). The book counts six Boons and eight Hooks (pp. 136-137).

Suggested: minor Contested Resources; minor Hermit, a Sufi or Gnostic mystic opposed to the use of the churches; major Beholden to regional inspectors; minor Rival, a Bedouin tribe. Boons: minor Hidden Resources, from a lost Nubian tomb or the ruins of walled Sabagura 5 leagues north; major Autocephelous, which spares the inspectors but may mean worse raiders (p. 137).

Fragile Vis Sources (Major/Minor Resources Hook, p. 134): a source of four or more pawns stops if a feature of the site is damaged, resuming if repaired. Major for three or more fragile sites; one that cannot be repaired counts as two. It may be unknown to the covenant.

Resources (pp. 137-139): up to three labs with living space in the two churches and the catacombs, or six without. Income only from fees and barter with spring and late autumn caravans, or Tapara's ventures. Few specialists and no teachers; a hermit might teach, and training can be had at Faras or Qasr Ibrim. A basketweaver, fishermen, herdsmen, potters and a smith would serve.

Vis (pp. 139-140): Abandoned Copper Mine, 4 Rego and 3 Terram a year, 35 points in all, Magic aura 3: gathers in copper nuggets or tools left against the seam, 25 leagues east on the Wadi Allaqi route, and stops for good if Hathor's statue at the door is taken. Black Sandbar of the Nile, 4 Creo twice a year, 40 points, no aura: rich black silt filling two amphorae as the flood rises in June and falls in October, two leagues north of the fishing camp. Temple Kiosk of Qertassi, 7 Imaginem a year, 35 points, Magic aura 3: haboobs leave it in the sand at the Hathor columns, 25 leagues northeast; it stops if the capitals are harmed and returns when they are mended.

Story themes (p. 140): survival in a harsh land, exploration for treasure-filled tombs, lost magics, Bedouin adversity, and a great legacy.

neighbours.name: The Village South of Adulis
neighbours.summary:
A fishing village on the open shore south of Adulis, rebuilt after the dragon Ceto destroyed it in antiquity. Its people are sailors and fishermen, handy with simple weapons, and go to church in town. Cool harbor breezes keep off sickness, and the country is dry but pleasant, with room for a few goats and camels and sloops at the docks.

An old stone lighthouse stands at the village's edge, overlooking the small deep harbor. The villagers have kept quiet about a hidden copse of myrrh on a nearby island's slopes and pearl beds in the cove of another.
neighbours.secrets:
Hooks: Dwindling Resources (Minor Resources; pearl beds poached by fishermen of Adulis or Dahlek, or a jinn who finds them delicious); Linked Vis Sources (Minor Resources); Poorly Defensible (Minor Site); Regio (Minor Site); Road (Minor Site); Tribunal Border (Major External Relations); Urban (Minor Site). Boons: Healthy Feature (Minor Site; harbor breezes, +1 to Aging Rolls for residents most of the year); Important Building (Minor Fortification; the lighthouse); Secondary Income (Minor Resources; myrrh); Unwitting Defenders (Minor External Relations); Sailors (Free Resident). The book counts four Boons and nine Hooks (pp. 141-142). It suggests minor Uncontrolled Portal, or major Monster, Ceto bursting up through the docks in storms (p. 142).

Linked Vis Site (Major/Minor Resources Hook, pp. 142-143): two or more sources of four pawns or more depend on one condition. If it fails their rates halve in the first year, quarter in the second and then stop; a story restarts them, over three years. The book's example is bees of 6 Animal and wildflowers of 4 Herbam in Iberia. Major links four sites; permanent damage counts as two.

Unwitting Defenders (Major/Minor Resources Boon, p. 143; listed as External Relations on p. 142): a force unaware of the covenant keeps bandits and pirates off. Revealing the covenant turns it into Local or Powerful Ally, or Rival or Unsafe. Major means a force that can stand a siege, paid for in taxes.

Resources (pp. 143-144): the lighthouse can hold four labs and sanctums, but then cannot serve as a lighthouse; magical light costs -5 to lab work unless the magus is Blind, until a story or project cures it. Two Typical Quality sources give 100 Mythic Pounds each: myrrh grove and pearl fishery, on unclaimed islands. Any force over twenty grogs draws notice. An ex-ship captain might be autocrat; potters make hard white brick with crushed coral.

Vis (p. 144): Fire Coral Beds, 6 Vim a year, 30 points; Magical School of Fish, 6 Animal a year, 30 points; both yield 1 pawn every two months or 6 each year, and a second early harvest in a year cuts both to 3 until left alone for a year. Storm Flotsam, 3 Perdo twice a year with the first spring and first autumn storm, 30 points, in the wreckage under the docks.

Relations (p. 144): the sultan of Dahlek would blackmail the magi into helping seize Adulis, but might sell safe passage of the Bab-el-Mandeb for an elephant and regular fodder. The bishop may urge the governor to attack; with the bishop discredited or replaced, the governor may accept them for aid in need and regular gifts, which other magi might frown on.

Story themes (p. 144): discovery and exploration from a base open to Egypt, Ethiopia, the Levant Tribunal and Arabia, and more distantly the Great Desert, Nubia and Soqotra, by way of Yemeni merchants. Christian magi may struggle to get books; Muslim magi are nearer the Levant and Arabia.

neighbours.name: Ceto's Well
neighbours.summary: The deep harbor where the great sea monster dived and destroyed the old village. A ridge of ruby-red fire coral grows on its northeast rim, among fish twice the common size, and fishermen of Adulis eye both in hard times.

details.tethers: Opens on the anniversary of the dragon's attack and in great storms.

levels.notes: The book prints no aura here.

levels.name: Level 2
levels.notes: The book prints no aura here.

levels.name: Level 3
levels.notes: The book prints no aura here. It leads to a part of the Magic Realm much like the Ionian Sea.

neighbours.secrets: A three-level regio opening to the Magic Realm, likely tied to the myth of Perseus and Andromeda, and outside a likely Aegis (pp. 141-142).

neighbours.name: The Great Sea Serpent
neighbours.summary: Ceto breaks ships that skip the sailors' sacrifices, near shore and among merchants, so that survivors spread its legend. Magi who bloody its nose become the rival it has wanted.

details.antagonist: The Dragon Ceto, playing the great rival

stages.title: It takes offence
stages.clues: The magi save a ship or drive it off.
stages.ignored: It hunts their allied ships and spares their own, earning them an unlucky name in every port.

stages.title: The rival revealed
stages.clues: It hides its flight until the moment is best.
stages.ignored: It may even defend the covenant's waters: only it may choose when the magi are destroyed.

stages.title: The last battle
stages.clues: They begin to treat it as a mere hazard.
stages.ignored: It forces a fight in which it 'dies' or destroys them.

neighbours.name: The Trees Listen
neighbours.summary: If the Divine aura lives in the church forests, can it be moved with the trees? What of their wood, carved into items, or used to imprison demons or stunt a magus? Might such trees exist for other Realms?

neighbours.name: The Birthright of Solomon
neighbours.summary: Menelik gave the Ark into the care of the Kahens, priests of the firstborn, and they kept his ring, one of Solomon's, with a seal. Its hiding place was lost among Tana's islands and monasteries. Finding it could fill the years of any magus curious about Theurgy or Ars Notoria.
neighbours.secrets: If it lies with an unburied Kahen, the ghost could speak of the Ark's powers against unbelievers and of old sites in Ethiopia, to one who has Ge'ez or Hebrew at 4 (p. 112).

neighbours.name: The Devil's in the Trees
neighbours.summary: A lesser false god demon raises or transplants myrrh stands near the covenant and shows them to villagers, merchants, nobles and covenfolk alike, feeding greed and murder, then works its way among the grogs toward the magi. Bloodshed brings inquiries, tangles with local rulers and perhaps a Quaesitor, above all if a Levant covenant is in the myrrh trade.

neighbours.name: Discarded Directive
neighbours.summary: When 'Amr ibn al-'As came for Ruqayyah's party, Jafar's Qur'an moved Armah to tears and the emperor refused to give them up. At his death the Prophet told his people to leave the Abyssinians in peace unless they attacked, and the sultanates have kept to that. A cabal of demons could wear away the sultans' respect for those words while goading the Ethiopian lords to aggression.

neighbours.name: On a Wing
neighbours.summary: A covenant might grow rich on bridges or short-flight items, drawing rivals who seize a bridge for tolls or ambush its agent for the device, while word of the magi's methods spreads.

neighbours.name: Serpents of Unknown Provenance
neighbours.summary: An ambitious magus seeks an elephant-eating serpent as a familiar, seeing magic in the Order's snakes. They may be fallen sacred snakes of the pharaohs, spawn of Jormungandr, or children of Eden's serpent. Missing cattle or grogs might start it, for they eat more than elephants.

neighbours.name: The Lost Temple
neighbours.summary: The ruin on Tana Qirqos can show where the Holy of Holies lay at Jerusalem.
neighbours.secrets: That may lead to a Divine regio made by Solomon and peopled by nephilim, or this temple may be another door to it, joining Ethiopia and the Levant. The nephilim knew the Ark, may have studied Ars Notoria or Kabbalah with Solomon, and might help recover the Ark or fight demons. Students of Hermetic Architecture may want the ruins too (p. 119).

neighbours.name: Beyond the Sultanates
neighbours.summary: South past the sultanates, through heat, poison and pagans, hyenas, lions and elephant-eating serpents, stand the Mountains of the Moon. Beyond may be the rim of Creation described by Diogenes, Eden, or a way to Arcadia or Paradise.

neighbours.name: The Nascent Saint
neighbours.summary: Pagan raiders from beyond the Jamma carry off the mother of young Takle Haymanot to wed one of their lords. Her return will prove the archangel's care.
neighbours.secrets: A young man attends the sleeping boy, calls magi by their birth names, ignores the Aegis and vanishes: Michael. A devout magus, or one with a Divine Ghostly Warder or Guardian Angel, may act as his instrument (p. 121).

neighbours.name: A Temple in Africa
neighbours.summary: A few Knights Templar in Cairo came home with Lalibela in 1187, hoping for a second base against the Levant. They fought for him against Kedus Harbe, and are now his secret allies, gathering knights in his cavalry and influence at his court.
neighbours.secrets: Finding a covenant, they may seek alliance, destroy it, or steer it. The storyguide sets whether the Order is Divine, Infernal or mundane (p. 118).

neighbours.name: The Angel's Share
neighbours.summary: The Ark would make the Templars independent of the pope, perhaps a nation. Letters come with the patriarch's couriers, and in 1219 one told of the Fifth Crusade at Damietta. The knights are near sixty, their sergeants near fifty. It is now or never.

stages.title: The knights move
stages.clues: They trick or enlist the magi, or arrange a double-cross.
stages.ignored: They take the Ark from Maryam Tsion.
stages.stopped: The magi might swap in a replica, an elaborate heist with no blood spilled.

stages.title: The race north
stages.clues: A long overland chase to the crusaders at Damietta.

stages.title: The march on Cairo
stages.clues: The crusaders advance in July.
stages.ignored: With the Ark the attack may not fail.

neighbours.name: How Many Angels Dance
neighbours.summary: Angels may still keep Roha's niches and gates, and appear to those at prayer or walk in human form, asking favours of the faithful, from feeding a senile anchorite to recovering captives from pagans. They do not always know the greater purpose.
neighbours.secrets: If the Templars go for the Ark, the angels may guide the magi to help or stop them: God let it leave Jerusalem once, and may want it moved, or kept (p. 118).

neighbours.name: For the Love of...
neighbours.summary: One of Roha's angels has fallen in love with a mortal worshipper. Fearing the sin of the nephilim, the others will not act themselves, but press the characters to take the mortal far away, even on a dangerous mission to Egypt or across the Great Desert.
neighbours.secrets: Desperate, an angel may urge a grog to kill the mortal. It may all be a test of the characters (p. 118).

neighbours.name: The Zagwe Succession
neighbours.summary: Who follows Lalibela, his cousin Na'akueto La'ab or his son Yetbarak?

stages.title: Lalibela abdicates
stages.clues: If history holds, he yields to Na'akueto La'ab to retire as a monk at Roha.
stages.ignored: War comes between Na'akueto La'ab and Yetbarak.

stages.title: Yetbarak's victory
stages.clues: Lalibela returns to help his son win.

stages.title: The Solomonic overthrow
stages.clues: The Solomonic dynasty overthrows Yetbarak.

neighbours.name: The Vacant Throne of Alexandria
neighbours.summary: The patriarchate stands empty, Cyril ibn Laqlaq and his foes at deadlock, with Abuna Yeshaq the Church's only head in Ethiopia.

stages.title: Abuna Yeshaq dies
stages.clues: If history holds.

stages.title: A patriarch and an abuna
stages.clues: If history holds, ibn Laqlaq becomes Cyril III and Giyorgis II becomes abuna, serving until 1284.

stages.title: Takle Haymanot
stages.clues: If history holds, the saint becomes abuna at 69.

neighbours.name: Sometime Lords of Siwa
neighbours.summary: Bedouin raiders carry off villagers as the magi arrive, and the elders offer a bargain for their kin's return and future protection. These raiders have a patron, a sahir or a bloodthirsty demon, and the captives must be found before it claims them. It need not die, and may trouble the covenant for years.

neighbours.name: Locating Laboratories
neighbours.summary: Old ghosts, desert spirits or bound jinn hold the rooms once used by hierophants and sahirs, and want some service, such as finding a lost idol or restoring a rite, before they accept a new tenant. Left unharmed they may augment a lab, guard it or assist in it.

neighbours.name: A Turb From Without
neighbours.summary: To spare the zaggalah, the magi hire Zenata tribesmen, who must be paid and kept busy. Bored, they raid caravans, and that draws Cairo's eye. Most such stories start with their reckless members in trouble.

neighbours.name: Filling the Coffers
neighbours.summary: The elders know the oasis's tales of strange places, and hence its vis, but the magi must earn them, by Mentem trickery, bartered luxuries from Cairo or proof they respect Siwan ways. Finding the sites alone takes seasons and teaches the land, but wins no friends.

neighbours.name: The Turb From Within
neighbours.summary: The zaggalah know outsiders and want adventure. Stories, a shared retributive raid or the chance to come home rich might win them, with proof of power and of real care for them. Many of them keep open same-sex partnerships alongside marriage, so a death abroad can drive a lover to despair or wild courage.

neighbours.name: The Crusaders Come Calling
neighbours.summary: In a saga where the Fifth Crusade will not sit in Damietta until 1221, it sends a force to Siwa for supplies and a new front against Sultan Al-Kamil. Its size, cunning and Divine protection decide whether this is one rout or a long struggle for the covenant.

neighbours.name: Getting Slaves
neighbours.summary: Buying grogs makes the covenant look rich, bringing raiders, bandits and tax demands. Freeing slaves from Nubian, Berber or Bedouin slavers is riskier: many flee, some serve in thanks, and frequent attacks bring better armed expeditions, perhaps with supernatural aid.

neighbours.name: New Landlords
neighbours.summary: The eparch of Nobatia owes the sultan under the Baqt. Arriving with his tax collectors, the magi might take on the town's debt and deliver it, and be made its governors in return for gold or slaves. A visiting Quaesitor may be less forgiving.
neighbours.secrets: The eparch ranks as a metropolitan and likely has strong Magic Resistance from Commanding Presence (RoP:D p. 42) or a relic, and Divine agents (p. 134).

neighbours.name: The Past of a Slave
neighbours.summary: A lot of slaves hides a general or tribal prince, who may rebel, or lead the magi on an adventure if they take him home. Or it holds cutthroats waiting to signal friends to the gates.

neighbours.name: The Bedouin Storm
neighbours.summary: Two strong Bedouin tribes demand surrender and tribute. They know about the well, and want water, then camp fees, word of weak caravans, wives or slaves. Each competes with the other, so neither will take less than submission.

neighbours.name: Lost Tombs and Treasures
neighbours.summary: A saga of unsealing the pharaohs' caches along the Nile, against tomb guardians, spirits and bound beasts, rival groups and eremites or expeditions of magi, with races out of closing tomb-regiones, fights for shelter from storms, and trips to Mythic Europe to sell the prizes.

neighbours.name: Any Port...
neighbours.summary: After a terrible storm the magi find the village wrecked, with only the lighthouse standing. Perhaps a greedy merchant or zealous missionary wants it finished off. The elders offer service, sailors and the lighthouse in return for help. The lighthouse is rumoured unsound, and the magi must keep up the lie or win legal title from the governor.

neighbours.name: Free at Last
neighbours.summary: European crusaders taken in Egypt are for sale here, and a merchant means to set them to work on the mosques at Massawa. Outbidding him draws the bishop's eye and his hopes of tithes. Stealing them means facing the mosque's Divine aura and devout guards. Those freed may join the covenant.

neighbours.name: Shipwreck of a Different Color
neighbours.summary: A wreck limps to the docks at dawn. It might carry crusaders with vengeful pursuers close behind; faerie sailors eager to act out a rescue, for a price; or a dying envoy seeking contact between the abuna and Mediterranean Christians, with his message intact and his guards stranded.

neighbours.name: Vis from Beyond
neighbours.summary: A local Christian woman died saving the village from Ceto. Her bones lie unspoiled in the fire coral, venerated but unrecognized by the Church.
neighbours.secrets: They hold a Faith point, and no vis can be gathered while they lie there. Whoever moves them has dreams, and her spirit promises the vis sites' secrets once they reach the bishop in Adulis, if the magi can manage that unnoticed (p. 139).

characters.name: Imhotep
characters.summary: Priest of Thoth in the reign of Djoser, inventor of architecture and medicine, whose healers trained in the House of Life. Thought to have needed two thousand years to become an akh (LotN pp. 37, 39).

characters.name: Marcus Antonius
characters.summary: Roman lover of Cleopatra, and the only Roman known to have had Egyptian burial rites. As governor of Italy for Julius Caesar he knew the Order of Mercury, and may offer insight into its magic (LotN pp. 39-40).

characters.name: Caesarion
characters.summary: Son of Cleopatra and Antonius, says the book, and perhaps the forefather of a secret society built on Egyptian rites (LotN p. 40).

characters.name: Cleopatra
characters.summary: Last queen of Egypt, Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator. Mythic Egyptians dismiss the Roman tales as her foes' lies: to them she was a just and wise ruler, a peer in the salons of her wisest subjects, and the author of a book of alchemy gathering her forebears' wisdom and her own medicine. She believed herself a reincarnation of Isis, and allied with Marcus Antonius against Octavian. She died by a sacred asp, some say a suicide in captivity, and her body was stolen for burial (LotN pp. 39, 44).
characters.secrets: The youngest possible akh, she may not have finished the change. Her ka may seek Hermetic aid to clear her ba's path, which disposes her well to magi; if so she is a remarkable communicator, and could be a peerless teacher of Egyptian mysteries. Cleopatra's Book is said to be the height of alchemy, and no Egyptian library admits to a copy.

characters.name: Nahrou
characters.summary: A jinniyya.
characters.secrets: One of the few who know where Cleopatra's tomb lies; her Magic Might protected her from its concealing enchantment (LotN p. 44).
